# Robust VGC Agent for Local Pokémon Showdown

Use this checklist to track implementation. Add dated notes under each phase as
work progresses. Training may use a faster headless/local simulation path, but
Pokémon Showdown remains the correctness reference and required battle platform.

**Active policy-improvement plan (updated 2026-10-31):** this section is the
current source of truth and supersedes older recommendation sections below;
dated entries remain the experiment ledger. Direct-policy self-play PPO with
auxiliary win-probability and hidden-set prediction is active. Round430 remains
the validated in-battle incumbent: its 55.32% head-to-head score against
Round424 (95% cluster interval [51.86%, 58.79%]) is not proof of strength
against external policies. Mixed-opponent PPO rounds 468–476 did not establish
a robust gain over Round430. Round477's first-five Max Damage intervention
helped four tested opponent classes and significantly hurt legacy Counterplay,
so it was not made a default rule. Rounds478–479 tested robust
counterfactual action distillation against Max Damage, Public Counterplay, and
Round476; the larger sample still produced almost no action changes and worse
validation loss. Round430 remains the default; change the counterfactual
objective or use stronger state-value / equilibrium targets before allocating
another large PPO run. Search remains optional and gated on held-out strength.
At inference, legal actions are selected from masked PPO policy logits; the
win-probability head is an auxiliary training target and does not rank moves.
The optional one-turn search can consult a state-value evaluator only when
explicitly enabled; the default play path leaves search disabled.
**Opponent-family coverage gate (added 2026-10-31):** Max Damage remains a
useful mechanics baseline, not the definition of strength. Do not promote a
change based on Max Damage alone, or on the same small response set used to
train it. Report side-swapped, team-clustered results against random, Max
Damage, public Counterplay, legacy Counterplay, and multiple frozen PPO
generations; when possible hold out an entire policy family/checkpoint from
training and action-value fitting. Report equal-weight league mean, median,
lower tail, and worst response. Any candidate with a credible regression on
one family requires investigation before promotion, even if its aggregate
improves. Counterfactual action values must be tested on an opponent set wider
than their training heads. Including several heuristic classes is not enough:
the learned-policy response must include multiple historical PPO checkpoints,
and evaluation must include at least one policy generation absent from fitting.
**Round485 controlled opponent-exposure ablation (2026-10-31; not promoted):**
matched Round473's Round430 start, PPO settings, Round402 selectors, and frozen
policy pool while changing only opponent proportions to 70% Max Damage, 10%
legacy Counterplay, 10% Public Counterplay, and 10% policy pool. Round485 scored
39.45% against Max Damage, −0.68 pp vs Round473 (95% CI [−3.12,+1.76]); its
equal-weight five-opponent change was −0.49 pp [−1.39,+0.39]. No per-opponent
paired interval excludes zero. The higher Max Damage share did not measurably
improve that matchup or the broader league; retain Round430 as default. The
10% policy-pool share was split evenly across five checkpoint opponents, so
each individual checkpoint supplied 2% of all games (400/20,000); the JSON
mixture weights are conditional within the policy slice, not shares of all
rollouts. Thus Round485 did not over-weight any single pool checkpoint. Full
results and speed appear below and in `site/round485_opponent_exposure.json`.
**Round484 split-sample candidate coverage audit (2026-10-31; offline
diagnostic):** added a reproducible held-out-repeat audit at
`scripts/analyze_round484_split_sample_action_selection.py`, with results in
`training/outputs/phase12_headless/round484_split_sample_action_selection_20261031/report.json`
and published as `site/round484_split_sample_action_selection.json`.
It selects among the existing legal candidate actions using four sampled
outcomes per response class and scores on the disjoint four repeats, across
128 whole team clusters. The candidate set averaged 6.09 distinct joint
actions/state (range 2–13); a switch was present in 74 states, Protect in 63,
setup in 20, and redirection in one. Equal-weight response selection changed
the baseline action in 67/128 states and gained +10.42 pp on held-out
Max Damage/Public Counterplay/Round476 outcomes (95% cluster CI [+7.36,+13.67]);
maximin selection changed 41/128 and gained +6.97 pp [+4.10,+10.03]. The
independent even/odd repeat split replicated the signs and magnitudes. This is
a one-step action ceiling with the incumbent continuation policy, not a full
policy result or Nash proof. It indicates the existing policy frequently
misses actions with repeatable local value; the failed Round482 actor projection
still shows that transferring these labels to a deployable policy is the hard
part. Next, build action-value supervision with cluster-disjoint train/validation
states and compare predicted rankings against these held-out counterfactuals
before any large PPO run. Expand candidate and response coverage before claiming
robustness beyond the three sampled response classes. **Information-boundary
qualification:** this action-selection screen branches from the real battle
snapshot, which contains the actual hidden opposing sets. The measured direct
selector is therefore an information-oracle upper bound, not an action rule
available to a closed-sheet player. Only the fitted model is restricted to
player-view features, and that model failed to transfer the gain.
**Round486 action-value transfer recheck (2026-10-31; no promotion):** trained
five independent response-conditioned value models on Round484's 128 states,
holding out whole team clusters and disjoint chance repeats. The 130 held-out
selector records covered 85 unique team clusters. Although the model changed
80 actions, the out-of-fold worst-response delta averaged only +0.64 pp
(95% cluster CI [-3.04,+4.85]); per-response deltas were +1.08 pp vs Max Damage,
+1.96 vs Round476, and +0.34 vs Public Counterplay, all with intervals including
zero. The repeatable +7–10 pp sample-oracle gain therefore does not transfer
through the current shallow value model. Reports:
`training/outputs/phase12_headless/round486_transfer_repeated_splits_20261031/report.json`.
**Round487 state-coverage and sample-budget study (2026-10-31; diagnostic):**
collected 256 fresh first-decision states, eight chance outcomes per candidate,
and the same three response classes. Eight workers completed 37,712 branches
in 736.63 s (51.20 aggregate matches/s), with zero missing states or rejected
actions. A five-split response-conditioned value model again failed to transfer:
across 177 unique held-out clusters, its worst-response delta was -0.25 pp
(95% CI [-3.33,+2.86]); Max Damage was +0.61 pp [-2.64,+3.81]. In contrast,
selecting actions directly from sampled counterfactual outcomes generalized
within each state. With one sample per action/response, equal-weight selection
gained +5.02 pp (95% cluster CI [+2.98,+7.09]) and maximin gained +3.72 pp
[+2.08,+5.49] on held-out repeats. At two samples, equal-weight gain was
+7.51 pp [+5.43,+9.68]; at four samples, +8.98 pp [+6.77,+11.33]. Maximin's
worst-response gain ranged from +5.36 pp with one sample to +8.98 pp with four.
First-vs-last repeat splits agreed. These are one-step candidate-set ceilings
with frozen-policy continuation, not full-match agent gains; the response set
is only three policies. **Information-boundary qualification:** the rollout
samples use the true hidden team from the captured battle snapshot, so these
gains are oracle-only and cannot be used by the live agent. Any follow-up search
must build branches from sampled public-compatible hidden worlds, such as the
existing `prepare_search_worlds` path, and verify that neither features nor
actions reveal the true team. Only then should it test one or two samples first,
adaptive sampling for close decisions, decision latency, and full-match results.
Do not replace the default until those gates pass. Reports:
`training/outputs/phase12_headless/round487_action_value_transfer_256x8_20261031/`.
**Round488 multi-phase action-value transfer (2026-10-31; not promoted):**
collected 128 opening states at decision 1, 128 at decision 3, and 118/128
reachable states at decision 5 (10 matches ended before that decision), with
eight chance repeats and paired Max Damage / Public Counterplay / Round476
response outcomes. The three phases produced 56,198 branch matches in 950.94
seconds (59.10 aggregate matches/s), with zero rejected candidates. Five
team-disjoint model fits covered 256 unique held-out team clusters. Action
outcome Brier scores improved over a constant-rate baseline, but the
worst-response action selector changed 54/75 held-out actions in the first
split and its five-split out-of-fold result was -1.56 pp (95% cluster CI
[-4.10,+0.80]); response deltas were -1.73 pp vs Max Damage, +0.49 pp vs
Round476, and -2.85 pp vs Public Counterplay (the last interval was
[-5.50,-0.26]). This is negative selector-transfer evidence, not a full-match
evaluation. Do not promote this model. It also reinforces the coverage concern:
three response heads are too narrow to support a broad robust-play claim. Next,
add varied held-out policy generations/families and random/legacy Counterplay
to the evaluation matrix, then train/evaluate on a family-disjoint split before
another value-selector iteration. Reports:
`training/outputs/phase12_headless/round488_multiphase_action_value_128x8_20261031/`.
**Round489 expanded response coverage (2026-10-31; no selector promoted):**
extended the Round488 collection to five responses: Max Damage, Random, legacy
Counterplay, Public Counterplay, and one frozen PPO (Round476). Across decision
indices 1, 3, and 5, 372 states were captured; 12 of 384 requested states ended
before their target decision. Eight chance repeats yielded 93,076 branch games
in 1,484.95 seconds (62.68 aggregate games/s); there were zero rejected
actions. Five team-disjoint model fits covered 250 unique held-out team
clusters. Action-outcome Brier beat a constant-rate baseline for every response
class, but this did not translate into better action selection. Maximin's
out-of-fold worst-response delta was -1.13 pp (95% cluster CI [-3.52,+1.29]);
equal-weight selection was -0.93 pp [-3.35,+1.53]. Both changed about 65% of
held-out choices. Against the only learned-policy response, Round476, maximin
regressed -3.40 pp [-6.35,-0.60], while equal-weight was -2.70 pp
[-5.65,+0.07]. These are one-step candidate-set results, not full-match
performance or a Nash equilibrium. More heuristic types alone did not fix
value-to-action transfer; the response set still contains only one learned
policy checkpoint. Keep Round430 as the in-battle default. The next value-model
comparison should include multiple PPO generations and a checkpoint family
held out from fitting, and should compare predicted-action ranking against a
regret-matched action distribution before PPO distillation. Reports:
`training/outputs/phase12_headless/round489_wide_response_action_value_128x8_20261031/`.
**Round492 pairwise action-value pilot (2026-10-31; not promoted; fresh
confirmation inconclusive):** Round491's fresh data showed the response-conditioned
win-probability model ranked worst-response action pairs correctly only 56.7% of
the time. A split-repeat empirical selector, choosing on four chance repeats and
scoring on the other four, gained +3.54 pp over the incumbent [+2.16,+5.05] on
the same 371 states. This is a hindsight ceiling diagnostic, not deployable
selection, because it directly uses sampled outcomes.

To target ranking, five calibrated response-wise models were trained on Round490
with BCE outcome loss plus a pairwise action-ranking loss; Round102 PPO remained
held out. On the same Round491 branch outcomes, the pairwise selector's
worst-response delta was -0.69 pp [-1.84,+0.37], versus -1.21 pp [-2.37,+0.02]
for a matched BCE-only model. The paired gain over BCE-only was +0.52 pp
[+0.03,+1.01], and the gain over the prior response-value selector was +0.62 pp
[+0.05,+1.21]. Worst-response pairwise ranking accuracy rose from 56.7% to
58.4%. This is encouraging but still does not show an improvement over the
incumbent or a full-match gain, so keep Round430 active.

Round493 evaluated both frozen selectors on fresh seeds: 128 states at
decisions 1 and 3, 115/128 at decision 5 (13 battles ended before the target),
eight chance repeats, seven responses, and 371 states total. It executed 135,211
branch matches at 64.5 aggregate matches/s with zero rejected candidates. The
pairwise selector scored +0.32 pp [-1.21,+1.89] versus the incumbent; BCE-only
scored +0.01 pp [-1.46,+1.60]. Their paired difference was only +0.31 pp
[-0.49,+1.15], so Round491's +0.52 pp pairwise-vs-BCE advantage did not
replicate. Pairwise worst-response ranking accuracy was 58.54% versus 58.40%
for BCE-only. Keep Round430 active; do not promote the pairwise selector.

An empirical selector using four repeats to choose and four to score gained
+5.90 pp [4.08,+7.88] on Round493, which confirms candidate-set headroom but is
still a hindsight diagnostic that cannot be deployed directly. Stop tuning this
selector on these states. The next action-value work should use multiple
public-compatible hidden worlds for each observation and evaluate ranking on
whole hidden-world clusters. It must preserve the closed-team-sheet boundary
and beat BCE-only on another fresh sample before any policy distillation or
full-match test.

Artifacts: `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round491_external_ppo_generation_eval_128x8_20261031/action_ranking_diagnostics.json`,
`training/outputs/phase12_headless/round492_pairwise_response_ranker_20261031/`,
`training/outputs/phase12_headless/round492_bce_ablation_20261031/`, and
`training/outputs/phase12_headless/round493_pairwise_confirmation_128x8_20261031/`.

**Round490/491 PPO-generation holdout and opponent-family weighting audit
(2026-10-31; selector rejected):** Round490 added two PPO generations to the
fitting response set (Round476 and Round430) while holding Round102 out, alongside
Max Damage, Random, legacy Counterplay, and Public Counterplay. Across 375 states
and 134,655 branches (62.20 branch matches/s), five split fits produced a
maximin delta of +2.13 pp [+0.05,+4.30] on the training response mixture, but
the held-out Round102 PPO delta was only +0.81 pp [-1.78,+3.44], inconclusive.
Round491 then scored those frozen fits on fresh seeds and 371 held-out team
clusters across seven response types. The maximin selector regressed by -1.31 pp
[-2.39,-0.28] on the worst response; equal-weight selection regressed -1.23 pp
[-2.31,-0.20]. It lost against legacy Counterplay (-2.13 pp) and both fitted PPO
checkpoints (-1.95 and -1.79 pp); held-out Round102 was -0.79 pp with an interval
including zero. Thus the fresh evidence rejects the selector despite its
positive internal Round490 result.

To test checkpoint over-weighting directly, PPO predictions were averaged into
one family before maximin and equal-weight action choice, then rescored on the
same Round491 branches. This did not change maximin actions in any of the five
fits; family maximin remained -1.31 pp [-2.43,-0.31]. Family equal-weight was
-1.22 pp [-2.34,-0.22], essentially the same as per-checkpoint weighting. The
selector's harm is therefore not explained by counting multiple PPO snapshots
as separate opponent families. PPO represented 2/6 fitted heads, but treating
checkpoints as one family did not recover performance. Keep Round430 as default;
do not tune this selector further on the same data. Next, diagnose
response-conditioned value ranking and candidate/action support. Any new method
must avoid hidden-team oracle leakage and pass fresh-seed, held-out-family
action-level and full-match comparisons before use. Reports:
`training/outputs/phase12_headless/round490_ppo_generation_holdout_128x8_20261031/`
and `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round491_external_ppo_generation_eval_128x8_20261031/`.

**Round482 equilibrium-target check (2026-10-31; reject both actor updates):**
combined the independent Round479 256-team / 8-repeat and Round481 128-team /
16-repeat counterfactual corpora (38,672 and 37,264 branch matches; 30.01 and
34.49 aggregate matches/s). Trainer and audit now split chance outcomes per
state (4/4 or 8/8) while holding out whole team clusters. The regret-matching
target improved its offline mean over the incumbent against each sampled
response class (+9.52 pp Max Damage, +6.19 pp Round476, +9.80 pp Public
Counterplay), but made average statewise worst response worse by 4.29 pp
(95% cluster CI [-6.09, -2.45]). After distillation, the held-out actor's
candidate-restricted mixed distribution was -9.16 pp worst response
([-12.07, -6.41]); argmax was -2.27 pp ([-4.71, -0.16]). The conservative
positive-worst-advantage actor kept the incumbent argmax on 75/77 held-out
states; its candidate-restricted mixture was -3.55 pp worst response
([-5.00, -2.22]). These candidate-set scores are offline diagnostics, not
full-match results. Neither candidate is promoted or sent to full-match
evaluation. The target is sensitive to per-state downside, while both actor
updates fail to transfer their training targets; investigate counterfactual
data coverage / policy projection before repeating the same distillation.
Reports are in `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round482_*`.
**Rounds483–484 actor-action coverage audit (2026-10-31):** the first
Round483 action-label screen is invalid and must not be used for policy
conclusions: its candidate checkpoint was scored with an empty opponent token
roster because the helper handled Pokémon objects but not generated-team
dictionaries. The model is trained with the six revealed opponent species, and
the LAN agent also receives those species. Round484 fixes this and explicitly
labels duplicate candidate actions, then evaluates the Round482 absolute-joint
regret actor on 128 fresh team clusters, eight chance repeats, and the same
Max Damage / Public Counterplay / Round476 response classes. Collection ran at
31.72 matches/s aggregate across four workers (18,976 branch matches), with
zero missing states or rejected actions. The actor's explicit action matched
its independently rescored legal-action argmax on all 128 states; it changed
the Round430 action in 29. On those selected actions, held-out chance repeats
gave -1.37 pp vs Max Damage (95% cluster CI [-3.32, +0.39]), 0.00 pp vs
Round476 ([-2.93, +2.93]), and -0.78 pp vs Public Counterplay ([-3.52,
+1.56]); mean statewise worst response was -4.69 pp ([-7.81, -2.15]). This is
a one-step action intervention with Round430 used for subsequent actions, not
a full-match result. Reject the actor; the action projection now matches its
full legal argmax, so remaining failure points to poor candidate targets or
insufficient opponent-response coverage rather than candidate-set argmax
selection. Report: `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round484_actor_argmax_outcomes_20261031/report.json`.
**Round430 stochastic-action diagnostic (2026-10-30):** added `--stochastic`
to paired evaluation and compared sampled PPO actions with deterministic
argmax on identical teams, previews, and battle seeds (128 team-pair clusters,

Preserve existing workspace changes while implementing and evaluating this
direction.

**Speed status (Round461, 2026-10-30):** the latest complete rollout-plus-PPO
reference remains 16.49 games/s (Round430). Two matched PPO-only updates with
cyclic GC disabled took 151.56 s on average (150.66–152.46 s), vs 227.17 s in
Round458 (33.3% lower wall time); mean sample preparation was 86.35 s
(85.45–87.25 s), vs 162.08 s (46.7% lower). All 28 numeric metrics and all 82
checkpoint tensors matched exactly in both runs; peak RSS was 7.32 GiB. The
CLI now disables cyclic GC during PPO updates by default and restores its prior
state afterward; `--enable-gc-during-ppo-update` opts out. This does not change
the complete-iteration games/s because the replays omit rollouts. Current prep
stages are transition extraction (~27.2 s), model-input construction (~20.4 s),
and load/parse/validation (~19.7 s); PPO optimization takes about 52 s. The
next performance gate is a full rollout-plus-update measurement with
peak-memory tracking.

**Latest measured throughput (Round479, 2026-10-31):** paired
counterfactual collection generated 38,672 complete local-Showdown matches in
1,288.62 seconds (30.01 games/s aggregate over four CPU workers; individual
shards measured 8.12–9.06 games/s). It covered 256 early-game states, six
candidate joint actions per state on average, eight chance repeats, and three
response classes. This is counterfactual branch throughput, not ordinary
self-play throughput. The Round478 full-match league ran at 4.28–6.65 games/s
over eight CPU workers, depending on opponent. The remaining general rollout
bottleneck is policy/action scoring plus observation encoding; the new
counterfactual bottleneck is sparse positive robust-action supervision.

**Current objective (2026-10-30):** move toward optimal, equilibrium-oriented
play in closed-team-sheet VGC. The earlier 80% goal against Max Damage is a
historical experiment milestone, not the project completion criterion. Measure
held-out performance across public counterplay, random, historical PPO, and
Max Damage, including side swaps, cluster intervals, lower-percentile results,
runtime, and action/protocol reliability. Do not optimize for one opponent's
percentage alone.

## Updated implementation direction (2026-10-30)

- **Primary training path:** improve the in-battle policy with terminal-outcome
  self-play PPO against a diverse pool of frozen historical policies and
  public legal baselines. Train the existing win-probability head against
  match outcomes and add auxiliary move, item, and ability prediction for the
  unrevealed opposing set. Keep the training labels in a separate
  `hidden_set_targets` field; observation construction must continue to use
  only species revealed at preview and per-turn public information. This
  auxiliary path has been implemented in `src/training/native_ppo_train.py`
  and the perspective-safe record projector. Syntax compilation passed; a
  full training run and leakage audit are still required before promotion.
- **Search:** keep search out of the first PPO training loop. Revisit it after
  the base policy demonstrates a reproducible gain, then compare at a fixed
  action-latency budget.
- **GPU/JAX decision:** do not translate the whole Showdown battle engine yet.
  The latest available profiling measured roughly 72 ms of policy inference,
  28 ms of observation encoding, and 33 ms of engine round-trip per match,
  plus persistence/setup. Even eliminating the measured engine portion would
  cap the speedup near 1.3x on that workload. Prioritize batched policy
  inference and feature preparation first; run a fresh component profile before
  investing in a JAX simulator. The local Showdown engine remains the
  correctness reference.
- **Reference strength:** Round402 scored 77.15% over 2,048 held-out games
  against Max Damage (95% team-cluster interval [74.90%, 79.35%], paired lift
  +4.30 pp vs damage preview). Keep this as one historical baseline, not as
  the sole definition of success. Current Round424's multi-opponent screen is
  recorded below and it is not promoted.
- **Round420 (2026-10-30):** trained Round402 for 16 epochs at learning rate
  5e-5 on the combined 20,000 Round401/407 current-policy outcomes. It
  completed with final loss -0.07857 and mean reward -0.0116. A fresh paired
  evaluation against Round402 used 256 team-pair clusters, two side-swapped
  outcomes per cluster, seed 20264600. Round402 scored 71.88% (1,024 games;
  95% cluster interval [67.48%,76.17%]); Round420 scored 73.54% (1,024 games;
  [69.43%,77.64%]). The paired lift was +1.66 pp (95% cluster-bootstrap
  interval [-2.25,+5.66]); 57 clusters favored Round420, 52 favored Round402,
  and 147 tied. Both completed with no timeouts or action adjustments. Speed
  was 14.10 and 13.25 games/s, respectively. This screen does not establish
  an improvement; retain Round402 as the incumbent and do not promote Round420.
  Reports are at `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round421_round402_freshscreen_20261030/`
  and `round422_round420_freshscreen_20261030/`.
- **Round423 auxiliary-PPO smoke (2026-10-30):** trained the Round190 in-battle
  policy for one update on 64 headless matches, using 25% each random,
  Max-Damage, counterplay, and current-policy opponents; Round402 selected the
  previews. Preflight accepted 128 safe player-view records, 513 trainable
  decisions, balanced seats, and no errors. The PPO update ran five optimizer
  steps on CUDA; auxiliary losses were win probability 0.690, hidden moves
  6.55, hidden items 5.95, and hidden abilities 5.63. The rollouts kept
  opponent team data species-only while putting complete sets in the separate
  training-target field. This validates data flow, not strength or calibration.
  The smoke output is `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round423_auxiliary_ppo_smoke_20261030/`.
- **Round424 self-play PPO (2026-10-30; completed):** trained 10,000
  matches with 25% random, 25% Max Damage, 25% closed-sheet public Counterplay,
  and 25% historical policy pool. The pool contains Round423, Round190,
  Round102, and Round176. PPO starts from Round423, uses the Round402 preview
  selector, four requested passes at 2.5e-5, 512 minibatches, and CUDA for
  optimization. The rollout preflight and held-out screens completed; it is
  not promoted because its scores did not establish a robust improvement.
- **Fresh Round424 profile:** total iteration 592.4 seconds for 10,000 matches
  (16.89 full-iteration games/s); rollout alone 437.4 seconds (22.86 games/s
  aggregate across 8 workers). End-to-end match time ranged from 136–344 ms by
  opponent class. The Showdown roundtrip was 27–34 ms (8–24%); the remaining
  time is primarily action selection, observation encoding, setup, and writes.
  Public Counterplay action scoring alone took 228 ms/match. GPU use is in PPO
  optimization; rollout policy inference remains CPU-side. See the speed
  breakdown and ranked speed-up plan below.

- **Fresh Round430 component profile:** per-match end-to-end means were 134.4
  ms vs Max Damage, 359.5 ms vs public Counterplay, and 193.5 ms vs the policy
  pool. Engine roundtrip means were 29.1, 27.9, and 33.9 ms, respectively
  (about 22%, 8%, and 18% of end-to-end time). Policy-pool action selection
  used 84.8 ms, including 73.1 ms inference; observation encoding used 27.4
  ms, writes 12.6 ms, and setup about 10.6 ms. Public Counterplay's baseline
  scorer used 239.0 ms per match. This confirms the shared priorities are
  batched policy/observation throughput and more efficient concurrent rollouts;
  counterplay scoring remains a workload-specific bottleneck. Do not add
  nested inference/scorer timings again to action-selection totals.
- **Round430 CPU rollout scaling (2026-10-30):** a fixed 240-game local
  Showdown workload against Max Damage measured 8.90, 24.76, 30.94, 29.09,
  and 26.04 games/s at 1, 4, 8, 12, and 16 worker processes. Peak aggregate
  RSS rose from 0.99 GB at one worker to 6.77 GB at eight, 10.02 GB at
  twelve, and 13.25 GB at sixteen. Eight workers were fastest in this short
  single-opponent sample; more workers consumed more memory and reduced
  throughput. Retain eight for now. The next concurrency gain should come from
  batching inference/features across the existing workers, not increasing
  worker count. Report:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round430_scaling_benchmark_240_20261030/scaling_report.json`.
- **Round430 policy batching benchmark (2026-10-30):** measured 256
  perspective-safe rollout states with one CPU thread, 5 warmup batches, and
  30 timed model-forward repeats. State/model-input preparation averaged
  0.429 ms/state. Native action-feature generation took 46.4 ms on its first
  call because it initializes the Gen 9 dex; the warm mean was 0.156 ms/state.
  For model inference plus device transfer and separately measured collation,
  CPU reached 2,522 states/s at batch 8 and 3,666 at batch 32; CUDA reached
  2,545 at batch 8 and 9,596 at batch 32. CUDA is roughly tied at batch 8,
  about 51% faster at batch 16, and 2.6x faster at batch 32, before queue wait.
  These are isolated model-forward results, not rollout throughput; queueing
  and inference-service overhead are excluded. The eight-worker arrangement
  may not supply large batches without keeping multiple games in flight.
- **Public Counterplay scorer damage cache (2026-10-30):** memoized
  deterministic damage estimates within a single joint-action decision, where
  many legal action pairs repeatedly ask for the same attacker/defender/move
  calculation. A paired 32-game CPU probe used the same Round430 checkpoint,
  format, seed, teams, and one worker before and after the change. Mean scorer
  time fell from 203.4 to 62.6 ms/match (69.2%); mean full episode time fell
  from 327.3 to 184.0 ms, and measured throughput rose from 3.03 to 5.36
  games/s. Both runs produced the same 13-19 win split, with zero timeouts and
  action corrections. Policy inference stayed near 31.6 ms/match, encoding
  near 19.3 ms, and engine calls near 28.7 ms. A follow-up 240-game,
  eight-worker Public Counterplay rollout completed at 23.51 aggregate games/s
  with 6.63 GiB peak RSS. Mean episode time was 247.9 ms, including 80.1 ms
  scorer, 44.2 ms policy inference, 26.8 ms observation encoding, and 36.8 ms
  Showdown roundtrip; there were no timeouts or action corrections. This
  validates concurrent rollout operation, but there is no pre-cache eight-
  worker control and the full 20,000-game mixed PPO iteration has not been
  rerun, so 16.49 full-iteration games/s remains the latest training rate.
  Compact report:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round430_counterplay_cache_benchmark_20261030/report.json`.
- **Measured action-feature micro-optimization (2026-10-30):** profiling 128
  saved states found thousands of scalar NumPy clamp calls in native action
  feature generation. Replaced scalar `np.clip` dispatches with a finite-float
  clamp helper while leaving vector clamps unchanged. On 256 rollout inputs,
  warm median calculation time fell from 0.1983 to 0.1165 ms/state (41.3%);
  all output arrays matched exactly when the new helper and the previous NumPy
  clamp implementation were run on the same inputs. This is a small per-state
  saving, not a demonstrated whole-match throughput gain. A separate comparison
  against stored rollout features found some switch-value differences when
  reconstructing features from the record's team metadata; the implementation
  comparison is exact, but record/team ordering must be audited before treating
  recomputed historical tensors as a correctness oracle. Benchmark code now
  separates one-time dex initialization from warm per-state cost. Reproduce
  with `scripts/benchmark_policy_inference_batching.py`; raw report:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round430_policy_inference_batching_20261030/report.json`.
  Keep CPU batching as the first rollout target and investigate multi-game
  in-flight scheduling across existing workers before a shared GPU service.
- **Action-feature replay parity audit (2026-10-30; resolved):** the original
  Round430 audit reconstructed the visible opponent from the initial team list
  rather than each step's `opponent_species` preview order, causing apparent
  damage/KO mismatches on legal actions. It also used `action_masks`, which
  PPO narrows for the conditional second action, while the feature encoder sees
  the raw mask. The headless rollout now preserves both `raw_action_masks`
  (feature generation) and `action_masks` (PPO behavior replay); perspective
  projection retains both and the per-turn public species order. New records
  include encoder version 1, and preflight reports version counts. A fresh
  64-game Round430-checkpoint rollout produced 128 perspective records and 481
  feature states; recomputation using the saved public order and raw mask
  matched all feature tensors exactly (0 differing values, max absolute
  difference 0). Artifact:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round430_feature_parity_smoke_v2_64_20261030/`.
- **Progress site:** `site/index.html` presents held-out results, the current
  speed snapshot, and training status. `.github/workflows/pages.yml` rebuilds
  its JSON from this plan and deploys through GitHub Pages on pushes to `main`.
  Setup is documented in `docs/TRAINING_PROGRESS_SITE.md`.

## Current execution focus (2026-10-29)

- **Round295 public-only Counterplay teacher (2026-10-29; no confirmed gain):**
  trained Round190 for 20,000 matches with 40% Max Damage, 30% public-only
  Counterplay, and 30% policy-pool opponents. A public-history teacher supplied
  58,021 legal action labels on Max Damage games across both trainable seats;
  rollout audits found no information leaks or choice corrections. PPO excluded
  those teacher-selected actions from its on-policy objective and used teacher
  cross-entropy weight 0.1. The run produced 157,844 transitions and completed
  in 1,160.3 seconds: rollout took 880.7 seconds (22.7 aggregate games/s),
  PPO and preparation took the remainder, with optimizer KL stopping after 774
  steps (2.50 of 5 requested passes). Per-worker throughput was about 2.9
  games/s against Max Damage, 2.9 against public Counterplay, and 5.1–5.8
  against policy opponents. Rollout collection and action selection remain the
  speed bottleneck; PPO optimization is not the dominant cost.
  On 256 matched held-out team clusters with the same Round94 selector and
  two side-swapped outcomes per cluster, Round295 scored 43.85% versus 45.41%
  for Round190. The paired change was -1.56 percentage points (95% cluster
  interval [-4.00, +0.78]); one candidate match timed out and there were zero
  action corrections. This does not show a strength gain. Keep Round190 as the
  training parent and continue with a materially stronger teacher-loss weight
  before judging distillation; still require a larger fresh screen for any
  apparent improvement. Training script:
  `scripts/train_round295_public_cp_teacher.sh`. Candidate, audit, and paired
  evaluation artifacts are under
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/direct_policy_round295_public_cp_teacher_round190_20k_20261029/`.
- **Round296 stronger teacher-weight experiment (2026-10-29; evaluation
  pending):** repeated Round295's 20,000-game mix from Round190 and changed
  only the teacher-loss weight from 0.1 to 0.5. Preflight passed with 40,000
  information-safe player views, 158,039 transitions, and balanced seats.
  Training completed in 1,131.4 seconds (881.9 seconds rollout, 22.7 games/s
  aggregate). Against Max Damage, workers averaged 3.02–3.04 matches/s and
  labeled 57,711 teacher actions for the trainable side; public Counterplay
  workers averaged 2.85–2.86 matches/s with baseline action scoring taking
  0.227–0.228 seconds per match. PPO prepared the tensors in 145.6 seconds,
  then hit its KL stop after only 14 optimizer steps (0.045 requested passes,
  KL 0.0344). Teacher loss was 1.607. The stronger weight therefore moved the
  policy too sharply for the current learning rate and was stopped almost
  immediately; reduce learning rate before another high-weight attempt.
  On 256 matched held-out team clusters, Round296 scored 45.21% versus 46.00%
  for Round190, a paired change of -0.78 percentage points (95% cluster
  interval [-4.30, +2.64]). There were no action corrections; one parent match
  timed out. This is not a demonstrated gain and remains far from 80%. Keep
  Round190 as parent. The strongest measured Max Damage result remains the
  separate 70.36% public Counterplay heuristic. Script:
  `scripts/train_round296_public_cp_teacher_strong.sh`; artifacts:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/direct_policy_round296_public_cp_teacher_strong_round190_20k_20261029/`.
- **Round297 lower-learning-rate teacher transfer (2026-10-29; evaluation
  pending):**
  follow Round296 by keeping its 0.5 public-only teacher loss but reducing
  learning rate to 1e-5, with Round190 as parent and the same 20,000-game
  opponent mix. This tests whether lower steps let PPO learn from the teacher
  without tripping its KL guard after a handful of minibatches. The 20,000-game
  rollout passed preflight with 158,130 trainable transitions, balanced seats,
  and 40,000 information-safe views. It finished in 1,134.8 seconds, including
  880.9 seconds of rollout (22.7 aggregate games/s); teacher labels totaled
  57,791 across the Max Damage games. Public Counterplay worker speed was
  2.57–2.67 matches/s with baseline scoring at 0.24–0.25 seconds per match.
  PPO preparation and aggregation took 146.1 seconds; reducing the learning
  rate tenfold extended the KL-limited update from 14 steps to 118 (0.382 of
  five requested passes), but still stopped at KL 0.0291 with clip fraction
  0.426. The 0.5 teacher loss is still driving policy drift too fast for
  meaningful PPO training even at 1e-5; test an additional order-of-magnitude
  reduction or use a separately controlled supervised phase. Matched fresh
  Max Damage evaluation on 256 clusters scored Round297 at 41.60% and Round190
  at 44.34%; paired change was -2.73 percentage points (95% interval
  [-5.66, +0.10]), with no timeouts or action corrections. Round297 is not an
  improvement. Repeating PPO teacher loss at progressively smaller learning
  rates is not a useful path: low weight barely transferred, and high weight
  still triggers KL or weakens play. The next experiment isolates the same
  public Counterplay action labels in a supervised-only training phase on the
  already collected Max Damage states, without PPO policy/value objectives.
  Script:
  `scripts/train_round297_public_cp_teacher_lower_lr.sh`; output:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/direct_policy_round297_public_cp_teacher_lower_lr_round190_20k_20261029/`.
- **Round298 supervised public-Counterplay distillation (2026-10-29; rejected):**
  instead of repeating PPO teacher-loss runs that
  tripped the KL guard or weakened play, reuse Round297's 57,791 public-only
  teacher actions from 8,000 Max Damage matches. Train Round190 on those
  57,791 labeled trainable transitions with a pure supervised objective:
  no PPO reward/value loss, no entropy bonus, no KL stop; five full passes
  completed in 565 optimizer steps. Teacher cross-entropy fell to 1.126.
  This changes the learning method while reusing already collected data, so
  no new simulation cost is needed.
  On 256 fresh paired Max Damage clusters, the candidate scored 29.00% versus
  45.41% for Round190; paired change was -16.41 points (95% interval
  [-21.29, -11.52]). No actions were corrected. Despite lower teacher loss, the
  student failed to transfer the Counterplay decisions and is rejected. Do not
  repeat this imitation setup. Reproduction:
  `scripts/distill_round298_public_counterplay_teacher.sh`; output:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/direct_policy_round298_public_counterplay_imitation_round190_20261029/`.
- **Round299 Max Damage preview selector (2026-10-29; no gain):** train the atomic
  4-of-6/lead selector from Round297's existing 8,000 Max Damage matches,
  using only trainable-side perspective rows, terminal outcomes, uniform
  behavior correction, and revealed opponent species. This targets a separate
  source of losses before the first move while leaving public Counterplay
  battle decisions unchanged. Evaluate its value directly against random
  preview on paired team clusters using the standalone public Counterplay
  evaluator. The selector scored 68.55% and random preview 69.34%; paired
  change -0.78 percentage points (95% interval [-6.45, +4.88]). Both had zero
  action adjustments or protocol errors. This targeted selector is not an
  improvement and does not establish general robust strength. Script:
  `scripts/train_round299_maxdamage_preview_selector.sh`; output:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round299_public_counterplay_maxdamage_preview_selector_20261029/`.
- **Round300 Counterplay loss trace (2026-10-29; evaluated):** preview selection
  did not improve the 68–70% public Counterplay baseline, so collect fresh
  per-turn traces from 64 paired team clusters / 256 side-swapped games. Score
  was 68.36% (175 wins, 81 losses), cluster bootstrap 95% interval
  [59.77%, 76.56%], at 13.17 games/s, with zero timeouts or action
  corrections. Losses already had worse total HP differential on turn 2
  (-0.34 versus +0.23 in wins), and were behind in faint count at that point
  (0.44 versus 0.27); the gap persisted at turn 3. Switch rate was similar in
  wins and losses, so this sample does not support a blanket switching penalty.
  This points toward first-turn tactical action quality and matchup-specific

  75.44% with damage-based preview, below the requested 80%. The confirmed
  preview improvement is +3.76 pp over random preview on 1,024 matched clusters.
  Do not treat a small tuning screen or the upper edge of an interval as
  reaching 80%. Next, improve preview choice using stronger team-role and
  matchup features, then confirm any candidate on at least 1,024 fresh clusters
  against the same-seed current preview incumbent. Continue evaluating public
  battle decisions separately so preview and action-policy gains remain
  attributable. Keep learned search disabled unless it beats this paired
  baseline under equal compute. The role and equilibrium experiments in
  Rounds341–345 did not help. Stop preview-weight micro-tuning; next return to
  decision-level counterfactuals and train a matchup-aware action policy using
  terminal outcomes under sampled legal opponent responses, with the damage
  preview held fixed so battle-action improvement is identifiable.

- **Rounds354–363 loss tracing and action-counterfactual audit (2026-10-29):**

  own knockouts by the second trace state. Opening move names were diffuse, so

  **Rounds371–372 turn-one action counterfactual follow-up (2026-10-30; no

  evidence that always setting up improves matches. Protect averaged +1.10 pp

  underperformed by 11.39 pp on average. Do not train a selector on these

  evaluate against Round333 directly to verify the new result transfers to
  the historic seed set. Broad action branching (about 7 matches/s) has not
  produced reliable action gains.

- **Round313 counterfactual action-value iteration (2026-10-29; planned):**
  Rounds301–311 show that one-turn material or learned-frontier search, broader
  candidate lists, equilibrium/maximin selection, and fixed/adaptive chance
  sampling do not reliably improve public Counterplay. The Round306 predictor
  is reasonably calibrated on observed behavior states, but it does not rank
  off-policy candidate actions better. The next player-improvement experiment
  must train directly from counterfactual action outcomes: sample public states
  from the current policy pool, build compact legal joint-action sets for both
  sides, advance each pair through the local simulator with paired RNG seeds,
  continue from each successor with a fixed continuation policy, and label
  player-view state/action outcomes by terminal win/loss. Fit an action-value
  model on those outcomes and use a small equilibrium matrix, then compare to
  raw Counterplay at the same decision budget. Start with a 20k-state pilot and
  report simulation throughput, samples per action pair, action-choice latency,
  and paired win-rate change. Do not scale to 1M predictor-only games until
  this action-level signal demonstrates improvement. Preserve the closed-sheet
  boundary in saved inputs and held-out tests.

- **Historical random-preview Max Damage checkpoint (Rounds 277–282; 2026-10-29):**
  the best score at that point was 70.36% for standalone public Counterplay with random team
  preview on 512 fresh team-pair clusters / 2,048 games. Its team-pair 95%
  interval is [67.19%, 73.54%], overlapping the previous Round264 score of
  67.87%; this is not yet a confirmed strength gain. Round94 preview selection
  scored 68.70% on the same fresh clusters; selector minus random was -1.66
  points (95% paired interval [-5.47, +2.05]). This checkpoint was superseded
  by the confirmed Round333 damage-preview result of 75.44%; the 80% target
  remains 4.56 points away. Current measured full-match speed is
  11.86–14.10 games/s with eight CPU workers; one million full matches would
  take roughly 20–23.5 hours at that observed rate, before training overhead.
  The present bottleneck is tactical action quality, not evaluation
  throughput. The switch-penalty, raw-damage move prediction, full sampled
  set, preview-selector, Helping Hand, sequential-damage, and joint-damage
  changes have not shown a reliable gain. Round282 and Round283 reproduced
  their matched controls' outcomes exactly; Round288's original HP-fraction
  threat objective also reproduced every Round284 outcome. A narrowed one-turn
  search was inconclusive and slower at 2.77 games/s; keep it experimental.
  Reports are recorded below.
- **Current plateau and immediate bottleneck (2026-10-29):** the raw direct
  policy is still around 40% against Max Damage; the best measured
  play variant remains Round190 with Max Damage controlling its first five
  decisions (51.86% on 512 paired clusters, +11.52 points over raw). New
  evidence continues to point to early action quality, while policy improvement
  from terminal-reward PPO and the first counterfactual ranker has not
  transferred. The response-conditioned
  selector had a positive but inconclusive first matched result under the real
  Round94 team-preview selector (+3.13 points vs Max Damage), but two fresh
  decision-3 screens did not confirm it. A first-action model was then trained
  on selector-matched counterfactuals; its 768-cluster full-match test showed
  no gain at all vs Max Damage (0.00 points; 95% cluster interval
  [-2.47, +2.47]) and -0.07 points overall ([-1.95, +1.82]). Round212 then
  trained a conservative direct actor update from paired first-action outcomes;
  Round213 tested it on the same 768 clusters as its baseline. It scored
  41.24% vs Max Damage vs 41.86% for the starting policy, a -0.62 point paired
  change (95% cluster interval [-1.53, +0.29]); only 83/768 clusters favored
  either side (32 candidate wins, 51 losses, 685 ties). The actor update did
  not improve play. Round214 retested replacing Round190's first action
  with Max Damage: +2.25 points on 256 paired clusters (95% interval [-0.98,
  +5.57]), so the intervention is directionally positive but unproven for this
  checkpoint. Round215 reduced the actor KL anchor tenfold; it still changed
  the selected candidate in only 1/52 held-out states, with zero estimated
  worst-response gain. Current bottleneck: learning to reliably turn the known
  opening action gap into a better action, not generating more evaluator data.
  Held-out Brier improvements and the tested selector/actor updates have not
  produced better action selection. Round216 focused the paired-action
  collection on policy-vs-Max-Damage, captured 800 states across 800 team
  clusters, and generated 23,728 replayed matches in 404.4 seconds
  (58.67 games/s aggregate, eight workers). The actor still selected Max Damage
  in only 3/160 held-out states with zero estimated robust advantage; a
  separate classifier gate selected 1/117 held-out states for a +0.21 point
  state-level estimate. Current full-match evaluation throughput is 9.43
  complete games/s for Round217 (2,048 matches / 217.3 seconds; the matched
  Round190 arm was 9.21 games/s);
  selector-matched data collection reached 40.64 games/s aggregate with four
  independent CPU workers, versus 12.08 games/s serial. Round217's 20k PPO
  rollout reached 41.96 games/s aggregate and 30.55 games/s end-to-end. Keep
  Round190 as the direct-policy baseline and Round195's first-five hybrid as
  the strongest measured play variant; do not promote Round217. Fresh Round241
  confirmed the first-five gain on 512 new team-pair clusters: 53.13% vs
  43.55% raw, paired +9.57 points (95% cluster interval [+6.10, +12.94]).
  Round242 then found fresh gains against public Counterplay (+11.33 points,
  interval [+6.35, +16.31]) and Round190 itself (+8.20 points,
  [+3.61, +12.79]). This is the first replicated multi-opponent play
  improvement in the current iteration. Round255/256 tested public-only
  Counterplay action scores as a logit prior on Round252: at prior weight 4.0,

  fresh Round257 confirmation scores 60.55% (1,240/2,048; 95% cluster interval
  [57.13%, 64.01%]) on 512 new team clusters. Round258 ran the zero-prior arm
  on the same clusters: 46.00% (942/2,048). The paired gain is +14.55 points
  (95% cluster interval [+11.23, +17.92]); 214 clusters favored the prior,
  80 favored zero prior, and 218 tied. Throughput was 9.65 vs 9.84 games/s;
  both arms had no timeouts or action corrections. The direct Round252
  checkpoint itself did not improve the Round190 baseline. A separate fresh
  Round264 full benchmark of the standalone public-only Counterplay heuristic

  `--policy-opponent-mixture-json` was supplied, per-policy episode counts were
  allocated according to weight index, but the selected checkpoint was rotated
  by `round_number`. This silently permuted the declared mixture and made the
  run report disagree with actual opponents. Explicit mixtures now keep weights
  aligned with pool checkpoints; default uniform sampling retains its round
  rotation. Each round report now records actual per-checkpoint episode counts
  alongside requested weights. The prior Round145-217 launch scripts did not use
  this explicit mixture option, so this does not explain those historical
  outcomes. Before a new PSRO-style training run, verify counts and freeze its
  exact pool/weights in run metadata.

  self-play data run completed 20,000 full Showdown games in 952.6 seconds,
  or 21.0 games/s aggregate with eight workers (2.78 games/s per worker). GPU
  utilization was about 94% during rollout; peak aggregate process RSS was
  17.1 GiB. Full-match generation and per-game record preparation remain the
  first bottleneck for million-game evaluator studies. The evaluator cache
  build on this corpus is CPU bound; record normalization took about 2 minutes
  and cache generation about another 2 minutes. Paired complete-match
  evaluation remains around 8–10 games/s. The Round199 snapshot-based,
  paired-response counterfactual collector ran at 12.4 replayed games/s across
  14,656 complete matches. Disk use is about 34%, with about
  577 GiB free; the 216 MB compressed rollout and 188 MB normalized value
  corpus fit comfortably within the storage limit.

  hybrid-vs-hybrid games with the Round94 preview selector and Max Damage
  action intervention on both players' first five battle decisions. Both

  from scratch and selected epoch 3 after calibration Brier began worsening.
  On 57,706 held-out states from held-out team rosters, Brier was 0.17290, log
  loss 0.51280, accuracy 73.22%, and ECE 0.01080. By turn bucket, Brier was

  parallel rollout, preparation, and PPO); rollout itself took 488.5 seconds

  intervention on eight workers. This independently confirms a real opening
  and early-turn action weakness; it does not meet the 75% target and does not
  show that the learned policy improved. Previous behavior cloning of narrow
  Max Damage labels regressed, so next training must use multi-response
  counterfactual action advantages / regret with policy-controlled continuation,
  and be tested against this hybrid as a strategic control. Artifacts and
  reproduction: `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round195_round190_first5_validation_512_2x_20261029/`
  and `scripts/evaluate_round195_first5_validation.sh`.

- **Round196 matched trace diagnosis (2026-10-29; descriptive):** traced raw
  Round190 and its first-five Max Damage intervention on the same 128 held-out
  team clusters, two outcome repeats, and both seats (512 matches per mode).
  Raw scored 41.4% and first-five 56.1%; each arm had zero action corrections,
  errors, or timeouts. In raw-policy losses, the policy was already behind at
  the first post-turn snapshot (mean team HP 4.96 vs 5.21 and 5.45 vs 5.80
  living Pokemon). In first-five losses, that first-snapshot gap was nearly
  closed (4.91 vs 4.99 HP; 5.39 vs 5.53 living Pokemon), then widened by
  snapshots three to five (HP 3.55 vs 3.98 at snapshot three and 2.50 vs 3.15
  at snapshot five). This is outcome-stratified and descriptive, not causal,
  but suggests the intervention improves early exchanges while losses still
  accumulate during continuation. Action frequencies differ too (31.8% pass in
  first-five losses vs 20.6% in raw losses), likely reflecting downstream
  knockouts/forced switches; inspect state transitions before assigning a
  strategic cause. Do not copy Max Damage as an optimal label. The next
  learning target is player-view action advantage over legal simultaneous
  responses and hidden-team hypotheses with policy-controlled continuation,
  especially across the first several decisions, then full-match evaluation
  against held-out opponent families. The trace analyzer now recurses through
  parallel worker directories. Reports:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round196_trace_first5_128x2_20261029/`;
  reproduce with `scripts/evaluate_round196_trace_first5.sh`.

- **Why the raw policy is still near 40% (2026-10-29; trace diagnosis):** the
  latest Round187 training batch changed the Max Damage score only from 39.81%
  to 40.43% on 768 held-out team-pair clusters (paired +0.62 points; 95%
  interval [-0.65, +1.89]). More games with the same terminal-outcome PPO
  signal are not the missing ingredient. The 128-cluster loss trace (256
  side-swapped games) scored 42.58%, with no invalid-action adjustments. Its
  outcome-stratified snapshots show the policy already behind after the first
  turn in losses (5.03 versus 5.24 team HP fractions) and further behind by
  snapshot five (2.62 versus 3.66); wins show the opposite trend. This is
  descriptive rather than causal, but points toward early joint-action quality
  as the place to improve. The current damage gate's +7.62-point Max Damage
  transfer shows that action choice matters, while its lack of a measured gain
  against learned opponents means it cannot serve as the learned solution.
  Next work should produce player-view-only counterfactual action values across
  legal opponent responses and hidden-team worlds, then train/test that signal
  on held-out states and paired complete matches. Do not launch another large
  PPO batch until such a signal passes a held-out decision-quality check.

  5.36–5.37 vs public counterplay, and 4.89–6.12 vs the policy pool. CPU PPO
  preparation/training took 180.2s for 80,402 transitions; the full update
  took 651.3s. Compression reduced 3.70 GB of raw rollout records to 202.5 MB
  in 14s. The selector-matched 256-cluster / two-outcome-per-side Showdown
  gate completed 1,024 games per checkpoint with zero timeouts or action
  corrections: Round173 scored 43.26%; Round176 scored 44.43%. The paired
  change was +1.17 points (95% team-cluster interval [-0.98, +3.32]); 32
  clusters favored Round176, 24 favored Round173, and 200 tied. This is a
  promising point estimate, not statistically established improvement, so
  Round176 is not promoted. Reproduce evaluation with
  `scripts/evaluate_round176_selector_matched_vs_round173.sh`; report:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round176_selector_matched_vs_round173_maxdamage_256pairs2_20261028/round176_minus_round173.json`.
  A second matched test against public-only Counterplay also completed 1,024
  games per checkpoint without errors: Round173 scored 46.00%, Round176 scored
  45.41%, and the paired change was -0.59 points (95% team-cluster interval
  [-2.73, +1.46]). Round176 therefore has no established gain against either
  opponent and is not promoted. The mismatch correction made the training
  distribution consistent with evaluation but did not break the policy
  plateau; do not repeat this PPO recipe as if selector consistency alone were
  a strength fix. Reports are under
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round176_selector_matched_vs_round173_public_counterplay_256pairs2_20261028/`.
  The fresh Round176 preview selector was then evaluated on 1,024 new held-out
  team-pair clusters, with two repeats and side swaps. Round94 scored 44.90%
  over 4,096 games (zero errors); the new selector scored 44.07% over 4,094
  games (one incomplete pair, zero action adjustments). The paired difference
  was -0.83 percentage points (95% team-cluster interval [-2.95, +1.29]); 194
  clusters favored the candidate, 212 favored Round94, and 618 tied. This is
  stronger evidence against a selector-only gain, not evidence that the agent
  is improving toward 75%. Keep Round94 as selector and stop spending training
  runs on preview-only updates. Report:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round176_preview_selector_vs_round94_maxdamage_1024pairs2_20261028/candidate_minus_round94.json`.
  The reproducible selector-data trainer now streams gzip shards and can filter
  to the trainable player's perspective (`--trainable-only`), fixing the prior
  decompression/mixed-perspective hazards; retain it for future use only if a
  preview-specific hypothesis warrants it.
  **Plateau response:** the ~40–45% raw result persists despite selector-matched
  PPO, a broad opponent mixture, and public-context features that encode
  mechanics such as Protect streaks and Fake Out windows. The legal matrix
  already includes switches, Protect, setup, redirection, and defensive
  responses; coverage and wider-row ablations show that adding candidates or
  chance samples alone does not resolve action ranking. A matched Monte Carlo
  terminal-return replay of Round176's 20k corpus also failed to improve its
  checkpoint (full result below). Do not repeat the same PPO mix, vary only
  GAE lambda again, or fit another scalar action ranker. Continue improving
  player-view-only joint-action payoff quality and robust response selection;
  validate candidate changes on held-out states and paired complete matches.
  Diagnose losses by turn and action category before another policy update;
  the first trace and causal opening intervention are recorded below. Keep Round173 as the battle-policy
  checkpoint and Round94 as its preview selector until a new checkpoint clears
  paired, multi-opponent promotion gates. Large Showdown score screens here ran
  at 8.3–9.5 games/s with eight workers; the latest 20k training update ran at
  42.5 rollout games/s aggregate and 30.7 end-to-end games/s. These are
  different workloads, not interchangeable speed claims.

  **What “stuck near 40%” means:** the number refers to the unmodified battle
  policy against the Max Damage baseline, not to all opponents or the best
  measured configuration. A prior Round176 screen scored 44.34%; its
  terminal-return replay scored 42.38% on a different matched screen. The
  larger fresh 512-cluster recheck scored Round176 at 38.87% versus Max Damage
  and did not establish a gain over Round173. Round173's five-decision Max
  Damage intervention
  reached 54.00% against Max Damage, but symmetric checks versus Round102 and
  Round166 did not establish transfer. This is evidence that a narrow
  opponent-specific action rule can raise this matchup while the learned raw
  policy remains weak; it is not evidence of broad improvement. No training
  process is currently active. Do not describe 40% as the current universal
  strength estimate.

  **Training-method pivot:** the restricted Round145–152 payoff-mixture runs
  already tested choosing a training opponent mix from an empirical policy
  matrix; they did not produce a dependable Max Damage gain. Another fixed
  PPO mixture or terminal-return variant is therefore not the next experiment.
  The next training candidate should be a true population-response loop:
  freeze an evaluated population, solve its empirical zero-sum game for a
  robust opponent mixture, train a new response policy against that mixture,
  then add the response only if a fresh, paired multi-opponent gate shows it
  improves the population's lower-confidence worst-case score. Keep the
  existing incumbent and first-five hybrid as controls. The first pilot must
  be small enough to validate the full loop before scaling: one response
  checkpoint, held-out team clusters, common seeds, both seats, and Max Damage,
  public Counterplay, and frozen learned policies. Report payoff-matrix
  uncertainty, per-opponent scores, action validity, training throughput, and
  complete-match throughput. This changes the response-generation process;
  it must not infer or exploit opponent behavior tendencies.

  **Implementation progress (2026-10-28):** `scripts/train_headless_ppo.py`
  now accepts `--policy-opponent-mixture-json`, a JSON object mapping every
  final policy-pool checkpoint path to a nonnegative weight. It validates that
  the entries exactly match the actual pool, normalizes them, allocates policy
  rollouts with largest-remainder rounding, and records the effective mixture
  in `rounds.jsonl`. Without this option, the existing uniform allocation is
  preserved. Syntax compilation and CLI help inspection succeeded. The
  feature has not yet been used in a training run; do not count it as a
  strength result.

  **Current-policy matrix and 512-cluster plateau recheck (2026-10-28):**
  evaluated Round136, Round166, Round173, and Round176 on 128 common
  team-pair clusters against Max Damage, legal public Counterplay, and the
  other learned checkpoints. Both sides used Round94 for team preview. All
  3,584 matches completed with no action corrections or errors at 5.18
  games/s summed over the sequential four-worker screens. Every checkpoint
  scored below 40% against Max Damage on this small fresh schedule; the
  95% cluster intervals were roughly 7 points wide. Regret matching put
  about 99.99% of the conservative response mixture on Max Damage and almost
  all policy-row weight on Round176. This matrix is too small to justify
  training from those weights, especially given the previous matrix-mixture
  PPO results.

  To resolve the discrepancy with earlier ~43–44% screens, ran 512 clusters,
  two outcomes per cluster and both seats, with Round173 and Round176 against
  both Max Damage and public Counterplay. This produced 8,192 complete local
  matches at 8.88 games/s aggregate across the four arms, with zero timeouts,
  action corrections, or incomplete pairs. Against Max Damage, Round173
  scored 38.57% (95% cluster interval [35.21%, 42.04%]) and Round176 scored
  38.87% ([35.50%, 42.33%]); the paired Round176 gain was +0.29 points
  ([-1.12, +1.71]). Against public Counterplay, scores were 41.75%
  ([38.38%, 45.21%]) and 42.72% ([39.36%, 46.14%]); paired gain +0.98
  points ([-0.54, +2.49]). Round176 is not a statistically supported
  improvement against either opponent. The current measured raw strength is
  therefore about 39% vs Max Damage and 42% vs public Counterplay on this
  fresh schedule; older 43–44% Max Damage point estimates are seed-dependent
  and should not be treated as a stable mean. Do not repeat Round176's PPO
  recipe. Reports and reproducible commands are in
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round178_current_policy_league_matrix_128_1x_20261028_retry1/`
  and
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round178_plateau_recheck_512pairs2_20261028/`;
  scripts are `scripts/evaluate_round178_fresh_policy_league_matrix.sh` and
  `scripts/evaluate_round178_plateau_recheck_512pairs2.sh`.

  **Round179 state-conditioned joint-action experiment (2026-10-28; evaluated):**
  inspection showed that the second native
  action was conditioned on the first through a state-independent action-index
  lookup. Added an optional zero-initialized head that scores the first action
  together with the current state when producing second-slot logits. The new
  branch is disabled for old checkpoints and can be enabled through
  `--state-conditioned-joint-action`; policy sampling, exact joint log
  probabilities, self-play batching, and PPO training all use the same
  conditional distribution. Round179 started from Round176, held the 50% Max
  Damage / 25% public Counterplay / 25% frozen-policy training mixture fixed,
  and changed only this model capacity. It completed 20,000 games and 80,388
  trainable transitions. Rollout took 468.1s (42.73 aggregate games/s), PPO
  took 183.0s for 1,580 optimizer steps, and end-to-end training took 651.1s
  (30.72 games/s). PPO approximate KL was 0.01135 and clip fraction 15.1%.
  Raw rollout data occupied 3.70 GB and compressed to 202.2 MB. Peak aggregate
  rollout RSS was 10.16 GiB. Per-opponent shard rates were 7.41 games/s vs Max
  Damage, 5.41 vs public Counterplay, and 5.27 vs policy opponents; mean action
  selection time ranged from 49.6ms to 99.9ms. During PPO, the GPU reached 84%
  sampled utilization with 1.23 GB of 8.19 GB memory in use. These are workload
  measurements, not evidence of strength. A fresh matched evaluation used 512
  team clusters, two outcome repeats and both seats against Max Damage, public
  Counterplay and Round166 (12,282 completed matches across six arms). Against
  Max Damage, Round176 scored 44.29% and Round179 45.02%; paired change +0.73
  points (95% interval [-0.73, +2.10]). Against public Counterplay the scores
  were 45.94% and 45.70%, paired change -0.24 ([-1.86, +1.37]). Against
  Round166 they were both about 51.56%, paired change -0.05 ([-1.81, +1.66]).
  Two incomplete timeout cases occurred in the public-Counterplay arms and one
  in the Round179-versus-Round166 arm; comparisons used the 512 matched team
  clusters. There were no invalid-action corrections. Arm throughput was
  7.27–7.30 games/s vs Max Damage, 6.50 games/s vs public Counterplay, and
  6.62–7.60 games/s vs Round166. The state-conditioned head did not produce a
  supported gain on any opponent, so Round179 is not promoted and this head
  should not receive another PPO run without a new learning-signal hypothesis.
  Audit found the generic trainer had serialized the post-update opponent pool
  beside the pre-update rollout weights. Corrected the trainer to snapshot and
  report the exact pool used for each round, and repaired Round179's manifest:
  its actual policy-pool mix was Round136, Round166, Round173 and the Round176
  starting checkpoint at 25% each. This is a provenance correction only; the
  recorded rollouts used those opponents, and it does not change the scores.
  Explicit opponent-mixture JSON is now restricted to one-round response runs
  until weights for a growing multi-round pool are defined.
  Reproduce training with
  `scripts/train_round179_state_conditioned_joint_policy_20k.sh` and evaluation
  with `scripts/evaluate_round179_joint_head_vs_round176_512pairs2.sh`; artifacts
  are under
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/direct_policy_round179_round176_state_conditioned_joint_ppo_20k_20261028/`
  and
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round179_state_conditioned_joint_vs_round176_512pairs2_20261028/`.

- **Turn-by-turn loss trace and opening-action intervention (2026-10-28):**
  added `--trace-decisions` to a fresh 128-team-cluster / two-repeat matched
  Showdown screen, retaining side-swapped per-turn actions and post-state HP
  and faint counts. The reproducible reader is
  `scripts/analyze_action_loss_traces.py`; it corrects the reversed-seat result
  convention, reports outcomes by the checkpoint's actual seat, and labels its
  action/state comparisons descriptive rather than causal. Round173 scored
  42.38% (217/512; team-cluster 95% interval [35.35%, 49.61%]), with zero
  action corrections, timeouts, or errors. In outcome-stratified simultaneous
  post-action snapshots, eventual losers were already down an average 0.32
  surviving Pokémon and 0.25 team-HP units after the first resolved action;
  by the eighth matched snapshot the gap was 0.95 Pokémon and 0.48 team-HP
  units. This localizes the losses early but is not itself proof that opening
  actions cause them. The trace report is
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_loss_trace_maxdamage_128pairs2_20261028/loss_analysis.md`.
  To test causality, replaced only the policy's first joint action with its
  legal Max Damage action on the same fresh 512 team clusters, repeats,
  previews, and side swaps. Raw Round173 scored 42.87% (2,048 games); the
  first-action intervention scored 47.22% (2,046 games; one incomplete pair).
  Paired gain: +4.35 percentage points (95% team-cluster interval [+1.46,
  +7.18]), favoring the intervention in 138 clusters and disfavoring it in 96
  (278 tied). Neither arm had action corrections; evaluation throughput was
  7.93 vs 7.69 games/s over eight workers. This confirms a material first
  decision weakness for this benchmark, while leaving the remaining 28-point
  gap to the 75% target. It does not justify teaching Max Damage as the final
  policy: prior narrow opening imitation updates failed to transfer, and the
  established five-decision Max Damage hybrid remains stronger (~50.6–51.2%).
  Use this causal signal to prioritize legal, player-view-only opening joint
  action improvement and robust response evaluation; preserve the measured
  later-game policy and verify any change across the opponent pool. Reproduce
  the 512-cluster intervention with
  `scripts/evaluate_round173_first_turn_max_damage_ablation.sh`; paired report:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_first_turn_max_damage_ablation_512pairs2_20261028/first_turn_max_damage_minus_policy.json`.
  **Cross-opponent transfer screen:** repeated the same first-action
  intervention against public-only Counterplay and frozen Round102 on 256 new
  team clusters, two outcomes and both policy seats per cluster. Against
  Counterplay, raw Round173 scored 46.29%, the intervention 49.41%, and the
  paired change was +3.13 points (95% cluster interval [-0.98, +7.23]); 74
  clusters favored the intervention, 55 opposed it, and 127 tied. Against
  Round102, the change was -0.78 points (95% interval [-5.57, +4.00]); 71
  clusters favored the intervention, 68 opposed it, and 117 tied. All four
  arms completed 1,024 games with zero timeouts, errors, or action adjustments.
  Neither cross-opponent comparison establishes a gain, but neither shows a
  clear regression. The Max Damage opening effect is therefore real on its
  benchmark and not yet a robust strength improvement. Do not train solely to
  copy this action. Continue with the closed-sheet response-matrix gate and
  require held-out transfer. Reproduce both comparisons with
  `scripts/evaluate_round173_opening_action_generalization.sh`; reports are
  under
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_opening_action_generalization_256pairs2_20261028/`.

- **Opening action-difference audit (2026-10-28):** traced 128 fresh
  team-pair clusters with side swaps (256 games per arm), using the same team
  and preview choices for raw Round173 and its first-five hybrid. At the first
  decision, the policy's joint action differed from Max Damage's in 232/256
  matches (90.6%). Across the 512 individual active-Pokémon action slots,
  354 differed: 224 selected a different move, 94 used the same move but a

  Later decisions are not state-matched after the first action, so their
  differences are descriptive only. The analysis read only the evaluated

- **Action-selection model input audit and repair (2026-10-28):** the earlier
  512-cluster model selected +1.39 points over policy on 90 held-out clusters
  (95% interval [-3.89, +7.22]) and -3.38 points against Max Damage
  ([-7.43, 0.00]). Its Brier score was good (0.1796 vs 0.2468 constant), but
  it saw only observation values and action IDs. The actor's native action
  semantics and 73 public-context features were missing. The data pipeline now
  records those player-view features for either seat; both action models and
  deployment inference consume per-slot action features, public context, and
  normalized policy log probability.
  The fresh feature-rich collection completed on 512 clusters: 448 usable Turn
  5 states, 3,453 candidate rows, 22,936 complete-match replays in 2,738
  seconds (8.38 replays/s), 64 games ending before the decision, and zero
  rejected candidates. The counterfactual baseline was 39.87% for policy and
  43.67% for Max Damage's action (+3.79 points, 95% interval [+1.73, +5.83]);
  these are single-action interventions under frozen continuation, not
  full-match strength. The feature-rich action model had held-out action Brier
  0.1816 vs 0.2468 constant, but chosen-action gain was only +1.11 points over
  90 clusters (95% interval [-1.94, +4.44]); against Max Damage it was -2.03
  points ([-5.41, +0.68]). The feature-rich pairwise ranker was -0.56 points
  ([-4.17, +3.33]). A 16-cluster full-match side-swapped integration smoke
  test submitted valid actions; its noisy -3.13 point result is only a wiring
  check. Better inputs fixed the information deficit but did not fix action
  choice. Stop spending more compute on this reranker.
  Full-prefix replay was 8.38/s; snapshot branching now reaches 16.63/s,
  separate from PPO training throughput (roughly 25-28 games/s end-to-end and
  37-43 rollout games/s in recent runs). The next experiment should improve
  the actor's training signal directly: build a held-out, team-clustered
  policy-improvement dataset from complete trajectories, compare
  terminal-return policy updates against the current PPO baseline, and promote
  only on repeated side-swapped complete
  matches against Max Damage and the frozen policy pool. Do not train on the
  action-value model's predictions; its held-out action ordering still fails
  against Max Damage.

  14.7%; it generated no new simulator games. On 128 fresh team clusters,

  ([-3.71, +1.37]), and -0.78 against symmetric-preview Round166

  learned policies used the Round94 preview selector in the Round166 matchup.
  No comparison establishes a difference, but all three point estimates are

  **Corrected response-coverage audit:** the first diagnostic matched by turn

  matches the exact joint decision and compares only contemporaneous move
  requests. Across 249 successful searched decisions, Max Damage's realized
  joint action appeared in at least one of two sampled hidden worlds 62.7% of
  the time, in both worlds 47.0% of the time, and in neither world for 37.3%.
  Eight worlds raised at-least-one-world coverage to 82.5% and mean per-world
  coverage to 68.5% on 63 decisions, but changed only 8 actions; the same-seed
  32-pair match difference versus two worlds was +1.56 points (95% interval
  0 to +4.69; one team-pair result changed) while throughput fell from 4.61
  to 1.76 games/s. Do not raise the default world count. The next improvement
  must improve response generation or payoff quality per simulation, not just
  draw more worlds. The audit is diagnostic only and never feeds the realized

  **Coverage-miss decomposition:** the diagnostic already records semantic
  action candidates, so the 128-pair report was re-audited without another
  simulator run. Of 93 decisions where the realized Max Damage joint action
  was absent in both sampled worlds, 17 had no world containing both realized
  move IDs (hidden-set sampling coverage); in 76, at least one world contained
  both move IDs. Across all 93 misses, the exact per-slot actions appeared in
  shortlisted responses for both slots on 19 decisions, for one slot on 67,
  and for neither on 7. Thus there are two distinct gaps: hidden-set sampling
  and, more often, shortlist/target selection even when moves are present.
  This is a coverage diagnostic, not a training target: the realized action is
  never passed to search. Next, inspect why high-damage legal joint responses
  are pruned and improve the response ranking using only each sampled world's
  legal state and mechanics; do not add more worlds or train to copy Max Damage
  choices as an opponent-tendency model.

  **Leave-one-opponent-out probability calibration:** fit a two-parameter

  overconfident for eventual match outcomes. A two-parameter logistic mapping,
