  **Current diagnosis and next action:** the plateau is primarily an action
  ranking/generalization problem. The current one-turn matrix changes many
  decisions without consistently changing match outcomes for the better, and
  the learned frontier is poorly scaled against final outcomes. Further
  chance samples, larger candidate sets, or another PPO run with the same
  weak action labels are not justified. Continue with the next acceptance gate
  below: build legal, strategically diverse candidate and opponent-response
  sets from player-visible information; compare candidate payoffs over
  repeated outcomes; then train/evaluate only on held-out team clusters and
  multiple opponents. Treat the 40% score as the current measured strength,
  not as evidence that more training epochs alone will fix play.

  **Same-width slot-coverage response selector (2026-10-28):** added an
  opt-in `slot_coverage` selector. It reserves the strongest raw-damage joint
  response, then greedily covers high-ranked legal actions for each opponent
  slot in the remaining rows. A 64-team-pair pilot showed why the reservation
  matters: pure slot coverage lifted per-slot coverage from 77.6% to 84.8%, but
  exact joint-response coverage fell from 56.4% to 20.0%; that first variant is
  diagnostic only. With the top-damage joint response retained, exact joint
  coverage returned to 55.1% while per-slot coverage rose to 89.2% on 192 fresh
  held-out team clusters (control: 54.9% joint and 77.9% per slot). The paired
  change in search-versus-raw match effect was +0.78 percentage points (95%
  cluster-bootstrap interval [-1.04, +2.60]); only 7 searched outcomes favored
  the variant versus 4 favoring control, with 373 ties. Runtime was comparable
  (4.70 versus 4.54 games/s on the larger seed; same 10 safe fallbacks in each
  arm across the two seed sets). This improves per-slot coverage but has not
  shown a strength gain; keep it configurable, not default. The diagnostic
  checks only whether the benchmark opponent's realized joint action was in
  the candidate set and never exposes that action to the search policy.
  Reports: `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_slot_coverage_control_maxdamage_64_seed5701_20261028`,
  `round173_slot_coverage_damage_variant_maxdamage_64_seed5701_20261028`,
  `round173_slot_coverage_control_maxdamage_128_seed5801_20261028`, and
  `round173_slot_coverage_damage_variant_maxdamage_128_seed5801_20261028`.

  **Counterfactual action-selector evaluation correction (2026-10-28):** the
  action-value and pairwise-ranker trainers now accept
  `--split-chance-repeats`. With eight common outcomes per action, they fit
  and early-stop on the first four, then report held-out action calibration,
  pairwise ranking, and selected-action outcomes on the other four. This
  prevents choosing an action and estimating its outcome from the same chance
  samples. The existing reports remain valid as diagnostics but their
  selected-action deltas are selection-biased; use the split mode for future
  promotion decisions. Python compilation and CLI help checks pass; the mode
  was applied to the prior 128-cluster Max Damage set as a pipeline check. The
  action-value model selected +5.4 points over policy on 23 held-out clusters
  (95% interval [0.0, +15.2]), while the pairwise model selected -2.2 points
  ([-5.4, 0.0]); both were too small and uncertain for promotion. The fresh
  feature-rich 512-cluster split test is complete; its results and stop decision
  are recorded at the top of this plan. Earlier artifacts are in
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_action_model_splitchance_128_maxdamage_20261028/`
  and `round173_pairwise_ranker_splitchance_128_maxdamage_20261028/`.

  The full-match action-selector path now also applies to whichever seat owns
  the policy, and captures that seat's own observation/mask for paired-state
  checks. Deployment-time evaluation now uses the same legal tactical
  candidate generator as training data, then verifies each candidate against
  the live Showdown request. A four-cluster smoke evaluation exercised both
  P1 and P2 with no reach mismatch or invalid action. A subsequent 16-cluster
  feature-rich smoke exercised live native action features, public context,
  and log probabilities for either seat, with all 64 complete matches valid.
  Its -3.13 point result is too noisy to infer strength. This validates the
  seat-swapped evaluation plumbing only; it is not a strength result. See
  `scripts/run_headless_showdown_self_play.py` and
  `scripts/evaluate_action_value_selector.py`.

  **Response-pruning code audit (2026-10-28):** the headless search scores
  individual move/target options, adds the two active-slot scores into a joint
  score, and sorts the resulting joint actions. Before taking the top rows, it
  reserves semantic categories such as switch, Protect, setup, and redirection;
  opponent rows can additionally reserve top raw-damage pairs. This explains
  how a response can contain both realized move IDs in a hidden world yet still
  miss the realized joint action because one slot's target/action combination
  was pruned. The score is a local damage heuristic, not a learned joint-action
  payoff, and it does not model support synergy or move-order interactions.
  Earlier two-damage-row and wider-response ablations did not improve match
  outcomes, so do not simply reserve more damage rows. Next test a same-width
  response selector that explicitly covers legal per-slot action/target
  combinations and selected joint profiles, then compare its payoff regret
  and paired full-match strength on identical held-out clusters before using
  it for training. Implementation to inspect: `individualOptions` and
  `generateJointCandidates` in `scripts/search_showdown_first_turn.js`.

- **Why the score appears stuck near 40% (2026-10-28 update):** this is a real
  policy-quality plateau, not evidence that the simulator is too slow or that
  we simply need more games. Round173's raw policy was 40.82% in the fresh
  512-game Max Damage screen; its first-five-decision hybrid was about 50% in
  a separate matched screen. More search did not lift the raw policy. A
  seat-balanced 512-game comparison of four-by-four material search against
  the same raw policy gave 221/512 (43.16%) for search and 226/512 (44.14%)
  without it: -0.98 percentage points (95% paired episode-cluster interval
  -5.66 to +3.71). Material search ran at 3.00 games/s versus 10.07 games/s
  raw; its median/p95 decision latency was 224/264 ms. This is not a detected
  loss, but there is no strength gain to buy with the 3.4x slowdown. Keep raw
  Round173 as the search control and do not train from these search labels.
  Report: `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_material_vs_raw_256perseat_20261028/paired_comparison.json`.

  The evaluator is also unreliable on the states search creates: in the
  128-game 4x4 search sample it predicted 66.0% mean win probability while
  outcomes were 39.8%; Brier score was 0.300 versus about 0.24 for a constant
  base-rate prediction. With eight opponent responses, mean prediction was
  61.8%, observed win rate 39.1%, and Brier 0.276. Treat this as a distribution
  and calibration failure signal, not proof that the value model alone causes
  the policy plateau. The diagnostic is
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_search_frontier_value_calibration_64x2_20261028.json`.

  **Next direction:** the closed-sheet one-turn 4x4 matrix now has paired
  complete-match evidence in both seats. At two hidden worlds and one chance
  sample, it gained +3.5 percentage points against Max Damage over 256 team
  pairs (95% cluster interval 0 to +7.0), and +2.3 points against frozen
  Round166 over 64 pairs (interval -6.3 to +10.9). These consistent positive
  point estimates are not yet reliable strength gains. Keep raw Round173 as
  the incumbent and do not train from the small candidate-selected outcomes.
  Four chance samples did not improve the result in a 64-pair check (+2.3 pp,
  interval -4.7 to +9.4) and slowed throughput from 4.59 to 1.95 games/s. A
  shortlist de-duplication change now selects distinct switch, Protect, setup,
  and redirection profiles when available while preserving the four-action
  cap. On 128 fresh team pairs it changed 168/249 valid decisions but had zero
  net win-rate effect (95% cluster interval -5.5 to +5.1). A same-seed
  equilibrium-versus-maximin comparison changed the selected action in 18/256
  cases and complete-match result in only 3/128 team pairs; maximin's net
  effect was -0.4 points (interval -2.0 to +0.8). These results point back to
  action-ranking quality rather than a need for wider matrices or fixed extra
  chance samples. Adaptive maximin sampling from 1 to 8 outcomes was also
  measured: on 64 decisions it used a mean of 5.91 outcomes (31 stopped at 4,
  29 used all 8, four used 5 or 7), changed only 2/64 actions relative to
  fixed four-sample maximin, and changed only 1/64 match outcomes. It ran at
  1.52 games/s versus 1.99 for fixed four-sample maximin. Keep adaptive
  sampling as an available experiment, but do not enable it for routine search;
  the confidence rule did not save enough work or change decisions often
  enough to justify its added cost. Do not distill these small screens. A closed-sheet data set
  still needs genuinely repeated chance outcomes before it can support
  calibrated policy labels. Current measured full-match rates:
  10.1 games/s raw, 4.59 games/s with one-decision search against Max Damage,
  and 3.73 games/s versus a frozen policy; the revised four-row shortlist ran
  at 4.66 games/s and maximin at 4.68 on a later held-out Max Damage workload.
  One-decision search latency was 157/262 ms median/p95 (decision call) and
  247/356 ms adapter-inclusive.
  The bottlenecks are decision-time simulation and candidate/chance coverage;
  raw simulator throughput is still adequate for policy training, while
  decision-time search needs more efficient sampling before wider use.

  **Chance-sampling follow-up:** on a separate 64-team-pair Max Damage screen,
  four chance samples yielded 34.38% versus 32.03% for raw play (+2.34 pp;
  paired 95% team-cluster interval -4.69 to +9.38). That is similar to, and no
  stronger than, the one-sample signal. Throughput fell to 1.95 games/s from
  4.59; successful search-call latency rose to 612/1,121 ms median/p95
  (adapter-inclusive 804/1,313 ms). 123/128 searched decisions succeeded;
  the five safe fallbacks were Illusion/Transform exclusions. Four samples
  therefore do not yet justify their roughly 2.4x full-match cost. Keep the
  low-sample search experimental; improve candidate ranking or use adaptive
  sampling on close decisions before spending a larger budget. Report:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_closed_sheet_search_vs_maxdamage_64_chance4_20261028/report.json`.

- **Adaptive midgame chance-budget pilot (2026-10-28):** exposed the existing
  sequential maximin stopping rule through the midgame runtime. Corrected its
  robust row interval to take the minimum cellwise lower and upper bounds over
  hidden worlds and legal opponent responses. On 32 held-out team pairs / 128
  matches, adaptive 1-to-8 sampling succeeded in all 64 searched decisions,
  but used 4 samples in 31, 5 in 3, 7 in 1, and all 8 in 29 (mean 5.91).
  Throughput was 1.52 complete games/s; adapter latency was 961 ms median and
  1,812 ms p95. On the identical seed/team schedule, fixed-four maximin ran at
  1.99 games/s. Adaptive sampling changed only two selected actions and one
  match result compared with fixed-four; the sample is too small to infer a
  strength difference, and the extra outcomes did not materially change
  decisions. Do not use adaptive sampling by default. Retain it as an optional
  maximin experiment for future payoff models with stronger uncertainty
  separation. Reports:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_midgame_adaptive_maximin_1to8_vs_maxdamage_32_20261028/report.json`
  and
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_midgame_fixed4_maximin_vs_maxdamage_32_20261028/report.json`.

- **Shortlist de-duplication and selector comparison (2026-10-28):** a report
  audit of 500 valid search decisions found that the old diversity loop could
  count a Protect candidate again as the generic defensive candidate, wasting
  a slot. Redirection moves were also not separately labeled. The shortlist
  now seeks a distinct row per class and explicitly marks Follow Me, Rage
  Powder, and Ally Switch as redirection while preserving a strict four-row
  cap and the policy proposal. Across 128 fresh held-out team pairs / 512
  matches against Max Damage, search and raw play both scored 38.28% from P1
  and 35.94% from P2; combined paired gain was 0.00 points (95% team-cluster
  interval -5.47 to +5.08). Search changed 168/249 valid decisions and ran at
  4.66 games/s. In the selected four-row lists, 329 rows were offense-only,
  304 included Protect, 244 included a switch, 108 included setup, and 3
  included redirection; the chosen action used redirection once. The coverage
  fix improves shortlist diversity but has not yet improved match outcomes.
  On the identical team/seed schedule, maximin versus equilibrium changed
  18/256 searched decisions, changed match outcome in only 3/128 team pairs,
  and scored -0.39 points relative to equilibrium (95% cluster interval
  -1.95 to +0.78), at 4.68 games/s. Neither selector is promoted. Reports:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_closed_sheet_search_diverse_candidates_vs_maxdamage_128_20261028/report.json`
  and
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_closed_sheet_search_maximin_vs_maxdamage_128_20261028/report.json`.

  The tactical candidate screen has now been expanded, but sparse action
  availability and weak transfer to complete matches still prevent promotion.

- **Side-swapped search adapter and paired screen (2026-10-28):** initial P2
  failures came from `swapSerializedSideReferences`: serialized Pokémon
  references such as `[Pokemon:p2a]` were not matched by the side-swap regex,
  so the sides and names changed but the active references still pointed to
  the original P1. A post-switch reproduction confirmed the cause. The regex
  now swaps both `[Pokemon:p1a]` references and protocol identifiers like
  `p1a:`; the worker checks that deserializing the normalized state reproduces
  the acting side's active slots in order. A corrected 8-pair pilot had zero
  action-translation failures (8/8 valid searches per seat); it was too small
  for strength inference. The subsequent 32-pair paired screen completed 128
  local headless matches at 4.35 matches/s. Search returned valid actions in
  63/64 attempted decisions; the one safe fallback was the intended guard for
  a publicly observed Transform state. Median/p95 search-call elapsed time was
  167/253 ms (adapter-inclusive median/p95 258/351 ms). At the first searched
  midgame state, P1-seat raw/search scored 25.0%/34.4% (+9.4 pp; paired 95%
  cluster interval -3.1 to +21.9); P2-seat scored 25.0%/21.9% (-3.1 pp;
  interval -12.5 to +6.3). Combined seat-averaged gain was +3.1 pp with a
  team-cluster bootstrap interval of -6.3 to +12.5. This is not evidence of a
  reliable gain or of strength improvement over the roughly 40% baseline.
  Keep the method experimental and do not train on these outcomes. Next
  inspect the robust action choices and increase evaluation power only if the
  selector has a concrete rationale; otherwise prioritize policy training
  signals from stronger, correctly calibrated multi-outcome data. Reports:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_closed_sheet_search_side_swap_pilot8_20261028/fixed_side_reference_report.json`
  and
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_closed_sheet_search_side_swap_32_20261028/report.json`.

- **Expanded corrected search comparison (2026-10-28):** to measure whether
  the small 32-pair signal was noise, ran 256 held-out team pairs / 1,024
  complete matches, with raw and one-decision search for both seats. Overall
  raw policy scored 35.94%; search scored 39.45%. The within-team-pair
  side-averaged gain was +3.52 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval
  0.00 to +7.03). P1-seat gain was +2.34 points (paired interval -2.73 to
  +7.42); P2-seat gain was +4.69 points (0 to +9.38). The directional result
  is promising, but the interval touches zero and this single-opponent test
  does not establish robust improvement. Search returned a valid action on
  500 of 512 attempted decisions; 12 safe fallbacks were all from the
  explicit public-Illusion or observed-Transform exclusions. Runtime was
  223.2 seconds / 4.59 complete games per second; for successful decisions,
  median/p95 search-call latency was 157/262 ms, and adapter-inclusive
  median/p95 was 247/356 ms. Search changed the policy's proposed joint action
  in 375 of 500 valid decisions. The search path may be a useful teacher or
  inference refinement, but do not promote it yet: replicate on independent
  team seeds and compare latency-adjusted strength. Report:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_closed_sheet_search_side_swap_256_20261028/report.json`.

- **Frozen-policy search control (2026-10-28):** added an optional frozen
  opponent checkpoint to the paired side-swapped evaluator and ran 64 team
  pairs / 256 complete matches against Round166. Raw play scored 50.0%; search
  scored 52.34%, a team-pair side-averaged gain of +2.34 percentage points
  (95% bootstrap interval -6.25 to +10.94). P1 and P2 gains were +1.56 and
  +3.13 points; all 128 search decisions returned valid actions, and search
  changed 100 of them. Runtime was 68.5 seconds / 3.73 complete games per
  second. This agrees directionally with the Max Damage screen but remains
  inconclusive; the current search selector cannot yet be credited with a
  robust strength gain, and its latency is a throughput cost. Keep raw policy
  as the incumbent and do not train from this 64-pair result. Report:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_closed_sheet_search_vs_round166_64_20261028/report.json`.

- **Turn 5 counterfactual replication (2026-10-28):** captured 114 player-view
  states on fresh held-out team seeds (14/128 matches ended before Turn 5),
  then replayed policy, Max Damage, one-slot hybrids, and random legal joint
  actions with four common chance seeds per action. Opponent responses were
  split between Max Damage (58 states) and frozen Round166 policy (56 states).
  Substituting Max Damage's joint action at Turn 5 changed outcome by -0.66
  percentage points versus Round173 (95% paired cluster interval -5.26 to
  +4.17); against Max Damage the delta was -0.86 (-7.76 to +5.17), and against
  Round166 it was -0.45 (-7.59 to +7.14). A one-slot hybrid gained +2.21 points
  overall (-1.77 to +6.19), also inconclusive. Random legal actions lost 7.80
  points overall (-13.31 to -2.82), confirming that the policy's action choice
  contains useful signal while simple random alternatives are worse. This
  rejects neither the value model nor the policy globally; it shows that
  copying Max Damage at this midgame decision does not explain the 40% plateau.
  Do not use Max Damage Turn 5 actions as a training target. Collection took
  214.3 seconds for 2,093 complete matches (9.76 matches/s), with 14 missing
  states and one rejected candidate. Report and raw repeated outcomes:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_midgame_counterfactuals_maxdamage_round166_128x1_step5_4chance_20261028/report.json`.
  A smaller 43-state pilot suggested a +6.40-point Max Damage action gain, but
  the fresh replication returned -0.66 points; the pilot was sampling noise.

- **Broadened Turn 5 tactical candidates (2026-10-28):** the collector now
  records the acting player's legal individual action descriptors at capture
  time and forms additional joint choices that preserve the other active
  slot's policy action. Candidate roles include switch, Protect, setup,
  redirection, spread, and other status moves. Each candidate replay still
  verifies identical observation/legal mask and uses four common chance seeds;
  opponent-private information is not stored in the action descriptors. On 47
  fresh states (one of 48 games ended before Turn 5), the candidate-level
  screen completed 1,120 full matches in 118.9 seconds (9.42 matches/s) with
  zero rejected actions. The broad-screen Max Damage action appeared +7.45
  points over policy (95% interval +2.13 to +14.36), but combining it with the
  prior disjoint 114-state replication yields only +1.27 points over 161
  states (95% interval -2.71 to +5.41). By opponent, the combined delta was
  +2.24 (-3.85 to +8.33) against Max Damage and +0.32 (-4.75 to +5.70)
  against frozen Round166. Thus the small screen does not establish an action
  gain; per-move labels are sparse, with switches available on 8 states,
  spread moves on 8, setup on 4, and redirection on 1. Protect candidates were
  available on 25 states and averaged +2.5 points over policy in this small
  diagnostic, still too weak for promotion. Do not treat the point estimates as
  learned values. Expand capture to hundreds of states and retain candidate
  availability, action semantics, outcomes, and chance seeds so ranking quality
  can be evaluated on held-out team clusters. Report:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_midgame_strategic_counterfactuals_maxdamage_round166_48x1_step5_4chance_20261028/report.json`.

- **Broadened Turn 5 replication and full-match intervention (2026-10-28):**
  the 128-cluster tactical collection captured 111 states, ran 2,676 matches
  in 278.7 seconds (9.60 matches/s), and found Max Damage's step-5 joint action
  +4.05 points versus Round173 (95% cluster interval +0.68 to +7.88). This
  counterfactual candidate subset was generated from states already selected
  by Round173, so it is a local diagnostic and not an unbiased replacement
  policy estimate. Random legal perturbations were -6.73 points (95% interval
  -11.06 to -2.88); Protect's pooled estimate was -3.0 points on 25 clusters
  and its interval included zero. Other tactical categories were too sparse
  to rank. Eight proposed pairs were rejected by Showdown in this 128-state
  run because both slots selected pass; that joint-invalidity filter is now
  fixed, and a replay confirmation captured 43 states with zero rejected
  proposals. Do not use the 128-state result as a policy-training target.
  Report: `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_midgame_strategic_counterfactuals_maxdamage_round166_128x1_step5_4chance_20261028/report.json`.

  To check transfer to complete games, raw Round173 scored 43.55% against Max
  Damage over 1,024 games (256 paired team clusters, two repeats; 9.76 games/s).
  Replacing only its Turn 5 action with Max Damage's action scored 44.92%; the
  paired delta was +1.37 points with a 95% cluster interval of -1.46 to +4.20.
  Against frozen Round166, the corresponding rates were 56.25% raw and 56.93%
  with the intervention, delta +0.68 points (95% interval -3.03 to +4.30).
  There were no invalid-action adjustments. Thus, the large local
  counterfactual estimate did not transfer to a reliable complete-match gain.
  This narrows the current diagnosis: extra games or a one-turn heuristic
  override alone will not clear the plateau; we need to find and fix a
  repeatable action-ranking error without using hidden opponent state. Reports:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_step5_maxdamage_intervention_vs_maxdamage_gate_256x2_20261028/paired_comparison.json`
  and
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_step5_maxdamage_intervention_vs_round166_gate_256x2_20261028/paired_comparison.json`.

- **Action-probability ranking audit pilot (2026-10-28):** captured the
  policy's log-probability for each legal joint action at the Turn 5 player
  view, then compared the policy, Max Damage, tactical, and random candidates
  across four common chance seeds. The run captured 43 of 48 held-out states
  (five games ended before the decision), completed 1,024 matches in 117.0
  seconds (8.75 matches/s), and had zero rejected actions. Each state had a
  mean of 7.4 strategically sampled candidates. Only 17 states had both
  varying candidate probabilities and varying four-repeat outcomes. In those
  states, within-state Spearman correlation averaged +0.12 (median +0.17),
  with positive correlation in 53% of states. The policy's selected action had
  median zero observed gap from the best sampled candidate; the mean gap was
  16.7 percentage points. The best-candidate gap is biased upward because
  candidate selection and measurement use the same four outcomes, and this is
  not an exhaustive action set or a calibrated policy-strength estimate.
  Result: the pilot neither validates the policy's ranking nor identifies a
  reliable corrective target. Increase held-out states/repeats and measure
  rank correlation with uncertainty before training from action outcomes.
  The batched action scorer exactly matched the existing single-action scorer
  to within 6e-8 log-probability over the seven parity states checked. Reports:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_action_ranking_audit_48x1_step5_4chance_20261028/report.json`,
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_action_ranking_audit_48x1_step5_4chance_20261028/ranking_summary.json`,
  and
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_action_ranking_score_parity_8x1_step5_1chance_20261028/report.json`.

- **Expanded action-ranking audit and slot-specific complete-match screen
  (2026-10-28):** repeated the same 128-cluster mixed-opponent Turn 5 sample
  with eight chance seeds. The 111 captured states were exactly identical to
  the four-repeat run (same observations, masks, and candidate action keys),
  and the two runs' first four chance seeds match. With eight repeats, 39
  states had enough variation to score ranking; mean within-state Spearman was
  +0.22 (95% team-cluster bootstrap interval +0.10 to +0.34). Split by
  opponent, the policy-response subset was +0.31 (+0.17 to +0.43; 19
  informative states), while Max Damage was +0.14 (-0.05 to +0.33; 20 states).
  This is a modest ranking signal, not a measured full-match strength gain.
  The run used 5,656 matches in 648.4 seconds (8.72 matches/s), with 17 games
  ending before Turn 5 and zero rejected actions. Report:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_action_ranking_audit_128x1_step5_8chance_20261028/ranking_summary.json`.

  A separate Max-Damage-only sample captured 117 states from 128 clusters and
  ran 5,720 matches in 549.3 seconds (10.41 matches/s), with 11 early
  finishes and zero rejected actions. With eight repeats, 37 states were
  informative; mean within-state Spearman was +0.246 (95% cluster interval
  +0.106 to +0.379). Replacing both slots with Max Damage gained +2.88 points
  locally (95% interval -0.75 to +6.73). The slot-1-only hybrid gained +3.10
  points (+0.11 to +6.53) while the slot-0-only hybrid was -0.11 points
  (-3.32 to +3.10). Since several candidate variants were examined, treat the
  slot-1 estimate as hypothesis-generating, not confirmed. Report:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_action_ranking_maxdamage_128x1_step5_8chance_20261028/ranking_summary.json`.

  Tested that slot-1 hypothesis in a P1-only screen of 256 complete headless
  Showdown matches against Max Damage, paired on the same 256 team clusters
  (229 reached Turn 5). Raw policy scored 33.98%; replacing only slot 1 scored 35.55%, a +1.56
  point delta with a 95% cluster interval of -0.78 to +3.91. Among games that
  reached the decision, the gain was +1.75 points (-0.87 to +4.37). Six of
  229 proposed hybrids were rejected by Showdown because the slot choices
  formed an invalid joint order; they safely fell back to the policy pair or
  another strictly legal pair. No action submission failed. Thus the local
  slot-1 effect did not confirm as a complete-match improvement. Continue with
  a closed-sheet response matrix and side-swapped evaluation before policy
  training. Report:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_step5_maxdamage_slot1_vs_maxdamage_256x1_20261028/report.json`.

  A fresh Max-Damage-only action-ranking set captured 117 states (11 of 128
  games ended before Turn 5), used eight chance repeats, and completed 5,720
  matches in 549.3 seconds (10.41 matches/s). Thirty-seven states had outcome
  variation sufficient for correlation; mean within-state Spearman was +0.246
  (95% cluster interval +0.106 to +0.379). The policy's sampled candidate
  rankings therefore contain some positive signal even against Max Damage,
  but these 37 informative states are still too few to establish a stable
  training target. The policy action's median gap to the best sampled
  alternative was zero; the 7.6-point mean gap is upward biased by choosing
  the best and evaluating it on the same repeats. Full summary:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_action_ranking_maxdamage_128x1_step5_8chance_20261028/ranking_summary.json`.

- **Opening-matrix information leak audit (2026-10-28):** the two fresh
  Round173 equilibrium-matrix runs produced positive paired full-match deltas
  in both seats, but the matrix builder read the simulated opponent's actual
  policy and Max Damage actions from its full private set. The resulting
  equilibrium mix therefore depended on unrevealed opponent moves, items, and
  abilities. These are privileged diagnostic outcomes, not legal closed-sheet
  performance evidence; do not promote the selector or count its gains toward
  strength criteria. The script also incorrectly reported a closed-sheet
  information-boundary string; the source metadata has since been corrected.
  Reports remain useful
  only to quantify the privileged upper bound: P1 deltas were +6.64 points vs
  Max Damage, +3.91 vs Round166, +8.20 vs Round136 and Round175; P2 deltas were
  +4.30, +5.08, +8.20, and +5.08 respectively, on 128 clusters per seat.
  Matrix generation took about 1.63 seconds/state and 8.7 games/s end to end.
  A legal follow-up must generate responses from public-only policies and
  sampled hidden-set/roster hypotheses, as in `src/search/local_showdown.py`,
  and must verify the selector's input provenance before reporting strength.
  The evaluator's report metadata has been corrected to say
  `privileged_diagnostic`; older JSON reports retain their original, inaccurate
  information-boundary string and must not be trusted for that field.
  Privileged reports:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_opening_equilibrium_p1_fresh_128x8_deploy2_heldout_20261028/report.json`
  and
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_opening_equilibrium_p2_fresh_128x8_deploy2_heldout_20261028/report.json`.

- **Legal hidden-world opening-search budget screen (2026-10-28):** ran
  Round173 with Round94 team preview on identical 256 episodes/seeds against
  Max Damage. The baseline scored 119/256 (46.48%). Legal learned search with
  two hidden-set hypotheses, 12 selected-roster hypotheses per set, four
  candidates per side, and four chance samples scored 118/256 (46.09%); paired
  change was -0.39 points (95% episode-bootstrap interval -6.64 to +5.86).
  It had no invalid actions or search fallbacks, but averaged 3.56 seconds of
  search latency, 1,536 turn advances per game, and 0.27 games/s, versus 10.63
  games/s for the policy. Profiling attributed about 2.35 seconds to search
  subprocess simulation and 1.20 seconds to frontier processing (0.21 seconds
  of that was model inference).
  A reduced budget (one hidden-set hypothesis, four candidates, one chance
  sample; 12 combined hidden worlds) produced the same 118/256 wins on these
  seeds, with a paired baseline delta of -0.39 points (interval -6.25 to
  +5.86). It reduced mean search latency to 0.52 seconds and raised throughput
  to 1.61 games/s; compared with full-budget search it used 8x fewer simulated
  advances and selected the same action in 209/256 states. Full-budget and
  reduced-budget match outcomes differed on 16/256 pairs, split evenly 8–8.
  Against legal public-only Counterplay on another 256 episodes, the reduced
  budget scored 121/256 versus 109/256 for policy alone (+4.69 points; paired
  interval -1.17 to +10.55), also inconclusive; it averaged 0.51-second search
  latency and 1.53 games/s. Thus reducing sampling substantially improves
  throughput without a detectable Max Damage loss in this screen, but no
  strength gain is established and chance-sample quality remains uncertain.
  Both evaluations were P1-only with fixed continuation policies and no seat
  swap. Keep search experimental pending fresh-seed and P2 validation. Reports:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_legal_opening_search_maxdamage_256matched_20261028/paired_comparison.json`,
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_legal_opening_search_budget1_256matched_20261028/paired_comparison.json`,
  and
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_legal_opening_search_budget1_publiccp_256matched_20261028/paired_comparison.json`.

- **Fresh seat-balanced Max Damage confirmation (2026-10-28):** repeated the
  one-world/one-chance-sample legal opening-search comparison using the newer
  Round174 value checkpoint on a fresh seed with 256 paired matches from each
  seat. Round173 without search won 101/256
  from P1 (39.45%) and 108/256 from P2 (42.19%). Search won 107/256 from P1
  (41.80%) and 111/256 from P2 (43.36%). The equal-seat paired gain was only
  +1.76 points (seat-stratified episode-bootstrap 95% interval -2.54 to
  +6.05), with no search failures or policy fallbacks. Mean search latency was
  0.52 seconds per decision, p95 0.65 seconds, and throughput was 1.60
  games/s versus 9.43 games/s for the policy. This confirms that the ~40%
  result is reproducible on a fresh sample; the search improvement is
  inconclusive and does not justify promotion or more search compute. Raw logs,
  records, and the seat-balanced summary are in
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_budget1_fresh_seatbalanced_256_20261028/`.

- **Candidate-budget follow-up (2026-10-28):** checked whether expanding the
  current legal opening matrix from four to eight candidates breaks the
  plateau. On 64 matched episode seeds per seat/config against Max Damage,
  Round173 without search won 62/128 (48.44%), while four-candidate and
  eight-candidate search each won 51/128 (39.84%). The paired search-minus-
  baseline delta was -8.59 percentage points for either budget (seat-stratified
  episode bootstrap 95% interval [-17.19, 0.00]); eight versus four candidates
  was 0.00 points ([-4.69, +3.91]). Treat this small screen as diagnostic, not
  a reliable strength estimate. Search had no fallbacks or invalid actions, but
  reduced throughput from 8.89-9.46 games/s to 1.55-1.57 games/s at budget 4
  and 0.54 games/s at budget 8. Median/p95 adapter latency was 524/658 ms and
  1,711/2,166 ms respectively. Increasing the candidate budget therefore has
  no demonstrated benefit and costs roughly 3.5x to 17x throughput. Stop
  spending compute on wider search until the value/action ranking is validated
  or improved. Current measured speed is about 9 games/s for raw policy
  evaluation; opening search is the dominant decision-time bottleneck. Search
  reduced throughput by about 5.7x at budget 4 and 17.5x at budget 8.
  Results: `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_search_candidate_budget4_vs8_64_seatbalanced_20261028/paired_comparison.json`.
  **Public Counterplay head-to-head (2026-10-28):** evaluated Round173 against
  the information-safe public-only Counterplay policy on 256 held-out team-pair
  clusters, two repeats, and both seats (1,024 complete games). Round173 scored
  456/1,024 = 44.53%, with a team-pair cluster-bootstrap 95% interval of
  39.75%-49.22%; there were no timeouts, errors, or action adjustments. The
  aggregate rate was 9.02 games/s on eight workers. This shows Round173 does
  not clearly beat this public heuristic; it does not by itself explain the
  Max Damage result or establish that the heuristic is robust against other
  opponents. It complements, but is not directly comparable to, the separate
  66.70% public-Counterplay-versus-Max-Damage result. Report:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_vs_public_counterplay_1024_20261028_retry2/paired_summary.json`.
  **Interpretation:** public-only Counterplay is a serious benchmark, but not
  an established teacher. Counterplay-only scored 43.07% against the
  Round136-gated Round173 incumbent (paired delta -5.47 points, 95% interval
  -9.28 to -1.76); a 50/50 Round173-Counterplay mixture pilot was inconclusive.
  Round175's 20k-game mix update improved only +0.88 points against Max Damage
  (95% interval -1.37 to +3.22). Do not repeat the Counterplay teacher or
  Round175 mixture recipe. Keep Counterplay as a held-out benchmark and use
  public-player-view counterfactuals for diagnosis until a distinct training
  target demonstrates paired transfer.

- **Round173 loss-action audit (2026-10-28):** analyzed all 512 baseline matches
  from that seat-balanced screen using the policy's recorded legal masks,
  actions, and public-information damage features. The policy won 209/512
  (40.82%), averaging 8.52 decisions per match. Of 5,114 selected move-slot
  decisions, the selected action's estimated damage was more than 0.05 below
  the best legal individual move's estimate in 33.5%. This rate was 33.1% in
  won games and 33.7% in lost games. It missed the highest estimated KO
  pressure on 381/1,389 high-KO opportunity decisions (27.4%); the rate was
  27.8% in wins and 27.0% in losses. These rough, public-species-based
  features do not measure full move value and cannot prove causality, but they
  provide no evidence that a simple maximize-damage correction explains the
  plateau. Continue to treat the cause as unresolved. Detailed metrics are in
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_budget1_fresh_seatbalanced_256_20261028/policy_loss_action_audit.json`.

- **Opening counterfactuals and first ranker attempt (2026-10-28):** updated
  `collect_opening_action_counterfactuals.py` to accept the frozen team-preview
  selector, then evaluated policy, Max Damage, both slot hybrids, and random
  legal joint actions with four repeated outcomes per action. At 48 fresh team
  pairs, Max Damage's opening action gained 9.38 points over the policy action
  (95% cluster interval +0.52 to +18.23). A 128-pair confirmation gave 38.87%
  for policy and 45.90% for Max Damage's opening action, a paired +7.03 points
  (95% interval +0.20 to +13.67). The one-slot hybrids gained 3.71–4.30 points
  but their intervals included zero. This isolates a possible opening-action
  weakness against this specific opponent class; it is not robust-strength
  evidence, since continuations stayed fixed and the alternatives were scored
  only against Max Damage. Collection ran at 11.88–12.17 full matches/s. Data
  are in `round173_opening_counterfactual_selector_48x4_20261028/` and
  `round173_opening_counterfactual_selector_128x4_20261028/`.

  Trained an experimental pairwise action ranker from the 128-pair data using
  the existing Round173 policy as its initialization. On 26 held-out team
  clusters, pairwise accuracy was 57.0% before training and 56.7% after the
  larger learning-rate run; pairwise loss fell from 4.782 to 4.588, but
  end-to-end behavior barely changed. In fresh 256-match comparisons, the
  lower-rate candidate changed the opening action in only 3/256 matches per
  condition. Its paired win-rate changes were -0.78 points vs Max Damage in
  both seats, -1.17 vs public-only Counterplay from P1, and 0.00 from P2; all
  intervals included zero. Do not promote this candidate. This exposes a gap
  between counterfactual action preferences and useful policy updates; more
  Max Damage-only training is not the next step. The ranker reports and
  evaluations are in
  `round173_opening_counterfactual_ranker_128x4_20261028/` and
  `round173_opening_ranker_fullmatch_256_20261028/`.

- **Mixed-opponent counterfactuals and robust-ranker screen (2026-10-28):**
  extended the collector to evaluate each candidate against Max Damage,
  public-only Counterplay, and frozen Round166 policy responses, with four
  chance repeats per candidate and identical player-view opening states. Across
  96 team pairs, the Max Damage opening action changed its paired win rate by
  +0.5 points against Max Damage (95% cluster interval -6.5 to +7.6), +5.7
  against public-only Counterplay (+0.3 to +11.5), and +0.8 against Round166
  (-6.5 to +7.8). Its equal-opponent-mixture gain was +2.3 points (-2.2 to
  +6.8). This does not replicate the earlier +7.0-point Max Damage-only
  opening result; that earlier gain is seed-sensitive. The random legal
  candidates lost about 9.9 points against the mixture, confirming that the
  baseline policy is materially better than unstructured action choice.
  Collection completed 5,532 matches in 616.8 seconds (8.97 games/s). Data:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_counterfactual_mixed_opponents_96x4_20261028/data.json`.

  Trained the robust-dominance objective only on preferences consistent across
  all three opponent classes. It used 76 training and 20 held-out team
  clusters. Validation pairwise loss improved only from 2.019 to 2.012 while
  accuracy fell from 71.6% to 69.5%. In fresh 128-match full-match comparisons
  from each seat, equal-weighted over both seats and all three opponents, the
  candidate changed win rate by -1.04 points (95% stratified interval -2.86 to
  +0.78). It tied the parent versus Max Damage, fell 2.34 points versus
  Counterplay from each seat, and had mixed results versus Round166. It changed
  the opening action in 13–14% of cases but produced no measured strength gain;
  do not promote it. Reports and match records:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round173_counterfactual_robust_ranker_96x4_20261028/`
  and

- **Clarification on the “~40%” score (2026-10-28):** the fresh ~40% result

- **Why the raw policy remains near 40% against Max Damage:** the latest raw
  Round173 result is 43.07%, but this is not simply a shortage of training
  games. Repeated PPO, broad and narrow action imitation, and an outcome-trained
  action scorer have not produced a statistically dependable full-match gain.
  The strongest causal signal so far is action selection: a state-dependent
  immediate-damage gate raised Round173 to 57.03% against Max Damage, but it
  reduced performance against Counterplay from 40.63% to 32.62%. That shows a
  matchup-specific exploit, not robust play. Do not scale another PPO run with
  the same policy labels or promote the damage gate as a general solution.
- **Active bottleneck:** convert observed state and joint-action consequences
  into reliable closed-sheet move choices across opponent responses. Current
  search pruning is heuristic, its response columns may omit Max Damage's
  selected action, and its equilibrium diagnostics cover only a restricted
  action matrix. The search frontier can use a learned value model, but prior
  search evaluations still fell below raw-policy performance. Also, the
  apparently promising midgame oracle experiment used the other player's
  private action and is not valid agent performance. More data or more chance
  samples alone are not justified until action ranking improves on held-out
  states and then transfers to complete matches.
- **Next acceptance gate:** do not repeat the Round175 PPO recipe or use the
  standalone opening payoff-matrix results as legal evidence. The fresh,
  seat-balanced reduced-search screen is complete and inconclusive. Mixed
  opening counterfactuals and a robust scalar ranker are also complete; neither
  produced a repeatable policy gain. Do not run another PPO cycle or fit
  another scalar ranker to the same restricted action set. The next step is to
  extend the legal candidate generator with strategically distinct joint
  actions, including switches, Protect, setup, redirection, and defensive
  choices, and compare them against a response set sampled from public-only
  policies and hidden-set hypotheses. Build a compact payoff matrix from
  repeated chance outcomes, then compare deterministic maximin choices with
  regret-matched mixed choices. Keep policy input player-view-only; score
  candidate quality on held-out team clusters and complete matches. Keep the
  Round173 first-five hybrid as a distinct reference alongside raw Round173.
  Its gain clears 50% versus Max Damage and transfers to public-only
  Counterplay, but the symmetric Round102 interval permits a material loss;
  keep it experimental. Test both seats against additional frozen policies
  with selectors matched before deciding whether to deploy it broadly. For the next
  diagnostic, stratify the first-five interventions by state and action
  category (including target choice, switching, Protect, and damage
  allocation). Opening traces now show that both move choice and target
  allocation differ frequently from the teacher; use these as separate
  diagnostic strata, not as action-cloning labels. Then test a learned/legal
  replacement on held-out clusters.
  Promote only after paired full-match gains transfer across the pool without
  a material worst-opponent regression.
  Extend search into midgame or distill searched actions only after those
  action-ranking checks show stable legal gains. Report match-level
  intervals, action corrections, per-opponent throughput, and
  information-boundary checks before promotion.
- **Current throughput reference:** the latest paired mixture evaluation
  achieved 19.85 complete matches/s with eight isolated workers when replaying
  identical seeds and teams; prior serial throughput was 3.20 matches/s. The
  recent Round173 gate screen ran at 8.44–8.58 games/s with eight workers.
  These are different workloads and should not be conflated. The current
  More recent single-process headless rates are directly comparable with each
  other: Round173 alone achieved 10.63 games/s, reduced legal search achieved
  1.61 games/s against Max Damage and 1.53 against public Counterplay, while
  full 2-world/4-sample search achieved 0.27 games/s. Reduced-budget opening
  search took about 0.52 seconds per decision versus 3.56 seconds for full
  budget. Do not combine these with eight-worker server evaluations or
  training throughput. The bottleneck is now both decision quality and search
  latency, while raw simulation throughput remains important for scaling.

## Latest status and speed reading (2026-10-28)

- **Midgame joint-action replay and response-matrix pilot (2026-10-27):**
  extended the headless runner to capture both players' observations, legal
  masks, policy actions, and Max Damage actions at a chosen midgame decision,
  and to force a joint action at that decision while replaying the same
  deterministic prefix. The new pilot evaluated a restricted matrix of policy,
  Max Damage, and two slot-hybrid actions at decision steps 1 and 5 against
  Round136-policy and Max-Damage responses. It completed 309 matches at about
  8.0–8.9 matches/s, with zero replay mismatches and zero rejected profiles.
  Only 17 of 32 requested decision states were available (some matches ended
  or had a forced/wait state before the target decision). The matrix selector
  did not improve the one-match deployment outcome over the unchanged policy
  in these tiny pilot samples; held-out matrix outcomes also showed no
  dependable gain. Do not scale this variant yet. More importantly, this is an
  oracle diagnostic: the P1 matrix mix uses P2's private policy action and
  legal/max-damage action. Its score cannot count as closed-sheet agent
  performance or be used directly at runtime. Any follow-up must replace that
  response input with beliefs over plausible hidden teams and legal responses,
  or use the outputs only as aggregated labels from multiple hidden worlds.
  The repository already has this closed-sheet foundation in
  `src/belief/closed_sheet.py` and `src/search/local_showdown.py`: sampled
  hidden-set worlds, public revealed-fact conditioning, legal response columns,
  and maximin/equilibrium selection. Future work should improve that path's
  midgame payoff/frontier quality and measured strength instead of duplicating
  its belief sampler.
  Artifacts:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/midgame_joint_matrix_oracle_8x2x4_step1_20261027/report.json`
  and
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/midgame_joint_matrix_oracle_8x2x4_step5_20261027/report.json`.
  Runner changes are in `scripts/run_headless_showdown_self_play.py`; the
  diagnostic driver is `scripts/evaluate_midgame_joint_payoff_matrix.py`.

  starting large training or corpus-generation jobs.

  deterministic Round156 gate ablation independently shows that action choice
  is the problem: its public immediate-damage gate raised the same policy from
  42.68% to 56.05% against Max Damage. Since broad action imitation already
  regressed (Rounds159–160) and narrow intervention imitation did not help

  clusters, six or fewer legal joint-action candidates per state, and four

  was only +0.29 points (95% interval -0.39 to +0.98), with zero action
  corrections or protocol errors. Thus better preference loss did not transfer

  the Round165 selector baseline, Round166 plus the same selector scored
  38.48% (197/512 wins), versus 38.28% for Round165 (196/512). The paired
  improvement was only +0.20 percentage points (team-cluster bootstrap 95%
  interval -2.93 to +3.13), so this PPO update did not establish a battle-policy
  gain. Both arms had zero timeouts/errors and zero action adjustments. Full
  local-server evaluation ran at 1.41 games/s for Round166. The selector's
  separate +7.42-point preview gain remains useful, but optimizing the battle
  policy under it has not yet moved the result. Round166 is not promoted over
  Round165. The immediate next diagnostic is a matched first-turn Max Damage
  action intervention with selector-controlled previews, to test whether the
  remaining gap is concentrated in opening move choice before choosing the next
  policy-training change. Reproduction:
  `scripts/train_round166_round165_preview_selector_20k.sh`.
  Training, records, and evaluation summaries are in
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/direct_policy_round166_round165_preview_selector_maxdamage75_counterplay12p5_policy12p5_ppo10_20261027/`
  and
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round166_selector_preview_vs_maxdamage_256pairs_20261027/`.

- **Why play is stuck near 40% against Max Damage (2026-10-27 diagnosis):** the
  recent raw PPO updates (Rounds 163–165) all landed around 42–44% on paired
  1,024-game evaluations and none established improvement. Changing optimizer
  strength or removing the damage gate did not move the result. The follow-up
  search experiments also failed to beat raw Round165: best point result was
  28.91% versus 30.86% on the 256-game search schedule, while wide search was
  about 6.8x slower per complete game. The search's reported low exploitability
  is only for its pruned 5x4 action matrix; it does not mean the full legal game
  is near equilibrium. Current candidate pruning uses simple move-power/action
  class heuristics, and the opponent candidate set is not guaranteed to include
  the actual Max Damage response. The matrix frontier then scores outcomes with
  a state value model trained on sampled policy play, rather than a validated
  estimate of each joint action's eventual win probability. Thus a low matrix
  exploitability can coexist with poor full-game decisions. Search changes
  actions frequently but has not improved results, so expanding chance samples
  or depth before validating action rankings would spend compute without a
  demonstrated strength gain.

  **Next diagnostic gate:** continue the action-level audit beyond the opening:
  save representative early and midgame states and compare policy, search, and
  Max Damage actions under shared opponent responses and RNG seeds. Validate
  candidate coverage and action legality, then measure continuation win rate.
  In parallel, audit whether the historical `pilot_clean` 96.2% result used the
  same format, opponent implementation, team pool, seat balance, and outcome
  handling as current runs; until matched, it is not a reliable baseline.

- **Opening-action intervention and Round167 training (2026-10-27):** the
  matched first-turn counterfactual has isolated a concrete policy weakness.
  Across 1,024 held-out team-pair clusters, Round166's opening action scored
  42.29%; replacing only that joint opening action with Max Damage's action,
  while keeping the Round94 team selector and all later play fixed, scored
  46.88%. The paired improvement was +4.59 percentage points (95% cluster
  interval +1.56 to +7.62), and the replacement changed 936/1,024 opening
  actions. The 2,048 local headless games ran at 12.03 games/s with no errors.
  This establishes that the baseline opening action is weak on these sampled
  matchups; it does not establish Max Damage as an optimal teacher.

  Round167 tests a conservative response: 12.5% of Max Damage episodes use Max
  Damage only for the policy player's opening joint action; those overridden
  rows are excluded from PPO's policy-gradient loss and receive a 0.1-weight
  teacher loss. Other episodes and all later actions remain policy generated.
  The Round94 frozen team selector is applied in all games. A one-game smoke
  rollout confirmed the action is legal and recorded as a teacher action.
  Training completed in 780.0 seconds: 394.8 seconds rollout, 173.1 seconds
  PPO preparation, and 385.2 seconds optimization. The rollout generated
  158,838 transitions at 50.7 aggregate games/s across eight workers, with
  7.94 average CPU cores and 7.79 GiB peak aggregate RSS. Lossless compression
  reduced the 3.43 GB rollout set to 191.3 MB. PPO stopped at the KL limit
  after 1,729 optimizer steps (5.56 equivalent passes), with KL 0.02699 and
  clip fraction 21.92%.

  The paired 256-team-pair local-server evaluation scored 37.70% (193/512)
  versus Round166's 38.48% on the exact same teams and previews. The paired
  team-cluster delta was -0.78 points, with a 95% interval [-4.88, +3.32];
  this does not establish a regression or an improvement. There were zero
  timeouts and action adjustments. The training intervention did not show a
  gain at this sample size, despite the positive opening-action
  counterfactual. This experiment exposes a teacher-transfer problem: forcing
  the better opening action can help immediately, but a small imitation slice
  did not yet make the learned policy better overall. Round167 is not promoted.

  The next evaluation is testing the opening intervention directly on local
  Showdown, in both player seats, with Round166 and the same team selector.
  This separates whether the headless counterfactual transfers to full local
  server play from whether PPO can learn that behavior. Outputs:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/direct_policy_round167_round166_opening_teacher12p5_maxdamage75_counterplay12p5_policy12p5_ppo10_20261027/`,
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round167_opening_teacher_vs_maxdamage_256pairs_20261027/`,
  and current in-progress direct-intervention output at
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round166_opening_maxdamage_override_vs_maxdamage_256pairs_20261027/`.

- **Round165 team-preview selector transfer test (2026-10-27):** clarified an
  evaluation-label ambiguity: the previously cited 43.46% Round165 result was
  Round165 versus another learned checkpoint in a paired comparison, not
  Round165 versus Max Damage. On a fresh 256-team-pair, side-swapped local
  Showdown evaluation against Max Damage, Round165 with random preview scored
  30.86% over 512 complete games (158 wins, 354 losses). Adding the existing
  Round94 team-preview selector scored 38.28% on the exact same team pairs and
  seeds (196 wins, 316 losses). The paired gain was +7.42 percentage points
  (team-pair bootstrap 95% interval +0.98 to +13.67); the selector changed
  preview choice in 253/256 pairs. Both arms had zero timeouts, protocol errors,
  or invalid-action corrections. The local-server evaluation rate was about
  1.5 complete games/s, versus 50.4 aggregate rollout games/s in the headless
  training runner; full-match local-server evaluation is currently the
  evaluation throughput bottleneck. This is transfer evidence that team
  selection explains a material part of the apparent plateau, not evidence
  that battle play is solved. Use Round165 plus the Round94 selector as the
  current measured challenger, and include the selector in subsequent training
  and evaluation comparisons. Files are under
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round165_random_preview_vs_maxdamage_256pairs_20261027/`
  and
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round165_selector_preview_vs_maxdamage_256pairs_20261027/`.

- **Round163 check and next experiment (2026-10-27):** the second 20,000-game

  transitions at 53.7 aggregate rollout games/s across eight workers. Peak

  182.4 MB. Record preparation (~164 s) and PPO optimization (~142 s) together
  took about as long as rollout generation (~373 s), so rollout simulation is

  Thus the 40%-range raw policy is still stuck, and Round163 did not improve the

  not training loss alone.
- **Round164 higher-update ablation (2026-10-27):** doubled the learning rate

  Rollout throughput was 53.3 games/s aggregate across eight workers, peak RSS

  Gated Round164 scored 56.54% versus Round136 gated 56.93% (difference -0.39;

- **Current measured rates:** Round164 rollout generation was 53.3 aggregate

- **Round165 raw-action PPO (2026-10-27):** trained 20,000 games without the

  Fresh paired raw and gated evaluations against Round164 ran on seed

  Round164 raw 43.54%; the paired difference was 0.00 points (95% team-cluster
  interval -2.05 to +2.05; 511 complete paired observations because Round164
  had one timeout). Gated Round165 scored 57.81% versus Round164's 57.62%, a

- **Search strength smoke versus raw policy (2026-10-27):** on the same 32
  single-player team seeds, a single post-opening equilibrium search per match
  scored 7/32 (21.9%) versus 9/32 (28.1%) for raw Round165. The paired point
  difference was -6.25 percentage points, with a very wide team-seed bootstrap
  interval (-18.75 to +6.25). This is too small to establish a strength change,
  but it gives no reason to promote search yet. Search ran at 3.85 complete
  games/s on one worker with 0.169 s mean action-selection time; it must be
  evaluated over a larger paired sample and at matched decision-time budgets.
- **One-turn equilibrium search evaluation (2026-10-27):** scaled the smoke to
  256 deterministic same-seed matches against Max Damage, with one post-opening
  simultaneous matrix search per match, one hidden world, four candidates per
  side, and one chance sample. Search scored 62/256 (24.22%) versus raw
  Round165's 79/256 (30.86%). The paired difference was -6.64 points, with a
  team-seed bootstrap 95% interval of -10.94 to -2.34; 223 seeds tied, 25
  favored raw play, and eight favored search. Search changed the policy action
  in 184/256 cases; four cases fell back because the public preview included a
  possible Illusion user. Neither arm needed action adjustments. Search ran at
  4.65 complete games/s versus 9.88 for raw play in this single-worker
  comparison, and mean action-selection time rose from 0.036 s to 0.144 s per match.
  This rejects the current search configuration for promotion. It used the old
  Round94 frontier model and very shallow chance/hidden-world coverage, so the
  result diagnoses the present search setup, not all equilibrium search. A
  recent-policy frontier model has since been trained and compared; its
  detailed validation and follow-up search ablation are recorded below. Continue
  search work only with matched seeds and decision-time budgets.
- **Round165 self-play value-model comparison (2026-10-27):** trained from
  scratch on recent, perspective-safe Round165 trajectories, using roster-held
  splits: 156,701 training states, 32,423 calibration states, and 67,583
  held-out states; the best checkpoint was epoch 2. Its held-out Brier score was
  0.1594, versus 0.2500 for a constant 50% predictor, and held-out ECE was
  0.0055. However, on the same held-out cache Round94 scored better Brier
  (0.1551 vs 0.1594), accuracy (76.54% vs 75.44%), and log loss (0.4676 vs
  0.4790). Paired cluster intervals show significantly worse Brier
  (+0.0025 to +0.0061) and accuracy (-1.54 to -0.67 points) for the new model;
  the ECE difference (-0.0103 to +0.0026) includes zero. Keep Round94 as the
  stronger general predictor and retain the Round165 model only for search
  ablations.
- **Updated frontier search ablation (2026-10-27):** on the same 256 seeds,
  replacing Round94 with the Round165 value model improved the one-world,
  one-chance search point score from 24.22% to 27.34%, but remained below raw
  Round165 at 30.86%. The direct new-vs-old search difference was +3.13 points
  (95% interval -0.39 to +6.64), so that uplift is uncertain. Expanding to two
  hidden worlds and four chance samples with Round165's model scored 28.91%
  versus raw 30.86% (paired -1.95 points; interval -5.08 to +1.17). It required
  about 40,096 simulated turn advances for 256 one-decision games, ran at 1.46
  games/s, and used 0.613 s mean action-selection time per match. This is much
  slower than raw play at 9.88 games/s and still has no proven strength gain.
  Four cases fell back because possible Illusion users prevent safe hidden-team
  construction. A matched wider search using Round94's frontier scored 25.78%
  versus raw 30.86% (paired -5.08; interval -9.77 to -0.39). The newer
  Round165 value model exceeded Round94's wide-search result by +3.13 points,
  but the interval (-0.78 to +7.03) still includes zero. Thus recent-policy
  training may improve the action ranking used by this search despite weaker
  global Brier score, but that effect is unconfirmed. Neither search version
  is promoted. The immediate next priority is to diagnose candidate generation
  and search/frontier ranking errors before adding more samples or depth; the
  current wide search costs roughly seven times the raw-policy match latency.

- **Round162 on-policy gated PPO (2026-10-27):** found and corrected a
  training-probability mismatch. Earlier gate rollouts stored the executed
  action with the log-probability of the actor's pre-gate proposal, then
  removed those rows from PPO and tried imitation. Round162 now keeps the
  proposal as PPO's sampled action while the actual battle executes the gate's
  action; reward and value targets therefore come from the resulting gated
  match. A 32-match smoke produced 145 overrides, passed all 64
  closed-sheet perspective checks, and replayed 228 transitions with initial
  approximate KL 3.36e-6. The 20,000-game run took 723.3 seconds total:
  371.6 seconds rollouts (53.8 aggregate games/s across eight workers), 164.7
  seconds record preparation, and about 142 seconds for PPO. It processed
  147,112 transitions over five passes at final KL 0.00551; peak aggregate RSS
  was 8.0 GiB.
- Round162 raw scored 40.14% in 1,024 held-out, side-swapped Max Damage games
  (8.43 aggregate games/s), so it did not break the raw-policy plateau. With
  the gate enabled, it scored 51.95% and made 4,211 overrides. Round136 with
  the gate scored 51.76% on the exact same seed/team schedule. Paired by 256
  team clusters, Round162 gained 0.20 percentage points (95% bootstrap
  interval 0.00 to +0.49); 254 clusters tied, two favored Round162, none
  favored Round136. This is not a measurable strength gain. There were zero
  action adjustments, timeouts, or errors. Keep Round136 as the stable
  incumbent and continue the corrected on-policy update for one controlled
  iteration before deciding whether this training signal helps.
- The training summary initially omitted the gate override total even though
  per-match records contained it; the runner now aggregates that count. Round162
  override totals were confirmed from raw records and independently from the
  4,211-override held-out evaluation.

- **Latest checkpoint still has not broken the ~40% Max Damage plateau.** The
  most recent no-oracle Round156 screen was 40.33% over 1,024 games. The
  immediate-damage action gate is a separate useful intervention (about 56%
  in its matched evaluation), but it has not yet transferred into the
  ungated learned policy. PPO teacher replay and direct behavior cloning
  regressed, so do not promote those runs as progress.
- **Chance-averaged action-value experiment (2026-10-27):** collected 87
  usable fifth-decision states from 96 generated team clusters, using four
  common future RNG seeds per candidate action (1,520 full matches total).
  Collection ran at 9.55 complete matches/s. At these states, taking the Max
  Damage action scored 43.68% versus 38.22% for the policy action; paired
  difference +5.46 points (team-cluster 95% interval +1.72 to +9.77). This is
  an action-level diagnostic, not a new complete-match win rate.
- A held-out action scorer trained on those samples improved Brier score over
  a constant predictor (0.258 vs 0.288), but its test set contained only 17
  team clusters. On a fresh 128-cluster full-match evaluation, using the
  scorer at decision five reduced overall performance from 42.97% to 38.28%
  (paired -4.69 points; interval -9.38 to 0.00); among games reaching that
  decision it fell from 39.32% to 34.19% (-5.13 points; -10.26 to 0.00).
  Therefore this action model does not generalize and is not promoted. The
  initial bottleneck hypothesis was sparse, noisy labels; the larger follow-up
  below shows that more labels alone do not solve action ranking. Next work should
  investigate why the gate helps while imitation and learned action scoring
  fail, then confirm candidate improvements in independent complete matches.
- **Current speed reading:** the largest counterfactual data path ran at 9.45
  full matches/s in one worker; the full-match selector evaluation ran at
  9.14 matches/s. The earlier eight-worker PPO rollout benchmark was
  47.7 aggregate games/s (see Round156 below); that rate is not directly
  comparable because it uses different rollout work. Decision-level action
  label generation is expensive because each state/action/chance sample
  requires a complete replay. Do not scale this collection to millions of
  matches until the candidate-selection method passes full-match validation.
- **Larger chance-averaged follow-up (2026-10-27):** expanded to 256 team
  clusters and eight common future RNG seeds per action: 235 usable decision
  states, 938 unique state/action rows, 7,504 binary outcomes, and 8,029 full
  matches in 849.8 seconds (9.45 matches/s). The Max Damage action beat the
  policy action at that sampled decision by +6.01 points (cluster-bootstrap
  95% interval +3.19 to +9.04). The larger action scorer reduced held-out
  action-outcome Brier from the constant baseline's 0.247 to 0.164, but its
  47-state holdout selected actions at only +1.33 points (interval -1.60 to
  +4.52). Fresh full-match validation on 256 new team clusters rejected it:
  overall 42.19% versus 43.36% for the policy (paired -1.17 points, -4.30 to
  +1.95), and against Max Damage specifically 34.38% versus 37.50% (-3.13,
  -7.81 to +0.78). Do not deploy or distill this scorer. More data improved
  probability prediction but did not yield better actions; the unresolved
  bottleneck is converting tactical state/action information into robust
  rankings, not simply label count or randomness variance.
- **Pairwise action-ranking follow-up (2026-10-27):** trained a within-state
  pairwise ranker on the same 235-state, eight-chance-seed dataset, comparing
  actions from matched continuations rather than fitting standalone win
  probabilities. The held-out state selector was +3.99 points (47 clusters;
  interval -0.80 to +10.11), still uncertain. On 256 new full-match team
  clusters it scored 40.23% vs 41.80% for the policy overall (-1.56 points;
  interval -4.69 to +1.17), and 31.25% vs 32.81% against Max Damage (-1.56;
  -5.47 to +2.34). This does not establish harm, but provides no dependable
  gain. Do not promote the ranker. Two distinct learned selectors now fail to
  improve fresh-match results despite better held-out predictive metrics.

- **Independent hybrid confirmation did not replicate (2026-10-27):** on 128
  new team clusters and four matched seeds per opening, policy scored 36.52%,

  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/midgame_counterfactual_round156_p1decision5_64x2_20261027/data.json` and
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/midgame_maxdamage_confirmation_round156_p1decision5_128x1_20261027/data.json`.
  Throughput was 11.71 and 12.61 complete matches/s, respectively.
- **Current speed/bottleneck (2026-10-27):** the multi-action opening
  counterfactual workload completed 2,454 full headless Showdown matches in
  213.6 seconds: 11.49 complete games/s. The measured throughput limit is

- The evaluator now has the private opponent-action oracle disabled by default;
  it forces counterplay priors to zero for policy inference and rejects
  policy-opponent prediction requests unless an explicit diagnostic-only flag

  counterplay baseline also remains separate from the legacy privileged path.
- **Strongest diagnostic so far:** an immediate-damage action gate applied at
  decision time raised Round136 from 39.65% to 56.93% against Max Damage
  (+17.29 points paired; 95% interval +13.67 to +20.80). This shows that many
  losses involve tactical action selection. It does not establish robust or
  near-optimal play: the gate only uses an immediate damage score and has not
  been shown to improve all opponent matchups.
- **Closed-sheet audit of the 69% counterplay number (2026-10-27):** reran the
  support-aware counterplay heuristic for 1,024 side-swapped complete games.
  It again scored 69.14% (95% normal interval 66.31%-71.97%), at 13.89
  aggregate games/s, with zero incomplete games or action adjustments. Source
  inspection then showed that this heuristic receives the other player's
  private `opponent_battle` object and reads its complete team roster and
  unrevealed active moves while estimating incoming attacks. This violates the
  closed-team-sheet information boundary. The refreshed score is therefore a
  privileged diagnostic only; do not use it as a fair benchmark, teacher, or
  evidence that the learner should be at 69%. The 40% learner result, 57%
  own-state damage-gated result, and the subsequently measured public-only
  baseline below are the relevant comparisons.
- **Information-safe counterplay baseline now runs complete matches:** its first
  1,024-game evaluation scored 73.14%, but used opponent-view stats in damage
  estimates and is superseded. After replacing those inputs with public species
  base stats and neutral unknown ability/item assumptions, it scored 66.70%
  (1,024 side-swapped games; 95% team-pair cluster bootstrap interval
  61.91%-71.48%), with zero adjustments and 13.95 aggregate games/s. This is a
  promising own-view heuristic result, not a trained-policy improvement or a
  matched comparison to the gate; it remains below the 75% target.
- Training the policy to imitate the gate has failed. PPO with gate teacher
  losses did not improve the ungated policy. Override-only imitation (Round158)
  fell to 26.81%; full gate-wrapper cloning (Round159) fell to 27.05%; cloning
  all of Round156 learner actions (Round160) reached 32.52%. The Round160
  decline versus Round136 was -7.13 points (95% paired interval -9.72 to
  -4.54); Round159 declined -12.60 points (-15.48 to -9.72). There were no
  invalid actions or adjustments. The Round159 trace found major behavior
  drift: first joint action matched Round136 on only 23/64 teams, and average
  decision states per side fell from 37.6/35.2 to 16.3/11.0. This points to
  policy distribution drift / poor imitation targets, not a protocol failure.
- **Round160 target audit completed:** `scripts/audit_behavior_clone_alignment.py`
  checked 12,000 saved Round156 decisions against Round136 and Round160.
  All actions were legal, all saved labels matched executed actions, and
  Round136 reproduced the rollout's ungated log probabilities almost exactly
  (9,176 rows; mean absolute error 2.3e-7, maximum 3.8e-6). This rules out
  feature, mask, and slot-alignment mismatch as the main cause of failed
  imitation. Round160 reduced joint-action negative log likelihood on these
  logged actions from 2.174 to 2.072, but its paired Max Damage score fell by
  7.13 points. The labels mostly represent actions sampled by the old policy;
  matching those actions is not a policy-improvement signal. Round160 changed
  the starting policy's greedy action in 30.2% of sampled joint decisions
  (per-slot top-1 agreement 83.1% / 83.0%). Report:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round160_behavior_clone_alignment_audit_12000_20261027/report.json`.
- **One-turn search pilot complete:** Round136 plus the immediate-damage gate
  was compared with the same policy, gate, teams, and seeds plus one equilibrium
  matrix search on 256 complete matches. The bot stayed P1 while generated
  rosters were swapped. Gate-only scored 54.69%; gate+search scored 55.08%, a
  paired +0.39 points (95% interval 0.00 to +1.17), with only one match outcome
  changed. This is no demonstrated strength gain and is not side-swapped
  evidence. Search changed the selected action on 181/245 successful decisions
  (73.9%), so it often changes the move without changing the match result.
  Search cost was 177.7 ms median / 204 ms p95 and reduced full-match
  throughput from 9.40 to 3.37 games/s. It advanced 40 simulator turns at a
  median of 363 advances/s; value inference took 5.6 ms median. Details:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round136_gate_vs_midgame_search_256_20271027_20261027/`.
- The pilot exposed a locked Solar Beam representation mismatch. Poke-env's
  fake target variants hid the targetless move that the local Showdown parser
  accepts. The action mask and order conversion now admit that forced
  continuation, and max-damage scoring decodes masked forced actions without
  repeating poke-env's stale target-order check. Both previously failing seeds
  (episodes 61 and 157) replayed with successful search, zero action
  adjustments, and zero fallbacks. Six possible-Illusion previews and three
  Transform states remain safe search skips. Regression checks for the mask,
  JavaScript search candidate, and max-damage selector passed (9 + 3 tests).
  The combined selected test run also exposed one unrelated existing
  counterplay speed-cache fixture failure (`SimpleNamespace` lacks `mega`); it
  does not exercise the changed max-damage path. See
  `followup_locked_move_fix.json` and
  `scripts/replay_round136_gate_search_locked_moves.sh`.
- **Next step:** keep Round136 plus the zero-margin immediate-damage gate as
  the strongest measured baseline; raw Round156 is near 40%, while the full
  gated agent is near 56%. Do not continue Round156 or use the public
  counterplay heuristic as a teacher: matched evidence showed no Round156 gain,
  and the public heuristic lost to the gate. Both the opening hybrid and the
  single fifth-decision Max Damage intervention failed independent
  confirmation. Do not promote either rule. The traced gate changes many
  actions across the match; build a state-action evaluator from a larger
  counterfactual dataset with varied legal opponent responses, held-out team
  clusters, and per-opponent calibration, then test its robust selector on
  untouched teams. Audit the state/action distribution mismatch before another
  behavior-cloning run:
  Round158-160 cloning shifted action frequencies and lost 7-13 points. Require
  a positive paired cluster interval on independent complete-match evaluation
  before promotion or another large PPO continuation. Do not start a
  million-game run until this smaller loop shows supported improvement. Keep
  search experimental: the fixed-P1 one-turn pilot did not establish a gain
  and reduced throughput from 9.40 to 3.37 matches/s.
- Latest complete 20,000-game simulator training remains Round156: 772.1
  seconds end to end (25.9 games/s), 419.7 seconds rollout (47.7 aggregate
  games/s), 169.2 seconds preparation, and about 147 seconds PPO; 146,526
  transitions, 7.45 GiB peak rollout RSS. Rounds157-160 were replay-only and
  added no simulator games. Current measured training throughput is therefore
  25.9 games/s end to end / 47.7 aggregate rollout games/s. CPU rollout and
  decision processing are the throughput limit; PPO record preparation is
  the largest post-rollout cost. Workspace use was about 444 GB of 915 GB
  (48.5%), below the requested half-disk ceiling.
- Latest complete-battle speed readings: standard paired evaluation processed
  1,024 games at 9.82 games/s (104.2 s); the four-arm, deterministic gated vs
  ungated ablation processed 2,048 games at 19.24 games/s (106.5 s). The latter
  uses four matches per team/repeat unit and eight workers. This is evaluation

  aggregate rollout games/s. CPU rollout decision work and PPO record
  preparation remain the training bottlenecks; benchmarked search still costs
  about 2.8x and is not enabled in the baseline.
- Rollout telemetry points to a CPU decision path as the current bottleneck:
  Round153 action selection took 57-66 ms/episode versus Max Damage and 71-85 ms
  versus Counterplay/policy opponents; policy inference took 30-34 ms versus Max
  Damage, 38 ms versus Counterplay, and 63-75 ms versus policy opponents.
  Observation encoding was 23-26 ms and simulator round trips 24-38 ms. GPU
  utilization was about 18% at a sampled training moment, and rollout
  throughput remains CPU-limited, so CPU-side decision-path profiling
  should precede any simulator CUDA work. PPO sample and
  transition preparation added 184 seconds. Peak aggregate rollout memory was
  7.49 GiB. Workspace size after gzip-compressing completed raw rollouts and
  evaluation records was about 444 GB of a 915 GB filesystem (48.5%); preserve

- Eight-worker paired evaluation completed at 7.81-9.57 games/s against Max
  Damage, 5.95-7.81 against Counterplay, and 5.88 against Round130. Training
  and evaluation results must remain separate measurements; the 41.5 aggregate
  rollout rate is not the end-to-end training rate.
- Training-objective audit: when `opponent_balance_power=1.0`, PPO normalizes
  each opponent class to equal total loss weight. Therefore the recent 75/12.5/
  12.5, 62.5/25/12.5, and 50/37.5/12.5 rollout mixes did not directly give
  Max Damage those fractions of the policy gradient; they mainly changed
  sample count, coverage, and within-class variance. At power 0.5, the
  75/12.5/12.5 mix instead contributes approximately 55% Max Damage and 22.5%
  each Counterplay and policy-pool loss weight. Round141 tested the setting
  without a clear strength change, Round142 added extra Max Damage loss weight
  and regressed, and Round144 returned to the Round136 objective while testing
  higher entropy regularization. Round145 removed the loss reweighting so the
  training mix directly controlled PPO sample proportions; Round147 increased
  direct Max Damage exposure from 15% to 20%. Its point estimates moved up
  slightly, but paired intervals still cover no change.
