policy result (28.91% in its paired 256-game evaluation) and from the separate

**Round 85 self-play win-predictor baseline (2026-10-22):** because
`pilot_clean` is unavailable, collected 20,000 full self-play matches with

runner. Both player's closed-sheet perspectives were recorded. Collection
completed in 558.0 seconds (35.84 aggregate games/s over eight workers),

**Search action-generation follow-up (2026-10-22):** reproduced a no-legal-
candidate error on a Solar Beam charge turn. Showdown's request includes
target-bearing options for the locked move, but `side.choose` rejects every
explicit target and accepts the targetless command. Updated the search
candidate generator to mark hard-locked moves as forced-targetless and added
a deterministic local-Showdown regression fixture. It now returns legal
candidate pairs for the state; the fixture also confirms the explicit-target
rejection and targetless acceptance directly. The existing bridge already
handles forced-targetless actions at submission. Focused regression and search
adapter tests pass (12 tests). A new 1,024-game paired evaluation on fresh
team/seed clusters confirms no no-legal-candidate failures in this run; the 25
search fallbacks were 21 possible-Illusion previews and 4 public Transform
states. No-search scored 35.55% at 9.92 games/s; equilibrium search scored
32.13% at 3.59 games/s (164.9 ms median, 188.2 ms p95), a -3.42 point paired
difference (95% interval -5.47 to -1.46). Search changed the policy action in
506/999 successful searches. In those 506 matched games, search won 38 games
that baseline lost while baseline won 73 that search lost. Unchanged-action
games had identical outcomes by construction. These are diagnostics, not
causal subgroup estimates, but they locate the regression in searched action
changes. This single candidate fix does not improve measured strength or
throughput; do not promote the search policy or train on its actions yet.
Current bottleneck is search decision quality and its CPU cost, not PPO data
preparation. Preserve Round 55 as the direct-policy incumbent and investigate
why the learned frontier ranks changed actions above the policy action before
another training update. Artifacts:
`training/outputs/phase12_headless/round55_midgame_equilibrium_search_eval_1024_20261022_candidatefix/`.

and superseded notes remain under `archive/current-training/`; this plan stays
the source of truth at the repository root.

1. **Speed is the first project goal.** Keep reporting collection games/s,
   games/s including PPO, state-value states/s, evaluation games/s, decision
   latency, CPU/GPU use, and disk headroom as separate measurements. The
   ordinary 20k direct-policy collection in Round 46 measured 40.5 games/s
   over eight CPU workers (493.5 seconds, 7.28 GiB peak aggregate RSS); the
   full train iteration was 28.2 games/s including PPO. Round 47's original
   support-aware teacher path measured 22.66 games/s on its mixed 20k
   collection and 18.45 games/s including PPO. Profiling found repeated strict
   order validation in the teacher's joint-action loop. The fast path now
   checks component orders once, checks pair conflicts during scoring, and
   strictly validates the selected pair. A post-change 8-worker, 2,048-match
   teacher-only benchmark reached 35.46 games/s with 119 ms mean
   action-selection time per match, three action adjustments, and zero
   baseline fallbacks. These teacher-path speed measurements are throughput
   diagnostics only; this teacher reads privileged state and is not an
   eligible closed-sheet policy. Round 48 completed on this path at 37.22 collection
   games/s and 26.29 games/s including PPO. Round 49 measured 37.17
   collection games/s and 27.40 games/s including PPO; Round 50's expanded
   policy pool measured 34.04 collection games/s and 25.09 games/s including
   PPO. Round 52's public-state gate mix collected at 36.09 games/s and ran at
   25.79 games/s including PPO. Its Max-Damage shards averaged 7.28 games/s
   per worker and 62 ms action-selection time per game, substantially faster
   than the retired privileged counterplay teacher. Round 53's 1,024-pair
   local-Showdown evaluation ran at 7.99 games/s ungated and 10.08 games/s
   gated across eight workers; the higher gated rate reflects shorter matches.
   Round 54's 256-pair policy-vs-policy condition took longest, making complete
   battle simulation plus recurrent policy decisions the current evaluation
   bottleneck. Round 55 collected 20,000 games in 556.8 seconds (35.92
   games/s) and completed training in 733.7 seconds total (27.26 games/s).
   Rollout shards ranged from 4.62–7.29 games/s each; the slower policy-pool
   games spent 76–91 ms per game in inference and action selection. PPO data
   preparation took 136.8 seconds of its 176.9-second training stage, making
   it the current within-training bottleneck after rollout. Round 58 collected
   20,000 games in 555.3 seconds (36.02 games/s) and completed training in
   774.4 seconds total (25.83 games/s; peak aggregate RSS 7.30 GiB). Its
   157,213 transitions completed all 1,232 optimizer steps / four passes at
   learning rate 1e-5, with approx KL 0.01728 and teacher loss 0.502. Round 60
   then replayed those 157,213 transitions with supervised-only gate
   imitation: 1,232 steps / four passes, teacher loss 0.4389, about 178 seconds
   total (133 seconds preparation + 45 seconds optimization). Round 61 tested
   it against Max Damage with the inference gate disabled and found a large
   regression. Round 62 collected 20,000 games in 550.6 seconds (36.32
   games/s) and completed training in 768.7 seconds total (26.02 games/s; peak
   aggregate RSS 7.25 GiB). Its 156,595 transitions completed 1,224 optimizer
   steps / four passes at LR 1e-5, with approx KL 0.00340 and teacher loss
   0.529. Round 63 found no significant strength change from Round 55 with
   the gate disabled. Round 64 found a small, inconclusive gain for Round 55
   when the public gate is enabled. The current bottleneck remains CPU rollout
   and evaluation throughput, especially recurrent policy-pool matches. Round
   65's one-turn equilibrium-search collection completed 20,000 games in
   1,156.9 seconds (17.29 games/s aggregate over eight CPU workers; peak RSS
   12.90 GB), with no baseline fallbacks. Rollout throughput is less than half
   the ordinary-policy rate because each game adds one sampled-world search
   decision. PPO record preparation took 18.9 seconds for 19,311 transitions;
   optimization took about 25 seconds (38 minibatch steps, one pass). Paired
   local-Showdown evaluation against Max Damage ran at 7.94 games/s for Round
   55 and 8.03 games/s for Round 65 over 1,023 matched clusters. Round 65 scored
   32.55% versus 32.89% (-0.34 percentage points; paired 95% cluster interval

   Its 20,000-game collection finished in 1,156.6 seconds (17.29 games/s over

2. Train the state evaluator from perspective-safe, varied-policy games. It may
   accept a rich set of observation inputs, but its public contract is exactly
   one number per state in `[0, 1]`: the evaluated player's probability of
   winning from that current observed state. It does not select moves. Round
   42 completed training on the 1M-game Round-33-gated corpus. Its best
   checkpoint is epoch 15. On 1,492,490 held-out states across 200,060 match
   clusters, it improved Brier from 0.15266 (Round 39) to 0.13811 (paired
   cluster 95% interval for candidate minus baseline: -0.01496 to -0.01415),
   log loss from 0.45897 to 0.41879, ECE from 0.01379 to 0.00306, and accuracy
   from 0.77018 to 0.79348. This is a strong, statistically supported
   evaluator improvement on the same held-out set; it is not evidence by
   itself that the player is stronger. Round 42 was used as the GAE baseline
   for Round 43; that policy update did not show a significant strength gain
   against max-damage, counterplay, or random. Continue with fresh, behavior-
   matched rollouts and retain Round 42 as the current evaluator candidate.
   Round 39 remains the earlier validated value baseline. Round 40's PPO
   update and Round 41's gate distillation did not establish policy-strength
   gains. Round 37's refresh had no significant
   Brier gain and did not change paired search outcomes; keep it diagnostic-only.
3. Improve the player using the evaluator and measured search only after speed
   work is advancing. One joint turn of lookahead is the current search cap.
   The sampled/pruned payoff matrix approximates Nash equilibrium only for that
   one-turn matrix. It is not a full-match Nash solver: persistent sequential
   information sets and beliefs through the match are not yet solved, and
   chance/action coverage is approximate.
   One-turn search remains diagnostic, not an enabled play policy. Repeated
   search showed a severe paired regression; one-search-per-match and the
   Round-37 evaluator comparison were inconclusive or unchanged. Search is a
   compact one-turn matrix, not a full-match Nash solver. See the Round-36/37
   search notes for action coverage, latency, and failure details. Round 43's
   two-pass PPO candidate using Round 42 values was not a significant win over
   its parent on fresh pairs and remains unpromoted.

   and the counterplay baseline reads private opposing-team state, so those

   teacher and its loss weights. Preserve Round 17 as incumbent while
   developing a public-information training signal. Artifacts:
   `outputs/phase12_headless/direct_policy_round51_round50_replay_lr1e5_20261022/`;
   reproduction scripts: `scripts/train_round51_round50_rollout_replay.sh` and
   `scripts/evaluate_round51_replay_paired.sh`.

   Closed-sheet information audit (2026-10-22): the support-aware teacher
   and `counterplay` baseline are privileged. In
   `scripts/run_headless_showdown_self_play.py`, teacher selection derives the
   opponent's current max-damage action from `match.battles[1]` and passes that
   opposing-perspective battle to `choose_counterplay_action`. The helper
   reads `opponent_battle.team` and `opponent_battle.active_pokemon` to resolve
   switches, moves, stats, and damage. In self-play, the counterplay opponent
   also receives `actions[agent_names[0]]` before its own choice, exposing a
   simultaneous action. `scripts/evaluate_native.py` likewise passes the
   other player's battle object to the counterplay scorer. Poke-env defines
   `.team` as the player's own team; because the scorer receives the opponent's
   battle object, it can see that opponent's private team and exact sets. The
   policy network still receives only its player observation, but Round 47–51
   counterplay labels/outcomes are not perspective-safe supervision, and all
   counterplay-baseline win rates are invalid for closed-sheet evaluation.
   Keep their timing and Max Damage match results as diagnostics, not promotion
   evidence. Do not train on or benchmark against this baseline as if it were a
   legal opponent. Round 52 executed a public-state gate training run and
   evaluated it against Max Damage, random, and frozen Round 33 on fresh pairs.
   The policy update was not significant. Round 53 compared Round 17 with and
   without the public gate on 1,024 fresh side-swapped team pairs: the gate
   raised score rate from 31.30% to 51.22% (+19.92 points; paired 95% cluster
   interval +17.09 to +22.80). Generalization to other opponents remains to be
   checked. Keep these reports separate from the invalid counterplay results.

   Round 52 public-state gate training (2026-10-22): started from Round 17 and
   collected 20,000 headless matches with 10,000 Max Damage (public immediate-
   damage gate active), 4,000 random, and 6,000 frozen-policy opponents. No
   counterplay opponents or privileged counterplay teacher labels were used.
   Collection took 554.2 seconds (36.09 games/s across eight workers; peak
   aggregate RSS 7.24 GiB); training/preparation took 221.3 seconds, giving
   775.5 seconds end-to-end (25.79 games/s). PPO used 156,825 transitions and
   completed all 1,228 optimizer steps / four requested passes, with approx KL
   0.00529 and no KL early stop. The Max Damage shards averaged 7.28 games/s
   per worker and 62 ms action-selection time per match. The Round 17 paired
   local-Showdown evaluation against Max Damage, random, and frozen Round 33
   policy completed on fresh teams. Without an inference-time gate, Round 52
   scored
   28.91% versus Round 17's 29.20% (difference -0.29 points; paired 95%
   interval -2.73 to +2.15) across 256 clusters / 512 matched cases. Against
   random, it scored 93.95% versus 92.58% (difference +1.37 points; interval
   -1.56 to +4.10) across 128 clusters / 256 cases. Against frozen Round 33,
   it scored 51.76% versus 50.39% (difference +1.37 points; interval -3.13
   to +5.86) across 128 clusters / 256 cases. No difference is statistically
   supported; retain Round 17. The trained policy alone does not capture the
   gate's measured Max-Damage benefit. A follow-up enabled the same public
   gate at inference for both checkpoints on fresh teams: versus Max Damage,
   Round 17 plus gate scored 47.27% and Round 52 plus gate 49.22% (difference
   +1.95 points; interval -0.68 to +4.49); versus random, scores were 99.22%
   and 97.66% (difference -1.56 points; interval -2.93 to -0.20); versus
   frozen Round 33, scores were 46.68% and 46.48% (difference -0.20 points;
   interval -4.49 to +4.10). This is not a demonstrated Max-Damage gain and
   the gate reduced score against random in this sample. Earlier Round 33
   results were too small to treat as a population estimate. Round 53 now
   resolves the larger Max-Damage comparison: on 1,024 fresh side-swapped team
   pairs (2,048 games per condition), Round 17 scored 31.30% ungated and
   51.22% gated. The paired gain was +19.92 points (10,000-cluster bootstrap
   95% percentile interval +17.09 to +22.80); 390 clusters favored gated, 116
   favored ungated, and 518 tied. The gate made 8,635 overrides across gated
   matches; there were zero timeouts/errors and zero invalid-action
   corrections. Ungated evaluation ran at 7.99 complete games/s over 256.2
   seconds; gated ran at 10.08 games/s over 203.2 seconds (eight workers).
   Higher gated throughput reflects shorter games, not faster decision code.
   Next compare the same fixed Round 17 checkpoint with and without the gate
   against random and a frozen policy on fresh paired teams before calling this
   a general improvement. Artifacts:
   `outputs/phase12_headless/round53_round17_public_gate_1024_pairs_20261022/`;
   reproduction: `scripts/evaluate_round53_gate_1024_pairs.sh`. Current
   evaluation bottleneck is CPU battle throughput across eight workers; the
   1,024-pair conditions took 3.4–4.3 minutes each.

   Round 54 gate generalization (2026-10-22): using the same Round 17 policy,
   compare its public gate off/on on 256 fresh paired team clusters against
   random and frozen Round 33. Against random, score rate rose from 95.12% to
   97.46% (+2.34 points; paired 95% interval +0.20 to +4.69). Against Round
   33, it rose from 47.27% to 49.02% (+1.76 points; interval -4.88 to +8.40),
   an inconclusive difference. Thus the gate has a large confirmed gain
   against Max Damage, a small edge against random in this sample, and no

   reproduction: `scripts/evaluate_round54_gate_generalization.sh`. This run
   took about 3 minutes for the four 256-pair conditions; policy-vs-policy

   decisions are the measured evaluation bottlenecks. Round 55 tested the
   public gate as an action-label source; Round 56 measured its checkpoint with

   Round 55 public-gate distillation (2026-10-22): continued from the Round
   52 checkpoint, collected 20,000 legal headless games (10,000 Max Damage,
   4,000 random, 6,000 frozen-policy pool), and increased the public gate
   teacher loss weight from 0.1 to 1.0. No counterplay teacher or opponent was
   used. Collection took 556.8 seconds (35.92 games/s, eight workers; peak
   aggregate RSS 7.46 GiB). PPO preparation and optimization took 176.9
   seconds, for 733.7 seconds total (27.26 games/s). The rollout contained
   157,448 transitions. The stronger teacher loss averaged 0.573, but the KL
   check stopped optimization after 73 minibatch steps (0.237 of a requested
   four passes; approx KL 0.0451), so this was a limited update. Round 56
   compared Round 52 and Round 55 with the inference gate disabled on 1,024
   fresh side-swapped Max-Damage clusters. Round 55 scored 32.86% versus
   30.42% for Round 52 (+2.44 points; paired 95% interval +0.24 to +4.64).
   This is a statistically supported but small transfer compared with the
   gate's +19.92-point wrapper effect. Round 52 evaluation ran at 7.76 games/s
   (263.9 seconds) and Round 55 at 9.22 games/s (222.1 seconds), both across
   eight workers; no timeouts/errors or action corrections. Round 57 checked
   transfer on 256 fresh paired clusters: against random, Round 55 scored
   95.51% vs Round 52's 95.31% (+0.20 points; 95% interval -1.95 to +2.34);
   against frozen Round 33, 51.56% vs 50.98% (+0.59; interval -4.30 to +5.66).
   Neither difference is conclusive, and no degradation was detected. Round
   58 continued from Round 55 with learning rate 1e-5, holding the 1.0 public
   gate teacher weight, 20,000-game mix, and opponent pool fixed. It completed
   all 1,232 optimizer steps / four passes (approx KL 0.01728, teacher loss
   0.502) in 219.1 seconds of PPO work; collection took 555.3 seconds, giving
   774.4 seconds end-to-end. Round 59 compared Round 55 vs Round 58 on 1,024
   fresh paired Max-Damage clusters with the inference gate disabled: 32.13%
   vs 32.42% (+0.29 points; paired 95% interval -1.66 to +2.25), an
   inconclusive difference. The two conditions ran at 7.83 and 7.64 games/s
   (261.6 and 268.0 seconds, eight workers), with zero timeouts/errors and
   corrections. Round 60 replayed the Round 58 gate-labeled trajectories with
   supervised imitation only, removing PPO and value objectives on unlabeled
   rows. It completed 1,232 optimizer steps / four passes at learning rate
   1e-5, with no KL stop, teacher loss 0.4389, and zero PPO/value losses.
   Preparation took 133.1 seconds and optimization 44.6 seconds. Round 61
   compared Round 58 vs Round 60 on 1,024 fresh Max-Damage clusters with the
   gate disabled. Across 1,023 matched clusters, Round 60 scored 23.02% vs
   Round 58's 31.43% (-8.41 points; paired 95% interval -10.95 to -5.96).
   The Round 58 condition had one timeout; Round 60 had none, and both had
   zero action corrections. The small unmatched set does not explain this
   statistically clear regression. Reject Round 60; Round 55 remains the
   strongest ungated learned checkpoint. Round 62 is collecting fresh
   trajectories from Round 55 with PPO retained and a moderate teacher weight
   0.3 to avoid pure imitation's loss of strength. Round 62 completed all
   four requested passes (approx KL 0.00340; teacher loss 0.529) with 156,595
   transitions; rollout took 550.6 seconds and the full iteration 768.7
   seconds. Round 63 compared Round 55 and Round 62 on 1,024 fresh paired
   Max-Damage clusters with the inference gate disabled: 33.38% vs 32.65%
   (-0.73 points; paired 95% interval -2.64 to +1.17), inconclusive. Round
   55 had one timeout; Round 62 had none; both had zero action corrections.
   Round 64 compared Round 17 and Round 55 with the public gate enabled on
   1,024 fresh paired Max-Damage clusters: 51.17% vs 52.39% (+1.22 points;
   paired 95% interval -0.63 to +3.13), not statistically conclusive. Each
   condition completed 2,048 games with zero timeouts or action corrections;
   the gate made 8,682 and 8,534 overrides, respectively. Evaluation ran at
   10.16 and 10.18 games/s across eight workers (about 201 seconds per
   condition). Thus Round 55 is the best ungated learned checkpoint at 32.86%
   on its Round 56 comparison, while gate-on Round 55 reached 52.39% on this
   sample; this does not establish a significant gain over Round 17 with the
   same gate. Next, shift from immediate-damage imitation toward outcome-based

   Round 65 (2026-10-22) is the first outcome-search teacher update from the
   Round 55 direct policy. One midgame joint-action matrix was searched per
   eligible game with two hidden worlds, four added candidate classes, and one
   chance sample. The equilibrium row strategy was stored as a joint-action
   distribution and distilled with a factorized policy loss; 19,311 player-1
   transitions were selected from the 20,000 games. Search-native indices did
   not always align with the live mask after semantic order translation, so
   soft-target pairs that were illegal or could not condition on the executed
   first action were dropped and the executed legal search action retained as
   a hard label. Post-training extraction found 19,290 usable soft targets
   (99.89%) and 21 hard-label fallbacks (0.11%); the mean remaining support
   was 4.97 joint actions. The update used one pass, LR 1e-5, terminal return,
   and 38 optimizer steps; soft teacher loss was 2.989. Evaluation versus
   Round 55 is not a promotion: 1,023 paired team clusters scored 32.55% vs
   32.89% (difference -0.34 points; paired 95% interval -2.49 to +1.81).
   Retain Round 55. Before another large run, improve action-identity mapping
   between search candidates and the live policy mask and measure how often
   soft labels survive; then test the resulting teacher on fresh paired teams.
   Artifacts: `outputs/phase12_headless/round65_soft_equilibrium_teacher_20261022/`
   and `outputs/phase12_headless/round65_soft_equilibrium_eval_1024_pairs_20261022/`;
   reproduction: `scripts/collect_round65_soft_equilibrium_teacher_20k.sh`,
   `scripts/train_round65_soft_equilibrium_teacher.sh`, and
   `scripts/evaluate_round65_soft_equilibrium_teacher.sh`.

   Round 66 (2026-10-22) continued training Round 65 for three additional
   passes over the same 19,311 transition search-teacher set, starting from
   Round 65. Its soft teacher loss dropped to 2.605 from Round 65's 2.989, but
   the fresh paired comparison showed no strength gain: 30.40% vs 32.55% on
   1,023 shared Max-Damage team clusters (difference -2.15 points; paired 95%
   interval -4.45 to +0.20). Round 66 had zero action adjustments; evaluation

   Round 67 (2026-10-22) tested outcome-based PPO on actions sampled from the
   equilibrium strategy. Collection completed 20,000 games in 1,156.6 seconds
   (17.29 games/s, peak RSS 13.00 GB), with 160 action adjustments and zero
   baseline fallbacks. From those matches, 19,355 P1 search decisions were
   selected; all had a finite behavior probability whose extracted log
   probability matched exactly. Of these, 19,334 retained a usable soft joint
   target and 21 used the executed-action hard-label fallback. PPO used
   terminal outcomes for the sampled search action and a 0.3 soft-equilibrium
   loss, with two passes and 76 optimizer steps. Its policy loss was 0.359,
   soft teacher loss 2.921, approximate KL 4.81, and clip fraction 0.9956.
   Despite a verified actor update, strength did not improve: on 1,023 fresh
   paired Max-Damage team clusters, Round 67 scored 33.77% and Round 55 scored
   34.07% (difference -0.29 points; paired 95% interval -2.39 to +1.81).
   Evaluation throughput was 8.75 games/s for Round 55 and 7.16 for Round 67;
   both had zero action adjustments. Do not promote Round 67. The large KL and
   near-total clipping show that the equilibrium behavior distribution is far
   from the parent policy, so the next training experiment should temper the
   behavior policy toward the parent before applying outcome PPO. Artifacts:
   `outputs/phase12_headless/round67_outcome_ppo_20261022/` and
   `outputs/phase12_headless/round67_outcome_ppo_eval_1024_pairs_20261022/`;
   scripts: `scripts/collect_round67_outcome_ppo_20k.sh`,
   `scripts/train_round67_outcome_ppo.sh`, and
   `scripts/evaluate_round65_soft_equilibrium_teacher.sh`.

   Round-33 immediate-damage gate follow-up (2026-10-22): on the same 256
   side-swapped max-damage pairs, the gate scored 55.27% versus 32.23% ungated
   (+23.05 points; 95% paired cluster interval +16.80 to +29.10). On 128 pairs
   versus counterplay, it was effectively tied (39.45% vs 39.84%, difference

**Evaluation CPU threading benchmark (2026-10-22):** the same 256-game,
128-team-pair max-damage run measured 0.87 games/s with eight evaluator
workers each using PyTorch's default eight CPU threads. Limiting each worker to
one thread (`OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1`)
raised eight-worker throughput to 9.18 games/s. A fair same-settings four-
worker run measured 5.63 games/s. This points to CPU thread oversubscription
as a major source of evaluation slowness. These are throughput-only runs and
do not count as strength evaluation. Peak system-available RAM after the runs
was about 26 GiB. The local Showdown server and benchmark processes were
stopped afterward.

## Immediate execution priority

**Why performance remains near one-third against max damage (2026-10-21):**
The round-27 result (172/512, 33.59%; paired-bootstrap 95% CI
28.52–38.67%) is not explained by observed action-submission or timeout
failures: the evaluation recorded zero of either. The opponent is a real
one-turn tactical baseline: it scores legal moves with approximate expected
damage, sums spread damage across foes, penalizes hitting its ally, and picks a
compatible joint action. It does not plan ahead, but it can punish poor target
choice, typing, focus fire, and team preview.

The training signals have been easier to overinterpret than the results
justify. The large historical corpus trained a state-outcome predictor on
states generated by its policy mixture; it did not train the policy for a
million games or label ideal play. In PPO, the accepted predictor supplies a
state-value baseline for terminal-outcome advantages; it does not directly
score candidate moves or act as a policy-improvement objective. Recent player
rounds each used one PPO update over 20,000 games (four epochs), and paired
round-to-round evaluations have not shown a statistically clear gain. Round
27's fixed-seed comparison to its starting checkpoint was -0.98 percentage
points (95% CI -4.88 to +2.93), despite scoring 33.59% on fresh seeds.

These match results also use randomly generated legal Champions teams and
random team-preview selections for both sides. They measure action-policy
strength in that setup, not the complete team-and-preview problem or broad
competitive VGC strength. The separate learned preview selector tested so far
did not improve on random preview. Accordingly, do not infer that more
predictor data alone will close the gap. Next diagnose policy decisions on
paired losing games, separately measure preview and in-battle choices, and
compare any tactical/search change against the same seeds before promoting
another checkpoint.

The one-turn search experiment remains invalid as strength evidence. Earlier
partial runs found action-index mismatches across hidden-team hypotheses. A
semantic-action adapter and live-legal-order filter passed representative
single-seed reproductions, but the subsequent 256-match run was stopped after
193 matches: 45/193 (23.3%) fell back, mostly because hidden-world shards had
no common candidate remaining after filtering against the live legal menu;
three were hidden-team sampling failures and four were Showdown move-order
errors. The representative seed was insufficient validation. Do not promote
or compare this partial search result. Resolve candidate-set consistency and
confirm low fallback rates across varied states before another paired strength
evaluation. This search integration issue does not explain the separate
policy-only round-27 score, which had zero action adjustments and timeouts.

**Full-turn immediate-damage gate (2026-10-21):** an exploratory 128-game
run replaced each P1 policy action whenever max damage's immediate heuristic
score was higher. It won 66/128 (51.6%), compared with 47/128 (36.7%) for the
policy-only diagnostic and 43/128 (33.6%) when replacing only the opening
action. This is a striking signal, but not yet a reliable strength estimate:
the intervention changes later states and policy trajectory, the baseline
comparison is not a documented paired-seed comparison, and immediate damage is
not win probability. Keep the unmodified round-7 checkpoint as incumbent. Next
run the gate and policy on matched seeds/rosters with side swaps, record the
number of overrides, then evaluate any apparent gain against the held-out pool.
Do not promote the gate as the policy without that validation.

Matched validation completed on 128 identical generated team seeds, once with
each roster orientation (256 games per condition). The policy scored 47/128
(36.7%) in the original orientation and 35/128 (27.3%) with rosters swapped;
the gate scored 66/128 (51.6%) and 64/128 (50.0%), respectively. Averaging the
two orientations per seed, the paired gain was +18.75 percentage points (95%
cluster bootstrap CI +12.11 to +25.78). The gate made 1,055 substitutions,
about 4.1 per game. This is strong evidence that action choices which sacrifice
the immediate damage heuristic are a major weakness in this evaluation setup.
It does not establish that maximizing this heuristic is generally optimal or
that the learned policy should be replaced: this is one team-seed batch against
one tactical baseline, and the gate changes future states. Recheck on a fresh
seed batch before promoting it. Reproducible logs and summary:
`outputs/phase6/round27_gate_matched/`.

Fresh-seed replication completed on 128 additional team seeds, also with both
roster orientations. The gate gain was +13.28 points (paired 95% cluster
bootstrap CI +6.64 to +19.92). Pooling both batches gives 256 matched team
seeds and 512 games per condition: policy 175/512 (34.2%), gate 257/512
(50.2%), paired gain +16.02 points (95% CI +11.13 to +20.90). The gate made
2,156 replacements, 4.21 per gated game. This replicated intervention supports
a real action-selection weakness, rather than a one-batch fluctuation. It still
only establishes that the heuristic gate beats this policy against max damage
on these randomly generated teams; do not generalize it to all opponents or
call it win-optimal. Combined report: `outputs/phase6/round27_gate_aggregate_report.json`.

**Round 28 teacher transfer and local-server check (2026-10-21):** the
headless collector now records the executed damage-gated action as a teacher
label, and PPO preparation parses those labels for imitation-only updates. A
20,000-game mixed-opponent batch completed with no action fallbacks; its P1
view contains 141,505 transitions and all teacher actions passed legality
validation. One conservative imitation pass produced a candidate checkpoint.
On 256 held-out side-swapped pairs against max damage on the local server, it
scored 155/512 (30.3%) versus 162/512 (31.6%) for its starting checkpoint; the
paired change was -1.37 pp (95% CI -6.25 to +3.32). The clone did not transfer
the gate's strength and is not promoted.

The gate itself was then tested directly through the same local-server paired
evaluator. On those identical 256 pairs, it scored 252/512 (49.2%) versus
162/512 (31.6%) ungated: paired gain +17.58 pp (95% CI +11.91 to +23.24),
2,221 substitutions, and zero invalid-action adjustments. Thus the headless
gate effect does transfer to local Showdown, while one-step behavior cloning
did not. Keep the gate as a measured tactical baseline, not as the trained
policy; diagnose the distillation gap and improve action evaluation/search.
Artifacts: `outputs/phase5/value_guided_20000_20261020/iteration_0028_damage_gate_teacher/`
and `outputs/phase6/round28_local_gate_comparison_report.json`.
On 1,440 sampled training labels, exact joint-action agreement with the gate
was 16.1% for the start checkpoint and 16.3% after one pass; after four passes
it fell to 15.3%. First-slot agreement was 30.7%, 35.5%, and 27.2%; second-slot
agreement was 28.2%, 30.2%, and 31.0%, respectively. This is an in-sample
diagnostic, not a held-out statistic, and is consistent with the weak match
transfer. The key next step is to improve the action-value/distillation method
and reserve whole games for teacher-agreement validation instead of increasing
imitation epochs blindly. Agreement report:
`outputs/phase5/value_guided_20000_20261020/iteration_0028_damage_gate_teacher/evaluation/teacher_action_agreement.json`.
The stronger four-pass clone scored 157/512 (30.7%) versus the same 162/512
(31.6%) starting checkpoint on the same 256 pairs. Paired change was -0.98 pp
(95% CI -6.05 to +4.10), with zero action adjustments. Four passes also
reduced sampled training-label joint agreement to 15.3%. Do not continue this
imitation recipe without fixing its conditional action/optimization behavior.
Report: `outputs/phase6/round28_clone4_comparison_report.json`.

**Evaluator and benchmark interpretation (2026-10-21):** keep the older value
model as a useful calibrated starting point, but interpret its output as the
win probability under the rollout policy/opponent mixture represented in its
training data. Its held-out Brier score near 0.135 is evidence about prediction
on that held-out distribution, not about ideal play. Max-damage-generated
games would be useful as an additional data stratum and for checking
calibration against that tactical policy; training only on max damage would
instead make the evaluator specific to max-damage continuations. Continue to
mix recent agent versions and varied opponents, preserve whole games/teams in
held-out splits, and report calibration separately by opponent and game phase.
To rank actions, use candidate-action rollouts or search with the evaluator at
the frontier; a state-only prediction alone does not tell us which action is
best.

Benchmark size should follow the effect we need to resolve. In the latest
256-team-seed, side-swapped experiment (512 matches per condition), cluster
bootstrap 95% intervals were 30.3–38.3% for the baseline and 46.5–53.9% for
the gate, with a paired gain of 11.1–20.9 points. This is enough to establish
that the gate intervention helped here, but not to rank changes of only a few
points precisely. Keep paired seeds and side swaps; plan around 1,000 or more
independent team-seed pairs for close (<5 pp) comparisons, then use the observed
paired variance to set later sample sizes. A 75% promotion claim must use a
predeclared held-out evaluation and have its lower confidence bound above 75%;
the current 256-pair batches cannot certify a result that is only slightly
above that threshold.

**Outcome-sampling benchmark rule (2026-10-21):** for strength comparisons,
sample battle randomness as well as team matchups. The current paired local
evaluator generates one team pair per pair index and two side-swapped games;
those two legs control roster and side effects, but use distinct environment
seeds, so they are not repeated stochastic outcomes of the same exact setup.
For follow-up close comparisons, evaluate each frozen team pair over multiple
independent battle launches, keep policy versions paired on the same team,
preview, and evaluator-seed cases, swap sides, and bootstrap at the team-pair
cluster level (with repeats nested inside). This separates matchup diversity
from within-match RNG variance and avoids treating games on the same teams as
independent.
Keep a smaller one-seed-per-team-pair sweep for broad screening; expand repeats
when paired results are noisy or the effect is small. Do not simply rerun the
same RNG seed and count the identical replay as extra evidence.

For evaluator calibration, compare the accepted old model and any candidate on
the same fresh held-out perspective states, grouped by whole match/team. Include
new-policy self-play and max-damage-opponent strata, then report Brier score,
log loss, calibration, and confidence intervals separately by opponent and
game phase. These are distinct questions: max-damage trajectories test whether
the evaluator predicts outcomes against that baseline; the mixed-policy test
measures its calibration on the intended training mixture. Neither result
alone establishes an “ideal player” win probability.

Implemented `--outcome-repeats` in `scripts/evaluate_native_paired.py`; repeated
cases keep generated teams and preview actions fixed and launch independent
battles, still running both side-swapped legs. The evaluator seed controls team
generation, preview sampling, and policy RNG, but poke-env does not pass it to
Showdown's battle simulator; Showdown generates each battle RNG seed
server-side. These are independent outcome samples, not replayable battle seeds
or exactly RNG-paired checkpoint trials. The runner records evaluation seeds
without labeling them as Showdown battle seeds. `scripts/summarize_paired_eval.py`
averages repeats within each fixed team pair and resamples team-pair clusters
for its interval. A live
local-server smoke run (one team pair, two outcome repeats, four complete
matches) confirmed identical rosters/previews across repeats, distinct repeat
cases, and zero action adjustments. This verifies the repeat plumbing only; one
team pair is not a strength estimate. For example, use `--pairs 256
--outcome-repeats 4` for a first repeated-outcome benchmark, then increase team
pair clusters if the interval remains too wide.

**Round-29 repeated-outcome gate comparison (2026-10-21):** on 256 fixed team
pairs, four battle launches per pair, and side-swapped legs (2,048 matches per
condition), the ungated checkpoint scored 32.57% (667 wins, 1,381 losses;
95% team-cluster bootstrap interval 28.08–37.11%). The same checkpoint with
the immediate-damage gate scored 50.93% (1,043 wins, 1,005 losses; interval
46.24–55.57%). There were zero invalid-action adjustments, timeouts, or
incomplete cases. The gate's paired gain was +18.36 percentage points (95%
team-pair-cluster bootstrap interval +13.77 to +22.90; 132 clusters favored
the gate, 52 favored baseline, 72 tied). This confirms a large tactical-gate
improvement over this weak policy, but it does not demonstrate strength over
max damage: the gated agent itself remains near 50% against max damage, far
below the 75% goal. Each Showdown battle used server-generated RNG; policy
versions shared teams, previews, and evaluator-seed schedule, not exact battle
RNG streams. The two runs completed at about 1.48 and 1.62 local Showdown
matches/s respectively. Reports and compressed match records:
`outputs/phase6/round29_repeated_gate_20261021/`. Reproduce from the repo root
with `POKEMON_SHOWDOWN_PATH=/path/to/pokemon-showdown PYTHONPATH=. venv/bin/python
scripts/evaluate_native_paired.py --checkpoint
outputs/phase5/value_guided_20000_20261020/iteration_0017_newvalue300k_maxdamage60/checkpoints/latest.pt
--opponent max_damage --pairs 256 --outcome-repeats 4 --seed 20262850
--output-dir /tmp/round29_ungated` and rerun with another output directory plus
`--max-damage-score-gate` for the gated condition.

**Round-27 decision trace diagnostic (2026-10-21):** added opt-in headless
debug tracing for the policy action, the same-state max-damage action, the
orders each would submit, and both actions' immediate-damage heuristic scores.
Across 128 deterministic games (47 wins, 81 losses), the policy's immediate
score was below the max-damage choice on 62.7% of logged decisions in wins and
65.0% in losses; the mean score gaps were -70.6 and -71.3 heuristic points.
Among below-score actions, 16.1% in losses versus 8.5% in wins contained no
positive-base-power move; Protect/Guard appeared in 6.5% versus 3.0%.
These features are suggestive but not proof of bad choices: score is not win
probability, and the policy also won many games while choosing lower-score
actions. A paired 128-game intervention that replaced only P1's first action
with max damage, then returned to the policy, scored 43/128 versus 47/128 for
policy-only. Difference was -3.13 pp (95% paired-bootstrap CI -11.72 to +5.47;
14 improved pairs, 18 regressed, 96 tied), so the first move alone does not
explain the poor result and max-damage imitation is not supported by this
experiment. Full report: `outputs/phase6/round27_maxdamage_decision_diagnostic/report.json`;
reproduce with `POKE_HEADLESS_DEBUG=1` and `--first-turn-max-damage` in
`scripts/run_headless_showdown_self_play.py`.

pairs it scored 32.0% (95% CI 27.1–37.1%; 164 wins, 348 losses), with no
protocol failures, action adjustments, or incomplete pairs. Its direct
round 7 comparison was 50.0% (95% CI 44.5–55.5%) on another 256 fresh pairs,
so it is not a demonstrated player improvement and remains unpromoted.
Training took 657.4 seconds for 20,000 games (30.4 games/s including PPO;
54.2 rollout games/s across 369.1 seconds). PPO preparation/update took
288.3 seconds; evaluator inference used 98.7 seconds for 185,279 states.
Rollouts averaged 10.70 CPU cores and peaked at 11.6 GiB RSS. Artifacts:
`outputs/phase5/value_guided_20000_20261020/iteration_0015_maxdamage60_newvalue/`.

Round 16 (2026-10-20): continued cumulatively from round 15 for 20,000 games
with the 240k-game evaluator, 60% max-damage / 15% counterplay / 15% random /
10% policy-pool rollouts, four PPO passes, and max-damage loss weight 2. A
first attempt stopped after rollout collection because one configured round 7
pool path was invalid; it is preserved at
`outputs/phase5/value_guided_20000_20261020/iteration_0016_failed_missing_pool_checkpoint/`.
The corrected run used the actual round 7 cumulative checkpoint and completed
in 656.2 seconds: 30.5 games/s including PPO and 54.2 rollout games/s over
368.7 seconds. PPO record preparation took 195.8 seconds for 22,000 records
(166,902 transitions); evaluator inference took 97.1 seconds over 185,240
states. Rollouts averaged 10.62 CPU cores and peaked at 11.5 GiB aggregate RSS.
The candidate scored 28.7% against max damage on 256 fresh side-swapped pairs
(95% CI 23.8–33.8%; 147 wins, 365 losses), with no draws, adjustments,
timeouts, or incomplete pairs. This does not improve on round 15 and is not
promoted. Its direct round 7 comparison scored 53.9% on 255 complete pairs
(95% CI 48.4–59.2%; one pair timed out), a small but statistically
inconclusive edge. The formal incumbent remains round 7. Artifacts:
`outputs/phase5/value_guided_20000_20261020/iteration_0016_continue_round15_60mix_retry/`.

Expanded predictor refresh from rounds 14–16 (2026-10-20): added 60,000 new
games to the previous 240k-game corpus, producing a 300,000-game combined
cache. The 240k training/calibration/test cache was preserved; 1,054,123 new
states were assigned to training using the existing roster-held-out lists,
while the original 414,866 calibration and 865,562 test states stayed fixed.
An incremental cache builder allows new trajectory sources to use prior roster
holdouts, and a zero-copy cache manifest combines old and new tensor shards.
Warm-started at learning rate 2e-5; early stopping selected epoch 1. On the
same 86,403 held-out match clusters, Brier improved from 0.135706 to 0.135502
(paired 95% CI for candidate-minus-baseline: -0.000280 to -0.000126), and log
loss improved from 0.412512 to 0.412009 (CI -0.000713 to -0.000291). Accuracy
improved by 0.00039 (CI +0.00008 to +0.00070); ECE improved by point estimate,
but its interval includes zero. This evaluator is accepted for the next player
update. Artifacts:
`outputs/phase5/value_guided_20000_20261020/evaluator_combined_100k_plus_rounds7_16/`.
Round 17 (2026-10-20): trained cumulatively from round 15 using the accepted
300k-game evaluator, 60/15/15/10 max-damage/counterplay/random/policy-pool
rollouts, four PPO passes, and max-damage loss weight 2. Training completed in
654.3 seconds for 20,000 games (30.6 games/s including PPO; 54.7 rollout
games/s over 365.3 seconds). PPO preparation took 197.7 seconds for 22,000
records / 165,982 transitions, with 98.8 seconds of evaluator inference over
184,371 states. The candidate scored 35.0% against max damage on 256 fresh
side-swapped pairs (95% CI 30.1–40.0%; 179 wins, 333 losses), with zero draws,
action corrections, timeouts, or incomplete pairs. This is the best recent
point estimate but remains far below the 75% target. Its direct round 7
comparison scored 54.1% on 256 fresh pairs (95% CI 48.6–59.6%), with no
action corrections, timeouts, or incomplete pairs. This is an inconclusive
edge, so round 7 remains the formal incumbent and round 17 is the best current
branch for the next iteration. Artifacts:
`outputs/phase5/value_guided_20000_20261020/iteration_0017_newvalue300k_maxdamage60/`.

GAE baseline batching benchmark (2026-10-20): a reusable benchmark script
tested record batches 64/256/512 and inference batches 512/2,048 on 1,024 real
rollout records (8,816 states, CUDA). Throughput ranged from 1,833 to 1,971
states/s across combinations; candidate score outputs differed by at most
6.6e-7. Repeated runs show batch-size effects are small and within observed
runtime variation, so retain the current 64/512 defaults. The larger measured
cost is CPU feature construction, not GPU batch dispatch. Reproduce with
`scripts/benchmark_gae_baseline_batches.py`; report:
`outputs/phase5/value_guided_20000_20261020/iteration_0009_balanced40/evaluation/gae_batch_benchmark.json`.

   28.14 games/s with 12 concurrent jobs on this 8-core CPU. Same-policy
   self-play now reaches 27.74 games/s at 8 workers after batching both

   unbatched 480-game run). A counterplay scorer optimization raised its

2. **Train the win-probability evaluator (first refreshed model completed):**
   generate closed-sheet examples with the faster pipeline and train/evaluate
   a model whose sole output is the current state's win likelihood in `[0, 1]`.
   The new calibrated checkpoint is measured on a roster-disjoint test set;
   keep it experimental until equal-budget search testing supports promotion.
3. Resume broader robust-policy training and search after those first two
   priorities are advancing on measured, reproducible throughput.
   Search speed guardrail (2026-10-20): keep production search to one joint
   turn of lookahead until equal-decision-time match tests show a strength gain.
   Do not expand every action pair across the full Cartesian product of random
   outcomes: e.g. the illustrative two-target Rock Slide case already has up to
   1,089 paired outcomes before merging. Benchmark outcome merging and any
   exact enumeration as isolated prototypes; bound work by a decision-time
   budget, share chance seeds across candidate actions, and fall back to the
   policy if the budget expires. Search remains an optional measured layer, not
   a prerequisite for evaluator training or rollout throughput. Current
   evidence: earlier one-turn searches needed roughly 0.13–0.35 s in warm
   profiles, while the larger 4/8-sample fixed-state probe took 0.83/1.52 s;
   these are different workloads and not a common-budget comparison. Search
   throughput is therefore still the bottleneck for adding search broadly.
   The fixed and adaptive 1M-checkpoint comparisons have completed; results
   are recorded below.
   A fresh epoch-2-checkpoint probe (seed 91019, two worlds, six candidates per
   side, one chance sample) measured 72 Showdown turn advances in 257 ms

   action as the material method on this one state; this is latency evidence,

## Goal and design constraints

- [ ] Build an agent for best-of-one, closed-team-sheet VGC that handles strong,
  unpredictable opponents without relying on opponent-specific tendencies.
- [ ] Train through self-play and evaluate against varied teams and opponents.
- [x] Complete full matches on the existing local Pokémon Showdown server.
- [x] Keep the LAN client implementation available as optional tooling; active
  second-device/LAN delivery was removed from scope by the user on 2026-10-20.
- [x] Permit the state evaluator to accept many useful input parameters. Its
  only output is one scalar in `[0, 1]`: the likelihood that the evaluated
  player wins from the current observed game state. Policy and search choose
  actions separately.
- [ ] Measure simulator throughput and decision latency at every phase; set
  explicit targets before scaling training or search.
- [x] Preserve Showdown as a usable match environment and correctness reference.
- [x] Enforce each player's closed-team-sheet information boundary for policy,
  evaluator, and training player-view inputs; keep persistent belief accuracy
  and broader search-world robustness tracked separately in Phase 7.
- [ ] Separate protocol, observation parsing, policy, search, and action
  submission so training and local-server play use the same decision code.
- [ ] Use reproducible strength/runtime evaluation and optimize measured
  bottlenecks. Do not begin with a CUDA rewrite.

  and supported rules.
- [x] Confirm target VGC format, generation, ruleset, and team-selection rules.
- [x] Define observations, decision timing, and legal returned actions.

- [x] Identify tests, simulator gaps, compute/memory limits, and decision
  deadlines.
- [x] **Deliverable:** design note for format, interfaces, information
  constraints, known gaps, and runtime limits.

  species-only preview roster at each decision; the perspective projector

- Data-size caution: the current 22,705 evaluator examples came from 1,002
  matches (about 22.7 player-view states per match); the 480-match scaling
  run averaged 12.73 joint turns (about 25 player decision states per match).
  Those states are correlated within a match, so one million games is not
  equivalent to 23–25 million independent observations. Reserve data and
  measure calibration by held-out game, team, and opponent pool; use
  game-clustered uncertainty estimates.

  out-of-core path to `scripts/train_state_value.py`: it hashes whole rosters
  in a first pass, converts one player-view record at a time, writes atomic
  tensor shards, and uses shard-local shuffled batches. The disk-cache manifest

  CPU thread, took 11.3 s, and peaked at 676 MiB RSS. The one-epoch CPU fit

  validates data flow only, not evaluator quality. At the 16,800-game training
  snapshot, rollouts occupy 3.0 GiB; linear planning estimates roughly 179 GiB
  of JSONL plus 59 GiB of tensor cache per million games. The filesystem then
  had 530 GiB free; check free space before a million-game collection. Usage
  is documented in `docs/PHASE4_DATA.md`.

- Open questions / limitations:

## Phase 5: Train robustly with self-play

- [ ] Train a policy with a practical reinforcement-learning method.
- [ ] Maintain a pool of past policy versions as a training mixture to stabilize
  training and reduce forgetting.
- [ ] Use self-play/equilibrium-oriented methods to improve worst-case
  performance; do not train opponent-specific exploiters or infer habits.
- [ ] After the 1M-game evaluator baseline, run repeated policy-improvement
  iterations of about 20,000 completed games each. Each iteration starts from
  the latest usable policy and value checkpoint, mixes the current policy with
  past versions and varied non-exploiter opponents, and trains both the policy
  and value from the new trajectories. Use the large frozen-policy corpus as
  the first stable evaluator baseline; then treat each 20k round as one cycle
  of policy improvement, improved-policy data collection, and evaluator
  refresh. The evolving evaluator estimates the win probability of the
  specified robust continuation policy, not an unknowable perfect-play
  probability. Connect the value to action improvement
  through full-state search or a validated value-guided actor/critic path; the
  current headless PPO entry point does not load the separate Phase 4 evaluator.
  A low-cost first experiment is to feed its player-view probability into GAE
  as a state-only baseline (map `p(win)` to expected terminal reward `2p-1`),
  while continuing to train the actor on actual terminal match outcomes.
  Compare this with the native critic at equal games and runtime, and check
  probability calibration by turn before adopting it; do not use the score as
  a policy reward or action preference without a valid action-value backup.
  The value targets should reflect improved continuation play and
  robust/equilibrium backups, rather than merely relabeling outcomes from the
  original frozen policy. Keep per-iteration checkpoints, game counts, seeds,
  and model/data provenance.
- [ ] Compare chance-sampling methods during these iterations: exact enumeration
  on manageable branches, independent Monte Carlo, common-random-number paired
  comparisons, stratified outcome sampling, and adaptive sampling that spends
  more samples when action values overlap. Compare them at equal decision-time
  budgets and record policy strength as well as value uncertainty; do not infer
  improvement from a lower Brier score alone.
- [ ] Evaluate every 20k candidate on separate held-out teams and match seeds,
  with side-swapped pairs against the previous policy and diverse strong
  opponents. Do not train on those evaluation games. Track mean and worst-case
  performance, confidence intervals, calibration, invalid actions, and
  decision latency before deciding whether to retain or roll back the candidate.
- [ ] Vary teams, seeds, and starting conditions; reserve teams/opponents for
  evaluation only.
- [ ] Track performance, invalid actions, runtime, and policy behavior.
- [ ] Publish each usable checkpoint atomically; each match keeps the policy
  version with which it started.
- [ ] **Deliverable:** trained policy, versioned checkpoints, training logs,
  and held-out results.

**Notes:**

  keeps record/agent/step alignment, and maps calibrated win probability to
  expected terminal score (`2p-1`) as a state-only GAE baseline. It requires
  terminal match rewards with `gamma=1` and `lambda=1`; PPO still optimizes the
  actual terminal outcomes, and policy-only PPO remains the default. Baseline
  state count, inference/encoding time, and checkpoint path are logged. Syntax
  compilation and both CLI help paths passed. The following controlled
  ablation used the option on preserved Round-27 trajectories. Independently,
  opt-in one-turn search can replace decisions during headless rollout
  collection and records its selected action as a teacher label. PPO still
  optimizes terminal outcomes; it does not directly optimize the matrix-game
  value or mixed strategy returned by search.

  critic PPO arms from the same Round-27 start checkpoint, on the same 20k-game

  checkpoints in the policy-opponent quarter. At the 2:45 snapshot it had
  completed 9,213 matches (~55.8 games/s including startup), versus about 30
  games/s for the previous websocket-backed rollout. The battle engine remains
  the local Showdown checkout; only the websocket turn loop is bypassed. This
  has completed. Final measurements: 20,000 games in 402.96 s (49.6 rollout
  games/s), then 325.34 s for PPO and setup, for 728.33 s total (27.46 complete
  training games/s; about 10.1 hours per million at this recipe, excluding
  held-out evaluation). The update used 174,648 transitions and 1,368 optimizer
  minibatches; feature preparation took 227.0 s, action/mask aggregation 4.8 s,
  and the optimized PPO loop about 50 s. The loop speed is about 5.7x the
  pre-hoisting batch-512 update. Rollout peak aggregate RSS was 11.3 GiB, with
  mean CPU use of 10.4 cores. Versioned and root `latest.pt` files match by
  SHA-256. Held-out evaluation is the next gate; this candidate is not yet
  promoted. Run output: `outputs/phase5/value_guided_20000_20261020/iteration_0002_batch512/`.
  Held-out evaluation is now running on fresh generated teams: 256
  side-swapped pairs (512 games) each against random, max-damage, counterplay,
  and the round's parent checkpoint. These matches are excluded from training.
  Results (2026-10-20): 2,032 games completed across 253–256 pairs per
  opponent; eight pairs were incomplete from timeouts. There were zero invalid
  action adjustments. Pair-bootstrap 95% intervals from 20,000 resamples were
  91.3% (88.4–94.1%) vs random, 29.9% (25.2–34.8%) vs max-damage, 30.4%
  (25.7–35.4%) vs counterplay, and 52.4% (46.8–57.7%) vs the parent policy.
  The parent comparison is compatible with both a small loss and a modest gain;
  this round does not establish a statistically clear strength improvement.
  Keep it as an experimental pool checkpoint and retain the parent as the
  incumbent until a matched evaluation shows a reliable gain. Reproduce the
  pair-cluster intervals with `scripts/summarize_paired_eval.py`; report:
  `outputs/phase5/value_guided_20000_20261020/evaluation_round_0001/report.json`.
  Evaluation throughput was slower than training rollout collection because
  each paired runner plays matches sequentially: the four opponent jobs were
  run concurrently and completed 2,032 games with eight timed-out pairs and no
  action adjustments. The report script resamples pair clusters, preserving
  the side-swapped design rather than treating each game as independent.
  Speed probe (2026-10-20): one saved 11-state match record took 7 ms to
  rebuild evaluator inputs and 3 ms to rebuild policy inputs. At 10:54 elapsed,
  the reused-input full PPO preparation was still CPU-saturated (one core) at
  about 4.4 GiB RSS, no checkpoint, and no additional swap use. This makes
  full-corpus JSONL decoding, repeated validation, and accumulated per-transition
  Python/tensor objects candidate costs; the single-record microbenchmark is
  diagnostic, not a corpus throughput estimate. A separate 500-record parse comparison on
  44.2 MB from the saved corpus measured 0.503 s with `json.loads` versus
  0.181 s with installed `orjson` (2.8x faster for decoding). The iterator now
  uses `orjson`; the previous attempt was stopped without a checkpoint and the
  same preserved data is being retrained with this change. Parsing plus current
  record validation took 0.706 s for that 500-record/44.2 MB slice, so one full
  40,000-row pass should take well under two minutes if rows have comparable
  sizes. This makes input materialization and retention more likely than raw
  JSON decoding to explain the multi-minute preparation; instrument those
  stages before changing feature encoding again. At 5:14 elapsed, the live
  trainer's `/proc/<pid>/io` `rchar` was 14.3 GB against 3.86 GB of source
  rollout files (roughly 3.7 corpus sizes of process reads, including runtime
  and checkpoint I/O). Root cause confirmed: the state-value evaluator was
  loaded from its 86.1 MB checkpoint once for every 64-record chunk. The
  cached-load benchmark took 2.33 s once; the same 64-record inference chunk
  then took 0.74 s, so across about 390 chunks the repeated load added roughly
  15 minutes and around 33.5 GB of avoidable checkpoint reads. The evaluator
  now loads once per PPO update. Initial live progress after the fix: 1,024
  records / 9,364 transitions in 9.34 s (0.446 s/chunk, including 0.298 s
  evaluator work); projected preparation is roughly four minutes at this early
  rate. A larger 64-record probe
  on another saved shard processed 649 states in 0.42 s total (0.10 s
  read/validate, 0.32 s feature encoding, with policy-input reuse enabled).
  That suggests feature construction alone should take only a few minutes for
  this corpus. Chunk-level logs are now enabled for the restarted run; use them
  to measure the remaining transition materialization, tensor aggregation, and
  optimizer costs before another optimization. The fast preparation attempt
  reached the PPO guard in 3.8 minutes but detected input drift (maximum
  log-probability error 0.1005, approximate KL 0.000120). Evaluator history
  enrichment had mutated two move-token tensors shared with cached policy
  inputs. Those tensors are now cloned before enrichment; the retry must pass
  the PPO consistency guard before producing a candidate checkpoint. On the
  corrected run at 7:19 elapsed, preparation had completed in 3.8 minutes,
  tensor aggregation/optimizer setup was CPU-bound, RSS was about 8.4 GiB with
  no new swap use, and process `rchar` was 7.9 GB, close to the expected two
  3.86 GB rollout scans. This confirms caching removed the repeated evaluator
  checkpoint I/O. No checkpoint had been written at that snapshot; measure the
  remaining aggregation time before optimizing it. Future runs now also log
  separate sample-collection, input-tensor aggregation, and action-tensor
  aggregation milestones, plus optimizer-step timing every 100 minibatches, so
  the remaining update cost can be isolated.

### Iteration 10 and recent-policy evaluator extension (2026-10-20)

  used the established evaluator as its GAE baseline and terminal match

- Held-out local Showdown evaluation completed 512 games over 256 fresh
  side-swapped team/preview pairs: 164 wins, 348 losses, zero draws; score
  rate 32.03% (pair-bootstrap 95% interval 27.15–37.11%); 55 pair sweeps,
  54 splits, 147 pair losses; zero incomplete pairs, timeouts/errors, or action
  adjustments. This is not a clear gain over round 7 (30.3% vs max-damage) and

  49.41% (pair-bootstrap 95% interval 44.14–54.88%), with 253 wins, 259

## Phase 6: Add search

- [x] Evaluate candidate joint actions for both players, accounting for
  simultaneous decisions; the implemented learned search currently applies at
  the opening decision only.
- [x] Use controlled, seeded Showdown outcome sampling for damage, accuracy,
  and secondary effects; exact probability branching is still experimental.
- [x] Repeat stochastic evaluations of candidate move combinations across
  independent chance seeds; paired comparisons report value uncertainty,
  transition count, and decision latency. Broad state coverage remains open.
- [ ] Add selective two-turn search; expand likely/important continuations and
  use the learned value model at the search frontier.
- [x] Preserve switches, Protect, setup, and defensive candidate classes in
  opening-search pruning.
- [ ] Spend more samples on close/uncertain decisions and compare depths at
  equal decision-time budgets.
- [ ] **Deliverable:** configurable search with measured strength, latency, and
  simulation cost.

**Notes:**

- Progress / evidence: 2026-10-19 — zero-sum regret matching, maximin action
  selection, and category-preserving candidate pruning are implemented. A
  local Showdown first-turn joint-action search now optionally evaluates
  leaves with the scalar closed-sheet value model. A small run evaluated 16
  transitions; a cold first inference took 163 ms. Warm batches took 2.1 ms
  (CPU) versus 2.5 ms (GPU) for 16 leaves, and 7.2 ms (CPU) versus 2.7 ms
  (GPU, including transfer) for 192 leaves. This is a plumbing benchmark, not
  a strength result. Selective two-turn search and equal-budget comparisons
  remain open.

  showed 1.43 s median frontier application versus 0.20 s model inference at
  1,536 leaves, so `apply_state_value_frontier` now shares the existing
  tokenized-team cache across leaves. On the same seed/state with 1,536 leaves,
  frontier application fell from 1,698 to 1,470 ms (13.4%); the selected
  action and matrix value were exactly unchanged. An 8-match follow-up measured
  1,204 ms median frontier application (203 ms inference), 1,173 ms Showdown
  search engine time, 2,480 ms median decision latency, and 0.355 games/s.
  This is a small timing sample; CPU feature construction and Showdown

- Separate evaluator-device profile (2026-10-21): the 1,536-leaf benchmark now

  ms; total frontier application fell from 1.35 s to 1.16 s on CUDA. Values

- Repeated-combination clarification (2026-10-20): yes, stochastic candidate
  joint actions should be evaluated on multiple chance outcomes. The current
  first-turn search already does this: it defaults to four chance samples per
  hidden-world/action-pair cell, with a configurable fixed or adaptive budget,
  and shares each sample seed across competing action pairs to make their
  comparison less noisy. A one-sample run is only a smoke test. The million
  training games are separate games from varied states and teams; they do not
  replace repeated chance trials for a specific fixed decision. Future move
  comparisons must report repeats, mean payoff, uncertainty, and latency, and
  should increase samples when paired action estimates are close. This is
  already a Phase 6 requirement; broad repeated-state evaluation and measured
  strength gains remain open.
- Equilibrium scope clarification (2026-10-21): the current implementation
  solves only a sampled, pruned one-turn zero-sum matrix. Regret matching
  approximates a mixed Nash equilibrium of that matrix; it is not a Nash
  equilibrium solution for the full sequential, partially observed VGC game.
  At the time of this note, search was opening-only. The authoritative
  Showdown `Battle` object is held by the Node worker, while the Python policy
  receives player-view observations. Midgame search must branch from that live
  state inside the trusted simulator boundary, replace unrevealed opponent
  sets with public-compatible sampled hypotheses, and return only the acting
  player's candidate payoffs/strategy; passing the live hidden sets to Python
  would violate closed-team-sheet constraints. An engine API probe confirms
  the local Showdown build supports
  `State.serializeBattle` and `State.deserializeBattle`, including live turn,
  side, field, queue, and PRNG state; this provides a candidate branch point.
  `scripts/showdown_hidden_snapshot.js` replaces never-active selected bench
  entries from a sampled set (including a different species selected from the
  public preview) and rebuilds previously active entries from a sampled set
  plus an explicit whitelist of public runtime facts, including protocol HP
  fraction and revealed move IDs. The probe now obtains the HP value from
  `Pokemon.getHealth().shared` and asserts that a sanitized branch retains the
  same displayed floor-percent after applying the sampled max HP. The helper
  rounds HP up within that public percentage interval.
  `buildPublicCompatibleSnapshot` applies the replacement across a full
  opponent roster, and the matrix script accepts
  these `sanitized_snapshots`. The probe now passes 28 checks for
  alternative back species, sampled move/item/ability/stat installation,
  public HP/status/revealed-move preservation, active lead preservation, a
  legal current-state matrix action, branch deserialization, and rejection of
  revealed Pokemon by the bench-only path. It also builds a later-turn fixture
  after both back Pokemon have appeared, aligns a different sampled back order
  without reordering live Showdown references, preserves active slots, and
  completes a 4x4 matrix search from the sanitized state. That midgame smoke
  evaluated 16 advances in 61 ms; the current-state matrix evaluated 16
  advances in 55 ms. A separate 4x4 opening regression
  evaluated 16 advances in 82 ms of engine time (430 ms subprocess wall,
  including startup). These are tiny one-sample timing probes, not strength or
  throughput estimates. The probe also confirmed Showdown retains only the four
  selected Pokemon after preview; the two unselected preview species are not
  search-state members. The later-turn probe was initially a fixture only;
  subsequent headless decision-loop integration is recorded below. The
  public-state whitelist still needs broad
  mechanics coverage, including Transform/form changes, item/ability
  suppression, and side effects.
  Integration boundary: the persistent headless Node worker owns the
  authoritative live `Battle`. Do not serialize that raw snapshot to Python.
  Build each branch from the live state and sampled hidden hypotheses inside
  that trusted worker, then return only player-view frontier features, legal
  candidate semantics, and timing/payoff summaries. This keeps the true hidden
  opponent roster out of the policy process.
  The sanitized current-state matrix is now wired into the headless decision
  flow. See the integration and fixed-seed pilot notes below. Selective
  multi-turn search remains a later step.

- Equal-seed complete-match pilot: material search won 1/8 against max-damage;
  learned search with either the earlier or turn-calibrated evaluator won 0/8.
  The selected opening differed from material on 3/8 seeds. These are only
  eight games per frontier and max-damage is not a broad opponent pool, so no
  strength conclusion is warranted. The learned frontier has not yet shown a
  complete-match benefit.
- Search-context integration (2026-10-19): the 971-feature learned frontier
  now receives the current native action mask, previous own joint action and
  active roster map, and public log-derived mechanics for each leaf. A
  one-world/four-candidate seed-20261097 run completed 16 simulated advances;
  Showdown time was 66 ms, first inference 167 ms, and warm frontier
  application 17.5 ms. Its 16 raw leaves had 252-entry masks and species-only
  opponent payloads. This proves data reaches the evaluator without hidden
  set payloads, not exact mask parity or stronger play. Direct poke-env mask
  parity and equal-budget complete-match tests remain required.
- Expanded value-frontier integration (2026-10-19): the corrected 1,331-input
  checkpoint loaded in first-turn Showdown search. Seed 20261040, two hidden
  worlds, two candidates per side, and one chance sample evaluated eight turn
  advances in 38.4 ms engine time. Cold frontier application was 171.3 ms
  (163.9 ms inference); warm application was 11.2 ms (2.9 ms inference). The
  scalar frontier value was 0.72235 and its opening matched material selection.
  This is small-budget integration evidence only, not a strength result. Full
  details are in `docs/PHASE6_SEARCH.md`.
- Corrected-corpus learned action selection (2026-10-19): the corrected
  checkpoint's scalar probabilities are now used to refill each joint-action
  payoff cell with the mean value across its chance samples. Search takes the
  worst opponent response per own action in each hidden world, then the worst
  sampled world, and chooses the own action with the highest minimum win
  probability. Across eight seeded, two-world/six-candidate opening
  benchmarks, this changed the material-heuristic selection in 3/8 states.
  Median search process wall was 656 ms; learned-frontier application was
  230 ms including 183 ms model inference in fresh processes. Repeated warm
  application was 60 ms including 4.6 ms inference. These are action-selection
  and latency observations, not evidence of improved match strength; equal-time
  complete-match evaluation is still required.
- Chance-outcome sampling (2026-10-19): the live first-turn adapter now
  supports multiple stochastic outcomes per joint-action pair, defaulting to
  four when search is enabled. A PRNG serialization bug was found and fixed:
  distinct samples now vary the current RNG state (`prng`), not merely the
  original seed field. Corrected 1/4/8-sample probes on one state required
  72/288/576 turn advances; child-process wall time was 614/1,103/1,803 ms
  and learned-frontier processing was 236/381/585 ms. The selected action
  stayed the same, but worst-case value shifted .60752/.60648/.60048. In a
  matched 16-game pilot against max-damage, one and four samples both scored
  6–10 with identical paired outcomes/opening actions; mean search adapter
  time was 424/1,337 ms and throughput 1.82/.71 games/s. One search failure
  occurred in each arm and fell back safely. This small pilot shows added
  latency without demonstrated strength gain. Previous timings before the
  PRNG fix are invalid. See `docs/PHASE6_SEARCH.md`.
  Follow-up 32-pair comparison after conditioning sampled worlds on an
  allied Ditto's publicly copied moves: one- and four-sample arms both scored
  12–20 (37.5%; 95% Wilson interval 22.9–54.7% against this fixed opponent),
  all paired outcomes and selected openings matched, and there were no
  search fallbacks. Mean action-selection time was 425 ms versus 1,345 ms
  (p95 457/1,406 ms); full-match throughput was 1.95/0.70 games/s. The extra
  samples changed no choices on these same-seed max-damage matches but cost
  about 3.2x decision time. This narrow run does not establish that one sample
  is enough across states or opponents. Keep repeated sampling for close or
  uncertain decisions and evaluate at equal time budgets.
- Multi-opening chance-count probe (2026-10-19): across eight seeded openings
  (two requested hidden worlds, six candidates), selected actions matched for
  1/4/8 samples in all eight. Median search wall rose 663 / 1,268 / 2,058 ms;
  median frontier probabilities were .45974 / .46173 / .44387. One hidden
  hypothesis implied a different acting-player action menu and was excluded;
  15 of 16 requested worlds were retained. Search now intersects candidate
  actions across worlds and excludes inconsistent action menus before scoring.
  This small opening-only sample is not strength evidence. Candidate targets
  use Showdown's `validTargetLoc`; diagnostic errors identify the rejected
  joint action. Outputs are in
  `outputs/phase6/chance_sampling_multistate_20261019/`.
- Chance uncertainty reporting (2026-10-19): search now reports a standard
  error for each chance-averaged payoff cell and, for learned-value search,
  paired selected-action-minus-candidate means and standard errors by opponent
  response using shared sample indices. One sample reports unknown (`null`)
  uncertainty; repeated equal outcomes can have zero estimated variance. These
  are conditional Monte Carlo errors, not confidence intervals over hidden
  teams or calibrated probability intervals. A seed-20261074 smoke benchmark
  with two worlds, four candidates, and two samples completed 64 advances,
  reported 32 cell standard errors and eight paired comparison rows, with zero
  inconsistent worlds. Adaptive allocation and equal-budget strength evaluation
  remain open. Details and the reproduce command are in
  `docs/PHASE6_SEARCH.md`; seven new search sampling tests pass.
- Same-opening sampling uncertainty probe (seed 20261076): with one hidden
  world and four candidates, the selected joint action matched at 1/4/8 samples,
  but robust value shifted .69741/.68344/.69741. The selected-action per-response
  standard error reached .039 at four samples and .030 at eight. Search-process
  time was 829/1,146/1,515 ms; learned frontier application was 838/1,092/1,588
  ms. This small fixed-state probe demonstrates chance variation and reports
  uncertainty, not improved action quality. Full details are in
  `docs/PHASE6_SEARCH.md`.
- Repeated stochastic evaluation requirement: one rollout per state/action
  pair is a noisy estimate because accuracy, damage rolls, secondary effects,
  speed ties, and hidden-set hypotheses can change outcomes. For search, average
  independent chance samples within each payoff cell; use paired seeds and
  shared sampled worlds across candidate actions where possible to reduce
  comparison noise. The first-turn Showdown adapter already reuses each
  world's sample seed across candidate action pairs (common random numbers),
  and defaults to four independent chance samples. Increase samples adaptively for close decisions and report
  latency with strength. Do not exhaustively repeat every combination by
  default: sample budgets grow quickly, so benchmark 1/4/8 samples and compare
  at equal decision-time budgets.
  For any claim that one move combination is better than another, run each
  candidate from the same fixed observation across multiple independent chance
  seeds; report the number of repeats, mean win-probability/payoff, and an
  uncertainty interval. A single sample is only a smoke check. Use common
  random numbers (same seed/world for competing choices) for paired differences,
  then add independent seeds to estimate variance. Repeat enough that the
  interval is useful for the size of the claimed difference; there is no
  universal repeat count. The running 1M match corpus samples independent games
  across diverse matchups for evaluator training, but does not repeatedly test
  every fixed state/action combination.
  This means each candidate joint-action pair is evaluated more than once when
  chance outcomes can affect its value. It does not mean exhaustively repeating
  every pair a large fixed number of times: one-turn matrix size multiplies by
  the sample count, so use a small baseline (four samples in the live adapter),
  then spend additional samples where paired action-value uncertainty is high.
  Current search has this repeated-sampling path and payoff standard errors;
  broader midgame and equal-latency strength evidence remain open.
  Adaptive first-turn chance sampling is now implemented as an opt-in mode:
  it samples at least the configured minimum (no fewer than four before an
  early-stop check when the maximum permits), and stops only when the leading
  robust action's empirical uncertainty band separates from every alternative;
  otherwise it samples up to the maximum. Fixed-budget behavior remains the
  default. The report records the actual sample count, stop reason, payoff-cell
  standard errors, action intervals, transitions, and latency. This heuristic
  does not yet allocate samples selectively by action row/cell, and its strength
  benefit and latency tradeoff remain unmeasured; the queued post-fit comparison
  will compare it with fixed budgets using the million-game evaluator.
  Chance-distribution design (2026-10-20): sampling can be prohibitive in
  high-branching states, so future search should represent a probability-weighted
  distribution of joint resulting states and compute the expectation of the
  evaluator over those states. Do not substitute expected HP or independent
  per-Pokémon marginals: the evaluator is nonlinear, and joint flinches or a
  knockout changing later turn resolution are strategically relevant. A
  simplified Rock Slide with two targets, 90% accuracy, 16 damage rolls, and
  30% flinch on hit has at most 33 target outcomes (miss, or 16 damage values
  each with/without flinch), hence at most 1,089 paired outcomes before
  merging equivalent states. This is a bounded single-move probe, not a
  guarantee that all full-turn/action-matrix trees are cheap. The design note
  in `docs/PHASE6_SEARCH.md` specifies exact finite-branch enumeration, safe
  state merging, branch-probability checks, and a measured hybrid fallback to
  sampling. Speed gate: a 32-pair one-versus-four-sample pilot measured 425 vs
  1,345 ms mean decision latency (457 vs 1,406 ms p95) and 1.95 vs 0.70
  complete games/s, with matching outcomes and opening actions. This narrow
  pilot gives no strength evidence for the extra samples, while showing their
  roughly 3.2x decision-time cost. A 4x4 matrix with 1,089 leaves in every cell
  would be 17,424 leaves per hidden world, 272x the 64 advances in the measured
  four-sample matrix. Linear extrapolation from its approximately 248 ms engine
  time is about 67 seconds per world, or about 6.7 minutes for six worlds,
  before replay and bookkeeping overhead. This is a warning estimate, not an
  exact-search measurement. Keep exhaustive expansion out of production. Before
  any exact or hybrid search experiment, use the Phase 1 provisional ceiling
  (end-to-end p95 under 2 s; hard deadline under 10 s), begin with selected
  cells, and compare strength at equal wall-clock cost. The 32-pair pilot's
  p95 is opening-action latency and does not verify full-match compliance.
