**Closed-sheet midgame search repair and smoke (2026-10-21):** fixed three
information/legality failures in the opt-in one-turn equilibrium teacher.
Revealed moves are conditioned on the hidden base set only when the public
species can learn them in Gen 9; copied/called moves and Struggle are excluded
from that constraint. Public active abilities are stored separately from
hidden set abilities, so Trace, Skill Swap, Mega abilities, and other visible
ability changes can be simulated without claiming they were the original set
ability. The hidden-world builder now maps active Pokemon from public
switch/replace logs and reconstructs public Mega forms in the sampled Showdown
world; it does not use the live opponent's baseSpecies or illusion fields to
choose the search input. Search is skipped when the public preview includes a
possible Illusion user, since the current belief model does not represent
that identity ambiguity.

Sixteen focused belief tests pass, and
POKEMON_SHOWDOWN_PATH=... node scripts/probe_hidden_bench_snapshot.js passes its
public-compatible snapshot checks, including a visible active ability
overriding the sampled active ability while leaving the sampled base set
intact. A 32-match random-opponent smoke completed 442 matrix decisions with
no search errors; six additional decisions were publicly skipped for possible
Illusion. Search decision median/p95 was 69.8/101.1 ms; complete-match
throughput was 0.49 games/s. This is wiring and information-boundary evidence,
not a strength result. The earlier 512-game attempt and first retry are
diagnostic-only: they exposed Trace follow-up, Skill Swap, copied-move,
Struggle, Mega-form, and Illusion handling issues and must not be used to
claim a clean teacher run.

## Phase 7: Model hidden information and robust action choice

- [ ] Track revealed opponent information and beliefs over plausible unrevealed
  Pokémon, moves, items, and abilities.
- [x] Evaluate opening actions against sampled hidden team configurations and
  legal responses, without modeling opponent behavioral tendencies. Persistent
  midgame belief-conditioned evaluation remains open.
- [x] Build an opening-search payoff matrix over a compact candidate action set.
- [x] Compare approximate mixed-strategy selection (regret matching) with
  robust deterministic maximin choices on paired complete matches.
- [x] Measure the effect of mixed selection in that paired comparison; the
  64-match sample was inconclusive and selectors rarely chose different moves.
- [ ] **Deliverable:** hidden-information tracking and a measured robust
  action-selection method.

**Notes:**

- Progress / evidence: 2026-10-19 — belief tracking accumulates parsed public
  opponent facts and samples legal hidden-set hypotheses from the local
  Showdown builder. Search uses those hypotheses and legal responses without
  modeling opponent behavior. Persistent turn-by-turn belief use is unfinished.
- Progress / evidence: 2026-10-20 — fixed a counterplay scorer tuple-unpacking
  error found by the complete local match check; its speed-control loop now
  reads all five action-record fields. `tests/baselines/test_native_damage.py`
  passes (4 tests). A one-match maximin and equilibrium integration rerun both
  completed with zero baseline fallbacks. The report proves the 4×24 payoff
  matrix and both selection paths execute, but the two methods selected the
  same action on this one state; a paired held-out strength comparison is
  still required before claiming mixed strategy helps. The 18 search tests and
  2 LAN adapter tests pass; a new LAN adapter regression verifies the
  equilibrium selector, seed, world/sample budgets, evaluator, and persistent
  search pool are forwarded to the local Showdown search. The regret-matching
  result now reports a best-response exploitability gap, propagated through
  the search summary and LAN log. Matching-pennies and pure-saddle tests pass.
  On a real learned-frontier opening matrix (seed 91019, 4 own actions × 4
  opponent responses), 1,000 iterations gave value 0.43180 and exploitability
  0.000446; the standalone maximin action matched the Showdown search action.
  Raw report: `outputs/phase7/matrix_solver_exploitability_91019_20261020.json`.
  This measures solver convergence on one matrix, not action strength or the
  benefit of randomization across matches.
- Progress / evidence: 2026-10-21 — `ClosedSheetBeliefTracker` now records the
  two opening species by public active slot and the species first seen through
  public switch/replace events. `possible_selected_rosters()` enumerates every
  four-Pokemon preview selection consistent with those facts, including both
  private back-slot orders. It also updates HP fraction, status, and revealed
  Tera type only from recipient-projected public protocol conditions/events;
  hidden-set sampling filters a Tera type when one is revealed. Ten focused
  belief tests now pass, including the rare revealed-item sampler regression.
  This is the public-input foundation for midgame
  hidden-world construction; the 2026-10-21 probe now builds one sanitized
  later-turn branch and runs a small matrix search on it, but that path is not
  integrated into ordinary decisions and does not yet provide persistent
  turn-by-turn beliefs or equilibrium selection in the live policy.
- Search-world coverage correction (2026-10-21): opening search previously
  enumerated each legal pair of hidden back Pokemon in only one roster order.
  It now uses the public-compatible roster enumerator to include both hidden
  back orders and reports sampled-team and selection-order counts. A local
  Showdown smoke search with one sampled team produced 12 public-compatible
  orders, a 4×48 adversarial payoff matrix, and 192 turn advances. Regret
  matching reported matrix exploitability 0.000107; engine search took
  212 ms and adapter wall time 900 ms. The selected action translated to a
  legal live order. This is one seed and one chance sample; it measures matrix
  coverage and latency, not playing strength. The 27 belief/search tests pass.
- Boundary-corrected regression (2026-10-21): reran the one-hypothesis
  opening-equilibrium smoke after recipient-specific log projection. It still
  produced 12 hidden selection orders, a 4×48 matrix, 192 turn advances, and a
  legal action; engine time was 247 ms and adapter wall time 942 ms. The
  focused belief/search/public-log suite now passes 37 tests. This checks the
  opening path against projected observations but does not complete the
  broader information-boundary audit or show a strength gain.
- Paired selector comparison (2026-10-21): maximin and regret-matched
  equilibrium opening search each played 64 complete local Showdown matches
  against max-damage on identical generated rosters and seeds. Search used two
  sampled teams, all 12 hidden back orders per team, four candidate joint
  actions, and four chance samples (a 4×96 matrix, 1,536 turn advances per
  decision). Maximin won 21/64 (32.8%); equilibrium won 20/64 (31.3%). The
  paired equilibrium-minus-maximin difference was -1.6 percentage points,
  bootstrap 95% interval [-4.7, 0.0]. They selected different opening actions
  in only 2 of 63 successful searches, with one maximin-only win; both methods
  fell back to policy once when hidden-team sampling could not satisfy public
  facts. Median search latency was 2.72 s (p95 2.88 s), and end-to-end rate was
  0.355 matches/s for either method. This small, one-sided sample does not show
  a strength advantage for equilibrium; it does show that the current expanded
  hidden-world/chance budget is expensive and that mixed selection rarely
  changed the sampled action on these states. Side-swapped and larger held-out
  evaluations remain open. Full records and logs are retained losslessly as
  gzip files beside the compact JSON report in
  `outputs/phase7/equilibrium_vs_maximin_64_seed20262900/`.
- Nash/equilibrium scope clarification (2026-10-21): opening search builds an
  approximate payoff matrix. Rows and columns are candidate joint actions for
  the two players, and each cell is scored by simulating the resulting state
  under sampled hidden-team worlds and chance outcomes, then applying the
  learned win-probability evaluator. The opt-in `--midgame-search learned`
  path also builds this kind of one-turn matrix on later move requests, but is
  P1-only and skips explicit forced switches. Outside that opt-in path, ordinary
  later turns still use the policy directly; the midgame search reconstructs
  public facts from the battle log at each decision rather than maintaining a
  persistent belief distribution. Regret matching approximately solves each
  finite matrix; maximin is a robust deterministic comparison. This is not a
  Nash solution of the full multi-turn, partially observed VGC game: action
  sets and sampled outcomes are truncated and the evaluator is approximate.
  The paired 64-game opening comparison found the selectors chose different
  openings only twice and showed no measured strength gain for equilibrium.
- Equilibrium selector default (2026-10-21): because the project assumes a
  strong opponent without exploitable behavioral tendencies, learned opening
  search now defaults to the regret-matched mixed row strategy in the
  headless runner, LAN client, and direct search API. Pure maximin remains an
  explicit comparison option. This follows the equilibrium objective; it is
  not a claim of a strength gain, since the prior 64-match comparison was
  inconclusive and the sampled selectors rarely diverged. The search-focused
  suite passes 22 tests. A complete local match with the selector flag omitted
  used equilibrium on a 4×48 matrix, reported exploitability 0.000281, had no
  search or fallback error, and finished in 1.95 s; one match is wiring and
  legality evidence only. Report: `outputs/phase7/nash_default_smoke_20261021.json`.
- Rare revealed-item sampler regression (2026-10-21): the paired comparison's
  only search failure reproduced at episode 47. Public facts required Rocky
  Helmet and Chandelurite simultaneously; the sampler previously waited for
  the random-set builder to draw both exact items and exhausted its attempt
  budget. Hidden-set generation now conditions sampled sets on observed item,
  ability, and Tera type directly, with Showdown's format validator checking
  the resulting sets. The exact two-world regression passed, and a complete
  match on the same episode/seed now searched all 24 worlds (4×96 matrix,
  1,536 turn advances) and finished without search or action fallback. This
  verifies the known failure path only; it does not change the earlier paired
  strength comparison. A full 64-game maximin rerun on the same match seeds
  then completed 64/64 search decisions with no search failures, matching the
  earlier maximin run's 21 wins and 43 losses. All 63 previously successful
  search decisions chose the same actions, and all 64 match outcomes matched.
  The post-fix arm ran at 0.350 games/s with 2.72 s median decision latency;
  this confirms reliability, not a strength gain. Full post-fix report and
  compressed records are `postfix64_report.json` and `postfix64.*.gz`; the
  exact regression match is in `postfix_seed_episode47.*`.

The headless/server parity comparison matched observations and legal-action
masks exactly across 202 player-state comparisons in an initial switch-loop

matched exactly (`[9, 25]` and `[26, 14]`); one later equivalent side also
matched (`[0, 0]`). Random outcome divergence later removed common legal
choices. `DoublesEnv.reset(seed=...)` only seeds its NumPy generator; its
challenge does not pass that seed to Showdown. Showdown's internal
`RoomBattleOptions` does accept a battle seed, but exposing it requires a
private test-server hook or a deterministic scripted state. Full
post-random-outcome equivalence still needs one of those paths. The comparator
is not counted as passed for a complete match; detailed results and the exact

## Search speed gate and chance-outcome handling (2026-10-20)

- Speed profile update (2026-10-21): current expanded opening search plus
  learned frontier runs at about 0.380 complete games/s (8-game matched
  profile; 2.28 s median decision), with a CUDA value evaluator and CPU
  policy/search bookkeeping. The latest experiment precomputed shared recent
  history features once across frontier leaves. On the same 8 seeds, it kept
  all actions, matrix values, and outcomes identical; median adapter search
  time changed from 2,281 to 2,274 ms and complete-match throughput from 0.38047
  to 0.38061 games/s, effectively no material speedup. The history-context
  work is therefore not a current bottleneck worth further tuning, and the
  shared-history code was removed. Main
  measured costs remain Showdown simulation/frontier construction and adapter
  overhead; warm CUDA value inference is only about 7 ms median. This sample is
  too small for strength conclusions. Disk free space was 28 MiB at that
  measurement; subsequent storage recovery is recorded below.
- Storage recovery (2026-10-21): two retained evaluator JSONL corpora were
  losslessly gzip-compressed: the 400,000-record combined corpus from
  31,122,516,271 to 1,822,511,978 bytes, and its 200,000-record source from
  15,909,792,216 to 928,842,684 bytes. Both decompressed streams matched their
  originals byte for byte and passed `gzip -t`; SHA-256 sidecars and corpus
  manifest paths were updated. Streaming readers now accept `.jsonl.gz` input.
  Archives are
  `outputs/phase5/value_guided_20000_20261020/evaluator_combined_100k_plus_rounds7_11/trajectories.jsonl.gz`
  and
  `outputs/phase5/value_guided_20000_20261020/evaluator_recent_100000/corpus/player_views.jsonl.gz`;
  each has a `.sha256` sidecar with the decompressed-content digest.
  The filesystem has 44,299,067,392 bytes free (41.2 GiB, 96% used), up from
  17 MiB before recovery. Monitor disk before large rollouts. Measured search
  throughput remains 0.380 complete games/s from the small 8-game benchmark;
  no training process is running, so this is not a fresh training rate.
- Frontier condition-age cache (2026-10-21): cProfile identified repeated
  `_condition_age_history` work within a decision. On the 64-leaf benchmark,
  192 context builds across three frontier applications had just one unique
  pair of public condition inputs. The frontier now memoizes those derived
  weather/terrain/field-condition age features per decision, using only the
  observation bits consumed by that encoder. The same seeded benchmark kept
  the selected action, all robust scores, matrix-game values and strategies,
  and simulated transitions exactly equal; warm frontier application fell
  from 89.85 to 50.48 ms. A paired 8-match local-server run retained all 8
  actions, outcomes, and fallback statuses. Median frontier time changed from
  1,009 to 996 ms and adapter search from 2,281 to 2,265 ms; throughput moved
  from 0.3805 to 0.3815 games/s. This end-to-end difference is too small and
  the sample too short to claim a throughput gain. The cache is retained for
  its exact microbenchmark reduction; simulation/search adapter overhead
  remains the dominant cost. Evidence:
  `outputs/phase6/frontier_condition_age_cache_8_20261021/`.

- Search remains experimental and must not slow the speed-first evaluator or
  make normal decisions unbounded. The current learned-search probe measured
  about 280 simulator turn advances/s (72 advances in about 257 ms); a separate
  warm hidden-world search plus value-frontier pass took about 1.12 s for one
  decision. These are small prototype measurements, not final latency targets.
- Do not enumerate the Cartesian product of every random event by default.
  For a two-target Rock Slide, exact per-target combinations can already reach
  33 outcomes per target (miss, or 16 damage rolls crossed with flinch/no
  flinch), hence 1,089 paired outcomes before considering other randomness.
  The evaluator is nonlinear in the resulting joint board, so averaging
  independent per-target values is not generally equivalent to valuing the
  combined state.
- Initial practical path: retain one-turn joint-action lookahead; impose a
  configurable wall-clock/simulation budget; evaluate chance with reproducible
  stratified or adaptive samples and common random numbers when comparing
  actions; merge only outcomes whose strategically relevant resulting state is
  identical; and stop sampling once the decision is sufficiently separated or
  the budget expires. Always return the best-so-far legal action on budget
  expiry. Keep exact enumeration as a small-state reference for validating the
  approximation, not as an unconditional production strategy.
- Before expanding search depth or sample counts, report decision latency
  percentiles, simulator advances/s, value-inference time, chance samples per
  joint action, and strength at equal latency against the baseline. Set the
  actual interactive latency budget from the intended local-server use case;
  until then, use policy-only decisions as the fast fallback and leave search
  opt-in. Search throughput should not be confused with complete games/s or
  evaluator training states/s.
- The optional LAN opening search now has a configurable 3-second total
  decision deadline (`--search-timeout-seconds`), shared across hidden-team
  sampling and simulator search. Expired requests are rejected before dispatch;
  timeout terminates overdue persistent workers, and their output is read in
  deadline-aware chunks so a fragmented response cannot block past the cap.
  The LAN player's existing failure path selects its policy action. This is a
  code-level cap, not evidence that search finishes within three seconds or
  improves strength. Python compilation and the CLI help path confirmed the
  new option is wired; measured latency and fallback-rate evaluation remain
  pending.

  samples measured 768 Showdown advances in 2.52 s (about 387 advances/s); the
  warm learned frontier then took 0.81 s, including 94 ms model inference. The
  2-sample version measured 384 advances in 1.55 s (about 372 advances/s); its
  warm frontier took 0.40 s, including about 43 ms inference. Both chose the
  same opening action on seed 91019, which is only one state and not strength
  evidence. Adaptive 2-to-4 sampling reached its four-sample maximum on this
  state, so its 2.53 s search plus 0.82 s frontier already exceeds the current
  3-second deadline before remaining adapter work. The opt-in LAN default is
  now two samples, while remaining configurable; the 2-sample result is a
  latency-oriented starting point whose strategic adequacy still needs paired
  match evaluation. Artifacts:
  `outputs/phase6/search_speed_deadline_20261020/`.

- Midgame matrix-search prototype (2026-10-21): the opt-in later-turn path
  reuses the local Showdown worker to construct public-compatible states for
  sampled hidden-team hypotheses, then forms a truncated matrix of legal joint
  actions for both players. The learned evaluator scores each resulting
  one-turn state, and regret matching selects our mixed strategy. This is a
  one-turn equilibrium approximation, not full-game Nash play; hypotheses,
  actions, and random outcomes remain sampled/truncated. A three-match smoke

### Round-36 evaluator in equilibrium search (2026-10-21)

- Same-seed local Showdown search comparison on eight opening states changed
  the selected action on one state between V10 and the Round-36 evaluator (7/8
  actions agreed). Four-sample median search time was 836 ms with Round 36 and
  818 ms with V10; median subprocess wall time was 1,211 vs 1,196 ms. This is
  action and runtime evidence only. Reports are
  `outputs/phase6/state_value_round36_search_eval_20261021/candidate.json` and
  `baseline_v10.json`.
- A paired 128-match P1-only evaluation used the Round-33 policy against
  max-damage on identical generated teams and seeds. Policy-only scored 40/128
  wins (31.25%). Applying Round-36 learned midgame equilibrium search at every
  eligible turn scored 5/128 (3.91%), a paired change of -27.34 percentage
  points (95% interval [-35.16, -19.53]). Search achieved 1.07 matches/s vs
  8.84 without search. It attempted 743 decisions: 723 succeeded and 20 fell
  back (11 Transform, 8 possible Illusion, 1 locked Solar Beam target mismatch).
  Invalid-action adjustments remained zero. Successful search adapter latency
  was 133 ms median / 156 ms p95, with 4.9 ms median value inference. The run
  used 32 simulator advances per typical decision. This is a severe strength
  regression; do not use repeated one-turn search for play or training.
- Deterministic maximin on the exact same 128 seeds also scored 5/128 (3.91%),
  with the same -27.34-point paired result. The regression therefore is not
  explained by equilibrium mixed-action sampling alone.
- Limiting search to the first eligible midgame decision per match scored
  32/128 (25.00%) vs 40/128 policy-only. The paired change was -6.25 points
  (95% interval [-14.06, +0.78]); 8 pairs changed in search's favor and 16
  against. Throughput was 3.63 vs 8.95 matches/s. Search succeeded on 123 of
  128 decisions; the other five fell back on Transform/possible-Illusion
  states. This one-decision result is inconclusive, not evidence of benefit.
- These runs keep P1 fixed, so they are diagnostic pilots rather than the
  side-swapped strength gate. The first-search estimated value averaged 0.259,
  while the repeated-search arm won 4.1% of 123 searchable matches; the
  one-search-only arm won 25.0% of 123 searchable matches. This points to
  repeated local replanning/horizon effects as a major risk. Next work should
  diagnose the per-turn payoff/frontier calibration and how choices change
  from the policy action, then require paired strength improvement before
  enabling search.
- The headless runner now accepts `--midgame-search-max-decisions` to compare
  one search decision with repeated replanning. `scripts/summarize_search_eval.py`
  now records midgame decision counts, failure reasons, simulator work, value
  inference and adapter latency. Reproducible match commands are in
  `scripts/evaluate_round33_round36_value_midgame_search.sh`; reports and
  player-view records are under
  `outputs/phase6/round33_round36_value_midgame_search_seed2026102100_128/`,
  `round33_round36_value_midgame_search_maximin_seed2026102100_128/`, and
  `round33_round36_value_midgame_search_equilibrium_max1_seed2026102100_128/`.
- Increasing the one-decision search to eight candidates and two chance samples
  produced 256 turn advances per search decision, 858 ms median adapter
  latency, and 1.03 complete matches/s. It scored 34/128 (26.56%) vs 40/128
  (31.25%) policy-only; paired change -4.69 points (95% interval [-12.50,
  +3.13]), so the extra search budget did not show a gain. Candidate search
  report:
  `outputs/phase6/round33_round36_value_midgame_search_equilibrium_max1_c8_s2_seed2026102100_128/paired_report.json`.
- A state-value comparison on the repeated-search trajectories had only 253
  held-out states from 27 match clusters. V10 and the Round-36 fine-tune had
  Brier 0.06813 and 0.06633 respectively; the paired interval for the change
  was [-0.01300, +0.01304]. ECE was high for both (0.1703 and 0.1565), and
  uncertainty is large. This dataset is too small to select either evaluator
  for these states. Its report and cache are in
  `outputs/phase6/round33_round36_value_midgame_search_seed2026102100_128/evaluator_diagnostic/`.
- The solver's measured matrix exploitability was usually below 0.002, yet
  repeated search's predicted frontier value declined by search ordinal:
  0.259, 0.143, 0.086, 0.051, then about 0.04, while final P1 win rate was
  4.1%. With only one search decision, final P1 win rate was 25.0%. Together
  with identical equilibrium/maximin match scores, the current evidence
  points to a repeated-search horizon/value/action-coverage problem rather

### Search action coverage and Round 37 (2026-10-21)

- [x] Instrument midgame search to log the policy proposal, semantic action
  candidates, and whether the proposal appears in the searched row set.
- [x] Fix the shortlist so the acting policy's legal joint action is always
  retained in the matrix. Previously, a four-row heuristic shortlist covered
  the policy action in only 1 of 4 sampled states. After the fix, the semantic
  proposal was present in all 4 matched-seed states. The extra row raises the
  maximum acting-side matrix from 4 to 5 actions; the policy row is retained
  even if that exceeds the requested shortlist size by one.
- [x] Evaluate one search decision per match on 128 paired local-Showdown
  matches against max-damage using the Round-33 policy and Round-36 evaluator.
  Policy-only scored 32/128 (25.00%); search scored 34/128 (26.56%), paired
  change +1.56 percentage points (95% interval [-2.34, +6.25]). This is
  inconclusive, so search remains an experimental teacher, not a demonstrated
  strength improvement. Search changed the policy proposal on 32% of 125
  successful searches; three search attempts fell back (two possible Illusion
  previews and one hidden-team sampling failure). Search speed was 3.37 matches/s
  versus 9.03 policy-only, with 171 ms median and 202 ms p95 search adapter
  latency. Report:
  `outputs/phase6/round33_round36_value_midgame_search_equilibrium_max1_c4_s1_seed2026102400_128/paired_report.json`.
- [x] Collect 20,000 policy-vs-opponent matches with one equilibrium-search
  teacher decision per eligible match, using the Round-36 opponent mix. The
  collection took 1,202 seconds (16.64 games/s aggregate including a 250-game
  completion shard), used 15.8 GiB peak aggregate RSS, and wrote about 359 MiB
  of compressed rollouts and logs. Across the 20,000 games, search succeeded
  19,369 times, failed 631 times (mostly possible Illusion/Transform states),
  and retained the exact policy proposal in 19,343 successful matrices. Search
  changed the policy action in 6,913 successful cases (35.7%). Zero fallback
  actions were recorded. Rollout and throughput report:
  `outputs/phase5/value_guided_20000_20261020/iteration_0037_search_teacher_20k/collection_report.json`.
- [x] Train a Round-37 student on 19,369 selected searched decisions in
  imitation-only mode, with no PPO or value loss. Four effective passes at
  batch 512 and learning rate 5e-5 produced checkpoint
  `outputs/phase5/value_guided_20000_20261020/iteration_0037_search_teacher_20k/checkpoints/latest.pt`.
  Filtering dropped zero records or teacher labels.
- [x] Evaluate Round 37 against max-damage on 256 matched team/preview clusters
  with both player sides tested. Parent Round 33 scored 29.69%; Round 37 scored
  19.73%. The paired change was -9.96 percentage points (95% cluster-bootstrap
  interval [-14.65, -5.27]); Round 37 was better on 24 pairs, worse on 59, and
  tied on 173. Both had zero action adjustments and no timeouts. This is a
  clear regression; keep Round 37 experimental and Round 33 as the parent.
  Comparison:
  `outputs/phase5/value_guided_20000_20261020/iteration_0037_search_teacher_20k/evaluation/paired_comparison.json`.
- [x] Fix locked-move search generation to distinguish truly targetless
  requests from targetable locks. The former code treated every single-move
  PP-less request as targetless; Solar Beam still requires a target in this
  doubles format. The fix uses Showdown's target locations and prevents those
  candidate actions from failing the live legal mask.
- [x] Fine-tune the Round-36 state evaluator on Round-37 match outcomes, assess

  update. Preserve the parent until a new candidate has paired strength gains.

## Why current training is not converging on strong play (2026-10-23)

The pattern is consistent across the project's direct-policy, value-model,
search, and PPO experiments. The limiting issue is the learning signal and
game-solving method, not a shortage of raw games or GPU time.

- **The old 96.2% pilot is not a reproducible starting point.** The archived
  report claims 96.2% against its Max-Damage heuristic over 500 games, but the
  `pilot_clean` checkpoint and its match records are missing. Its opponent and
  evaluation setup have not been matched to the current closed-sheet runner.
  The nearby 64-game checkpoint is a different model and lost badly to Round
  55. Treat the 96.2% number as an unverified historical result, not as a
  baseline we can continue training from.
- **The million-game predictor learned the data policy's outcomes, not ideal
  play.** Its held-out aggregate scores are strong (Brier 0.13396, log loss
  0.40806, accuracy 79.77%, ECE 0.00221 across 3.68M states), but opening-turn
  Brier is 0.21672. Most labels are outcomes from the policy mixture that
  generated the games, and many states are late enough that the winner is
  becoming obvious. More samples tighten the estimate of that distribution;
  they do not change the target into the value of an optimal continuation.
- **A scalar state value is not an action value.** The predictor estimates
  `P(win | current observation, behavior-policy mixture)`. In the PPO runs it
  is used as a state-only GAE baseline; it does not tell the actor which move
  is better. A baseline can reduce gradient variance, but it supplies no
  counterfactual comparison between Protect, attack, setup, switch, or target
  choices. The Round-85/88/200k scratch predictors did not beat the incumbent
  predictor, and using the mixed predictor in Round 91 reduced paired play.
- **The actor updates have not produced measurable policy improvement.**
  Direct terminal-outcome PPO and HP-shaped reward runs, 50–90% Max-Damage
  exposure, multiple policy pools, more PPO passes, and state-value GAE mostly
  remain near 27–35% against the current Max-Damage implementation. Rounds
  88, 90, and 92 did not establish a paired gain; Round 91 was significantly
  below Round 88 on its matched set. Approximate KL around 0.003–0.006 and
  policy losses near zero show modest updates, but those optimization metrics
  do not demonstrate that the chosen actions got better. Repeatedly restarting
  from Round 88 also prevented evidence from accumulating across policy
  iterations. The update-path audit now confirms that the headless loop trains
  only P1 policy transitions and does not mirror actor seats, even though
  evaluation swaps sides. This is a concrete distribution mismatch and a
  plausible contributor; its strength impact has not yet been isolated.
- **The current team distribution may not match competitive VGC.** Both
  training and recent paired evaluations generate teams with Showdown's
  `RandomChampionsTeams.randomTeam()` builder. The battle format and mechanics
  are correct, but this does not establish performance on curated player-built
  six-Pokemon teams or a tournament-derived roster distribution. Team-building
  and team-preview strength therefore remain separate unverified capabilities.
- **The search experiments solved only a small approximate game.** One-turn
  equilibrium and maximin search used pruned action matrices, sampled hidden
  worlds, sampled chance, and a learned value at the frontier. Repeated search
  and search-teacher imitation both hurt or failed to improve complete-match
  results; the 100k-evaluator search was about 3 points worse than policy-only
  and roughly three times slower. Low exploitability inside a pruned matrix
  only says the small matrix was solved; it does not say the matrix contained
  the right actions or that its frontier values ranked continuations
  correctly. Increasing samples on that same matrix is not the next fix.
- **The benchmark has measured some useful limits.** The immediate-damage gate
  raised Round 33 from 32.23% to 55.27% against Max Damage on one paired set,
  but other gated evaluations landed near 50% and no 75% edge was established.
  This is a useful baseline and action prior, not an optimal policy. The current
  90/10 mixture produced 31.77%, indistinguishable from Round 88. Training at
  90% against one heuristic risks optimizing that benchmark without improving
  robust play.
- **Evaluation is much better than training validation, but it still has
  limits.** Recent comparisons use 1,024 side-swapped team-pair clusters and
  paired cluster bootstrap intervals, which correctly avoids treating two
  sides of one team pairing as independent. Showdown battle RNG is not
  controlled by the evaluator seed, however, and the current default uses one
  match outcome per side and team pairing. Borderline candidates need repeated
  outcome replicates. We also need a permanently held-out team set and broader
  opponent suite so repeated tuning against the same Max-Damage seed range does
  not become benchmark overfitting.
- **Compute is not the primary blocker.** Recent rollout throughput is about
  35–45 complete games/s; Round 92 collected 20k games in 448 seconds. The
  200k evaluator cache build took 36m51s on CPU, while CUDA PPO optimization
  took about 22 seconds. Rollout policy-pool decisions and CPU trajectory/value
  preparation dominate current PPO time. A million games at recent rollout
  rates is hours, not an infeasible amount of computation. Better targets and
  evaluation are likely to return more than merely scaling the same weak
  update.

## Recommended plan toward robust, near-equilibrium play

> **Historical recommendation — superseded 2026-10-29.** It records earlier
> hypotheses and proposals. The active strategy is
> [NEXT_AGENT_PLAN.md](NEXT_AGENT_PLAN.md); follow the active plan where this
> section conflicts with later evidence.

Use `PLAN.md` as the experiment ledger. Keep Round 88 as policy incumbent and
Round 85 as state-value incumbent unless a candidate passes the promotion
gates below. Do not resume Round 93's partial collection. Do not spend another
large batch on a new scalar evaluator or one-turn search variant until the
counterfactual-action experiment demonstrates that its signal ranks actions.

1. **Freeze the target and benchmark.** Specify the local Showdown format,
   closed-team-sheet observation, team-generation distribution, action
   legality, and what “optimal” means operationally. The current use of
   `RandomChampionsTeams.randomTeam()` must be explicitly accepted as the team
   distribution or supplemented with a held-out curated VGC team set. The
   achievable target is
   a low-exploitability policy against a specified team and opponent
   distribution; no finite experiment certifies perfect play in this large
   stochastic imperfect-information game. Preserve a development benchmark
   and lock a separate held-out team/opponent benchmark. Include Max Damage,
   the immediate-damage-gated baseline, Round 55/85/88, historical pool
   policies, counterplay, and self-play league mixtures. Log exact checkpoint,
   teams, side, format, and run provenance for every result.
2. **Training-seat correction — already completed historically.** Round124
   introduced mirrored learner seats and Round125 recorded 85,014 P1 and
   85,075 P2 learner transitions from 20,000 games. Current
   `train_headless_ppo.py` allocates each opponent group across seats and
   invokes `train_native_rl.py --training-team trainable`; the trainer filters
   to the designated `trainable_agent`. This rules out P1-only data as the
   current explanation. Keep log-probability, reward-perspective and action
   mask consistency in the optimizer audit, but do not repeat seat-balancing
   as a proposed fix. See Round124/125 and current source.
3. **Build and validate action-conditioned values.** On a stratified set of
   opening, midgame, and endgame observations, enumerate legal own actions and
   a compact but strategically complete set of opponent responses. Always
   retain policy proposals, switches, Protect, setup, spread attacks, and
   defensive responses. For each joint action, play complete continuations
   under a frozen continuation-policy league. Use paired/common random
   numbers where available and repeated outcomes where server randomness is
   not seedable. Train `Q(observation, own action, opponent response)` as a
   win-probability output in [0,1], and measure both calibration and action
   ranking accuracy against held-out rollouts. Only scale this data if better
   action ranking predicts better complete matches.
4. **Use a robust policy-improvement target.** Construct small payoff matrices
   from the validated action-conditioned estimates, average over beliefs about
   unrevealed legal sets and chance outcomes, and use regret matching or a
   comparable equilibrium solver to produce a mixed target. Train the direct
   policy toward those distributions with a conservative trust region, while
   also measuring against the frozen league. Avoid one-hot imitation of a
   single sampled equilibrium action. Check candidate coverage and value
   calibration before applying search online; keep search disabled until it
   beats policy-only at equal decision-time budget.
5. **Run policy-space self-play in measured 20k-game iterations.** After the
   action-value target passes Step 3, train against a rotating league that
   includes past best policies and varied tactical opponents. Randomize seat,
   team order, and starting conditions; train from the best validated policy
   and retain the prior best as an opponent. Do not overweight Max Damage as
   the sole target. Refresh the value/action-value data from each improved
   policy, but keep train, development, and final test match clusters disjoint.
   Track average and lower-tail results across opponents, not just Max Damage.
6. **Use promotion gates that account for game randomness.** For each 20k
   candidate, first run at least 1,024 side-swapped team-pair clusters against
   the incumbent and the core opponent suite. Repeat stochastic outcomes on
   borderline comparisons (initially two outcomes per side/team pair; increase
   to four or more if the paired interval still overlaps both meaningful
   improvement and regression). Bootstrap at team-pair cluster level. Promote
   only when the candidate improves against the incumbent with a paired
   interval excluding zero, has no material lower-tail regression against the
   suite, and has zero invalid actions/protocol failures. Reserve a final
   untouched benchmark for periodic checks.
7. **Optimize speed at the measured bottleneck.** Preserve the current headless
   runner and Showdown reference. Profile rollout action selection, CPU
   trajectory/value preparation, and cache construction separately. Reuse
   caches and optimize CPU materialization before increasing model size or
   moving simulation to CUDA. Benchmark independent CPU rollouts and GPU model
   inference at actual search batch sizes; do not begin a simulator CUDA port
   without a validated prototype showing a large real-workload gain. Keep
   project storage below half of the filesystem and avoid duplicate raw
   corpora.

**Next work after this plan:** implement and verify mirrored-seat policy
collection/training before launching another 20k PPO iteration. Then run the
small counterfactual action-ranking pilot in Step 3. The current read-only audit
confirmed the P1-only update path; it did not establish whether this mismatch
alone explains the weak play. Measure it with a paired seat-balanced update
before drawing that conclusion.

## Round-92 team-preview selector transfer checks (2026-10-23)

- A selector trained from Round-92 rollout data improved the Round-88 battle
  policy's team preview over random selection on three independent paired
  evaluations. It sees the evaluated player's own six-Pokemon roster and
  species-only opponent preview. The opposing player's preview remained
  random and unchanged between baseline and selector arms. This isolates the
  evaluated player's preview choice; it does not establish full-agent strength.
- Against Max Damage on seed 20268800, the selector scored 40.03% versus
  32.60% with random preview on 1,023 matched team-pair clusters: +7.43 points,
  95% cluster-bootstrap interval [+4.50, +10.46]. On independent seed
  20272800, it scored 40.97% versus 33.54% on 1,024 clusters: +7.42 points,
  interval [+4.35, +10.55].
- Against Counterplay on seed 20274800, it scored 39.93% versus 34.60% on
  1,023 matched clusters: +5.33 points, interval [+2.35, +8.36].
- Against the Round-55 checkpoint on seed 20275800, it scored 61.20% versus
  52.98% on 1,022 matched clusters: +8.22 points, interval [+5.09, +11.40].
- Each arm had one incomplete pair in the Counterplay and Round-55 comparisons;
  only common complete team-pair clusters were used. Completed games had zero
  action adjustments. Battle RNG is server-side and not paired exactly; paired
  team clusters account for team variation, while repeated outcomes would
  further reduce chance noise.
- These results validate a useful, separable preview component across three
  opponent families, but the battle policy still wins fewer than half its
  games against Max Damage and Counterplay. Keep the selector checkpoint
  experimental until it is tested on held-out curated VGC teams and used in a
  complete-agent comparison across the core opponent suite. Reports:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round92_team_preview_selector_20k_20261023/comparison_seed20268800_selector_vs_random.json`,
  `comparison_seed20272800_selector_vs_random.json`,
  `comparison_counterplay_seed20274800_selector_vs_random.json`, and
  `comparison_round55_seed20275800_selector_vs_random.json`.

**Next work:** before another PPO batch, correct and verify mirrored-seat
policy collection/training, as described in Step 2. Keep the validated preview
selector as a separate candidate component and add curated-team evaluation.
Then run the small counterfactual action-ranking pilot in Step 3. The seat
mismatch is a concrete defect, but its impact on strength remains to be
measured in a paired seat-balanced update.

team choice but does not change that conclusion.

- A conservative warm-start fine-tune from Round85 completed on the same

## Round95 opening-action counterfactuals (2026-10-24, completed)

- Added a closed-sheet-safe snapshot of the acting policy's first legal
  observation, legal mask, executed action, and action source. The opponent's
  player-view row does not receive this data. A replay preflight reproduced
  an entire earlier match exactly (12 P1 decisions, 13 P2 decisions, 14 joint
  advances, terminal state), confirming that saved states can be reconstructed
  reliably.
- Ran a matched 2,048-opening comparison against Max Damage. In each seed/team
  cluster, the first Round95 action was either the policy action or the
  Max Damage action; the remainder of the policy's match was unchanged. Both
  arms had identical opening observations, masks, teams, and previews in all
  2,048 clusters. Win rate was 34.03% with the policy action and 40.67% with
  the Max Damage action. The paired difference for policy-minus-Max-Damage
  was -6.64 points (95% cluster bootstrap [-8.79, -4.49]).
- Repeated the comparison against frozen Round88 with 2,048 matched clusters.
  The policy-action arm scored 48.29%; the Max Damage first-action arm scored
  52.15%. Difference was -3.86 points (95% interval [-6.01, -1.66]). The
  direction transfers to this learned opponent, although it is still only an
  opening-action intervention and does not establish a generally superior
  policy.
- The initial 512-cluster pilot had wide, inconclusive intervals; the two
  larger comparisons provide clearer evidence. Reports and raw data:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round95_counterfactual_maxdamage_2048_20261024/summary.json`,
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round95_counterfactual_round88_2048_20261024/summary.json`,
  and `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round95_counterfactual_opening_pilot_512_20261024/pilot_summary.json`.
- **Training implication:** Round95 is consistently leaving opening value on
  the table relative to the immediate-damage baseline in these two matchups.
  Do not turn the sparse terminal results directly into action-value labels:
  there is one sampled continuation per action and state, and the action
  ranking may depend on opponent and hidden sets. Next, collect balanced
  action-conditioned outcomes on held-out teams with multiple response
  policies, estimate uncertainty/calibration, then test a low-rate policy
  improvement against the frozen baselines before starting another full PPO
  batch. Keep Max Damage and Round88 as evaluation opponents, not assumed
  opponent behavior models.
- Reproducible runners:
  `scripts/run_round95_counterfactual_maxdamage_2048.sh` and
  `scripts/run_round95_counterfactual_round88_2048.sh`. Summarizer:
  `scripts/summarize_counterfactual_action_pilot.py`.

  row. The row includes public mechanics and native action features, and the
  opponent's perspective still contains species only.

  Max Damage and 2,048 against Round88. Fitted four teacher-only passes from
  Round95 at learning rate 1e-5 using CUDA; 4,096 transitions were prepared in
  4.2 seconds and 32 optimizer steps ran. This is an experimental challenger,
  not an automatic promotion.

  (95% cluster bootstrap [52.44%, 59.96%]), with 1,024 games, no timeouts, and
  no action adjustments.

  scored 37.89% versus Round95's 39.55%; paired delta -1.66 points (95%
  interval [-4.69, +1.46]). This screen was inconclusive. With two outcomes

  delta -1.51 points (95% interval [-3.71, +0.59]). There is no measured

  Round96 scored 54.10% versus Round95's 51.51%; paired delta +2.59 points
  (95% interval [+0.39, +4.79]). One Round95 control case timed out; 1,023
  cases were matched. No action adjustments occurred.
- The 512-cluster single-outcome screens took 175-267 seconds per model arm
  (about 3.8-5.9 complete local-server games/s with four workers). The
  repeated screens took 380-573 seconds per arm. The repeat-aware summarizer
  now clusters bootstrap resampling by team seed, averaging repeated battles
  before resampling. Round96 remains experimental because its Round88 gain has
  not transferred to Max Damage, the primary target. Keep Round95 frozen as
  the accepted comparison baseline.
- Reports and candidate:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/direct_policy_round96_opening_maxdamage_imitation_4096_20261024/checkpoints/latest.pt`,
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round96_opening_imitation_eval_512_20261024/`,
  and `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round96_opening_imitation_eval_512x2_20261024/`.
- Round97 completed from Round96 with 20,000 headless games, the Round94
  fine-tuned evaluator for terminal GAE, 25% Max Damage, 25% Counterplay, and
  50% historical policies including Round95, Round88, and Round85. It uses

## Round101 strategy-class-balanced PPO (2026-10-24, evaluated)

- Diagnosis: loss weights were unbalanced by decision count. A 25/25/50 match
  mixture produced approximately 20/20/60 of the sampled decision steps
  because policy-pool matches last longer. The optional loss balancing also
  treated each policy checkpoint as a separate group, so adding pool versions
  could increase the pool's total objective weight.
- Corrected `src/training/native_ppo_train.py` to group samples by strategy
  class (the opponent label before its `|` metadata). Equal loss weighting now
  means equal aggregate weight for Max Damage, Counterplay, and the whole
  policy pool. This is a targeted objective correction; the rollout mix and
  learning rate remain unchanged.
- Round101 started from Round97 and used 20,000 games with 25% Max Damage, 25%
  Counterplay, and 50% policy pool; it enables class-balanced loss at power
  1.0 and uses two PPO passes at 7.5e-5. Pool candidates include Round100,
  Round99, Round98, Round95, Round88, and Round85. Its validated checkpoint is
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/direct_policy_round101_round97_class_balanced_round94_value_gae_ppo_20k_20261024/checkpoints/latest.pt`.
- It completed in 1,011.6 seconds: 679.3 seconds of rollout collection (29.4
  games/s at the slowest-shard wall rate) and 332.3 seconds for PPO, or 19.8
  games/s end-to-end. The rollout stage took longer than earlier rounds
  because five historical-policy shards plus four heuristic shards created
  nine jobs for eight workers; the final 2,000-game shard ran after a worker
  slot freed. Average worker CPU was 5.57 cores, peak aggregate RSS 7.55 GiB.
  Per-shard rates were 6.85-6.95 games/s against Max Damage, 5.37-5.38 against
  Counterplay, and 4.72-4.86 for four 2,000-game policy shards; the fifth
  2,000-game policy shard ran at 6.34 games/s after queuing.
- PPO preparation took 254.7 seconds for 30,000 records / 171,956 transitions;
  evaluator inference used 133.8 seconds across 260,462 states. Tensor
  aggregation took 5.8 seconds, and 672 optimizer steps took 23.7 seconds.
  Approximate KL was 0.00374 and clip fraction 3.54%.
- Paired evaluation on the same 512 Max Damage team clusters as Round97 gave
  Round101 a 38.96% score, versus Round97's 41.60%; difference -2.64 points
  (95% interval [-5.66, +0.39]), so the result is inconclusive and the point
  estimate favors Round97. Directly against Round97, Round101 scored 54.00%
  over 512 complete side-swapped clusters (95% interval [50.20%, 57.81%]); no
  timeouts or action adjustments. This is some evidence of an improved
  head-to-head result, but class balancing has not yet improved the primary
  Max Damage score. Round101 remains an experimental pool member.
- Reports: `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round101_paired_screen_512_20261024/`.
  Training telemetry and round record are in
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/direct_policy_round101_round97_class_balanced_round94_value_gae_ppo_20k_20261024/`.
- Reproduction command: `scripts/train_round101_round97_class_balanced_gae_ppo_20k.sh`.

## Latest speed and bottleneck measurements (2026-10-26)

- Latest full training iteration: Round121 completed 20,000 games in 787.9
  seconds (25.4 games/s end-to-end). Rollouts took 477.5 sec (41.9 aggregate
  games/s) and PPO preparation/optimization took 310.4 sec. Eight rollout jobs
  ran on eight workers. CPU rollouts remain the largest phase; PPO input
  preparation is the next largest cost.

  evaluated 256,096 states in 125.6 sec; record preparation plus tensor
  aggregation took about 243.8 sec. The optimizer ran 664 steps in about
  24 sec (approximate KL 0.00329, clip fraction 2.98%). CUDA training leaves
  CPU simulation and trajectory preparation as the main throughput limits.
- Round121 action selection averaged 54-55 ms/turn against Max Damage,
  88-89 ms against Counterplay, and 76-78 ms against the policy pool.
  Observation encoding took 24-26 ms/turn; policy inference took 32 ms against
  Max Damage and 66-69 ms against the policy pool; headless engine roundtrip
  took 28 ms against Max Damage and 32 ms against Counterplay/policy. Aggregate
  rollout RSS peaked at 7.57 GiB and average CPU use was 7.57 cores. The
  slowest shards were policy-pool jobs at 5.26-5.34 games/s; these four shards
  determine rollout wall time.
- The measured optimization priority is trajectory preparation and state-value
  inference (about 244 sec of PPO work), followed by slow policy rollouts.
  Optimizer execution (24 sec) is not a useful first GPU optimization target.
  Max Damage evaluation remains faster than policy-versus-policy evaluation;
  latest repeated screens were 4.69 games/s vs Max Damage and 3.44 games/s vs
  Round102. Keep separate throughput measurements for both.

## Round145 estimate a policy payoff game and use its robust mixture (2026-10-27; evaluated)

- To replace hand-tuned opponent weights with equilibrium-oriented evidence,
  measure the Round102, Round109, Round130, and Round136 policies against one
  another and against Max Damage and Counterplay. All matchups share one
  held-out team/seed schedule. Use 128 team-pair clusters and one repeat per
  side as an exploratory matrix screen; confidence limits must be considered
  before choosing a training distribution.
- Construct a zero-sum payoff matrix, solve it with regret matching both at
  the point estimates and at per-cell lower 95% confidence limits, and use the
  conservative opponent-response mixture only as a candidate training mix.
  This restricted strategy game is not claimed to be full-game Nash.
- Evaluation script: `scripts/evaluate_round145_policy_league_matrix.sh`;
  matrix summarizer: `scripts/summarize_policy_league_matrix.py`.
- All 14 matchup screens completed: 3,584 side-swapped matches across 128
  fixed team-pair clusters per matchup, one battle repeat per side, zero
  action adjustments, timeouts, or errors. Aggregate throughput was 4.55
  completed games/s (2.39-5.70 by matchup; 787.6 seconds summed across the
  screens). The payoff matrix's point-estimate response mixture assigned
  15.7% to Max Damage and 84.3% to Counterplay; the lower-confidence-limit
  game assigned 16.6% and 83.4%, with negligible weight on historical policy
  columns. The conservative row mixture favored Round130 (65.5%) and Round136
  (34.3%), while the point estimate favored Round102. These differences and
  broad per-cell intervals show substantial sampling uncertainty; this is an
  empirical restricted-strategy mixture, not a full-game equilibrium.
- The next training trial scales the conservative heuristic response mix to
  leave 10% policy-pool coverage: 15% Max Damage / 75% Counterplay / 10%
  historical policy pool. It disables opponent-class reweighting so those
  sample proportions are the actual PPO loss proportions, unlike the prior

## Round161 one-turn robust search pilot and locked-move fix (2026-10-27; evaluated)

- Compare the Round136 policy with its immediate-damage gate against the same
  policy/gate plus one equilibrium matrix search on matched Max Damage games.
  Use two hidden worlds, four candidate actions per side, one chance sample,
  and at most one search decision per match. This is a fixed-P1 runtime and
  action-quality pilot; the existing search adapter is still P1-only.
- Reproduction: `scripts/evaluate_round136_gate_vs_midgame_search.sh`.
  Round136 gate control and gate+search each completed 256 games. Gate-only
  scored 140-116 (54.69%); gate+search scored 141-115 (55.08%). The paired
  change was +0.39 points (95% interval 0.00 to +1.17); only one outcome
  changed. Do not call this a strength gain. Search changed the policy action
  on 181/245 successful decisions (73.9%) and had zero action adjustments.
- Gate-only throughput was 9.40 matches/s (mean 0.105 s/match); gate+search was
  3.37 matches/s (0.294 s/match). Search latency was 177.7 ms median / 204.0
  ms p95. Each successful decision advanced 40 simulator turns at a median
  362.9 transitions/s; value inference took 5.62 ms median. The added search
  cost is large compared with the inconclusive match result.
- The first run had 11 search fallbacks: six possible-Illusion previews and
  three publicly observed Transform states were deliberate safety skips; two
  were a Solar Beam mismatch. The local Showdown fixture confirmed that its
  parser accepts the forced targetless charge continuation and rejects the
  fake target-bearing orders, but `ShowdownDoublesEnv.get_action_mask` and the
  max-damage helper did not support that valid action. The mask, order
  conversion, and max-damage decode paths are fixed. Exact-seed replays of
  episodes 61 and 157 both completed a successful search decision with zero
  action adjustments and zero fallbacks. Reproduce with
  `scripts/replay_round136_gate_search_locked_moves.sh`; raw logs are in the
  pilot directory's `solarbeam_replays/` subdirectory. The six Illusion and
  three Transform skips remain.
- The updated focused mask/search tests passed (9), and the three max-damage
  selector tests passed separately. A broader selected run had 12 passes and
  one unrelated counterplay speed-cache fixture failure because its
  `SimpleNamespace` lacks a `mega` attribute; it does not cover the changed
  max-damage path. Full P2 search support, broader side-swapped strength
  evaluation, and any policy improvement from search remain incomplete.
- Paired report and exact-fix follow-up:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round136_gate_vs_midgame_search_256_20271027_20261027/paired_report.json`
  and `followup_locked_move_fix.json`.

## Counterplay baseline closed-sheet re-audit (2026-10-27; diagnostic only)

- Re-ran the support-aware counterplay heuristic against Max Damage on 256
  distinct team pairs, two repeats per pair, with sides swapped: 1,024 complete
  games, 708 wins, 316 losses, zero draws, zero action adjustments, and 69.14%
  score (normal 95% interval 66.31%-71.97%). Throughput was 13.89 aggregate
  games/s. Reproduce with `scripts/evaluate_counterplay_paired.py --pairs 256
  --repeats 2 --workers 8 --seed 2026102701 --output-dir
  training/outputs/phase12_headless/counterplay_vs_maxdamage_paired_1024_20261027`.
- Source audit found the result is privileged: `evaluate_native.py` passes the
  other player's battle object to `choose_counterplay_action`, which reads
  `opponent_battle.team` and its active moves. That object includes the full
  roster and unrevealed moves from the acting player's closed-sheet view.
  Therefore this score is diagnostic only and must not be compared as a fair
  agent result or used to produce training targets. The files are small (6.9
  MiB); preserve for audit, labeled as information-leaking.
- Next: implement an information-safe threat model using only the acting
  player's observation and publicly revealed opponent details. This has since
  been done in the experimental baseline described below. Keep the current
  learner at 39.9% and its own-state damage gate at 56.9% as the measured
  learned-policy controls.

## Public-only counterplay baseline, neutral hidden stats (2026-10-27; evaluated)

- Added `choose_public_counterplay_action`, which sees only the acting player's
  battle view and `PublicBattleHistory`. It filters opponent active move data
  against the public protocol history, ignores unrevealed moves, and models

  object or their action mask. The evaluation runner supports this as both
  player 1 and player 2.

  683 wins, 341 losses, zero draws, and zero action adjustments. Score was
  66.70%; a 20,000-resample team-pair cluster bootstrap interval is
  61.91%-71.48%. Aggregate throughput was 13.95 games/s on eight workers.

  attacker projection. Reproduction:

  records:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/public_counterplay_neutral_attacker_vs_maxdamage_paired_1024_20261027/`.

## Closed-sheet inference check for Round156 (2026-10-27; confirmed)

- Evaluation code previously passed the opponent's selected Max Damage action
  into policy action-feature construction. The current Round156 model does not
  consume that input: its checkpoint has `counterplay_prior_weight=0` and its
  action-feature variant is `damage_ko_friendly_fire`. The check therefore
  finds a latent unsafe interface path, not a leak that changed this
  checkpoint's prior 39.89% result.

  policy counterplay priors off, and rejects frozen-policy prediction requests
  unless `--allow-privileged-opponent-action-oracle` is explicitly supplied
  for a diagnostic. Per-match records include the flag value.

  repeated side-swapped outcomes each, completed 1,024 games: 413 wins, 611
  losses, zero draws, score 40.33% (95% team-pair bootstrap interval
  35.35%-45.31%). There were zero action adjustments, timeouts, and errors.

  training/outputs/phase12_headless/direct_policy_round156_round136_maxdamage75_public_gate_w003_ppo5_round94_value_gae_ppo_20k_20261027/checkpoints/latest.pt
  --opponent max_damage --pairs 256 --outcome-repeats 2 --workers 8 --seed
  2026102704 --output-dir
  training/outputs/phase12_headless/round156_no_oracle_maxdamage_1024_20261027
  --team-selection-checkpoint
  training/outputs/phase12_headless/round94_selfplay_mirrored_20k_20261023/selector.pt
  --device cpu`.

## PPO + auxiliary prediction implementation (2026-10-30; candidate not promoted)

- Added auxiliary heads and losses to native self-play PPO. The policy trains a
  terminal win-probability target plus opponent hidden-set move, item, and
  ability targets. Hidden-set labels live only in `hidden_set_targets`; the
  observation builder does not copy those targets into model input. Revealed
  moves are masked from hidden-move supervision, and item/ability labels are
  supervised only where they are still hidden.
- New PPO runs enable the ability head and use loss weights 0.10 for win
  probability and 0.05 for hidden-set prediction by default. Action generation
  and policy logits remain the same interface as earlier native PPO.
- 64-game implementation smoke (Round423) passed rollout preflight and ran
  five CUDA optimizer steps. The telemetry recorded finite auxiliary losses:
  win probability 0.690, hidden moves 6.554, item 5.947, ability 5.635. This
  establishes that targets and losses flow through the training step; it is not
  evidence of calibration or better play.
- Round424 completed 10,000 matches (2,500 each vs random, Max Damage, public
  counterplay, and a four-policy historical/self-play pool) in 592.4 seconds:
  437.4 seconds rollout and 123.5 seconds PPO preparation/optimization, for
  16.9 matches/s over full training wall time. The 8-worker rollout produced
  80,079 transitions; 12,500 PPO-valid player-view rows; seats were balanced
  (5,002/4,998), with no preflight errors. CUDA PPO ran 628 steps in about 26
  seconds, with KL 0.00630, clip fraction 7.43%, win-probability loss 0.544,
  hidden-move loss 5.813, item loss 4.866, and ability loss 5.166. These loss
  values alone do not tell us if predictions are calibrated or actions got
  stronger.
- Match-rate bottlenecks vary by opponent. A policy-pool shard averaged 5.8
  matches/s with about 32 ms policy inference, 23 ms observation encoding,
  and 32 ms Showdown roundtrip per episode. Public-counterplay shards averaged
  2.9 matches/s; baseline action scoring was 226-229 ms, versus 27 ms Showdown
  roundtrip, 22 ms encoding, and 32 ms policy inference. Thus the engine is a
  minority of current wall time, especially for the counterplay mix.
- JAX/GPU simulator rewrite is not justified by these measurements yet. The
  correctness reference is the local Node/Showdown engine, and porting its
  mechanics/state semantics would be substantial. Prioritize profiling and
  reducing counterplay action-scoring cost, batched policy inference, and
  trajectory throughput first. Reconsider a batched JAX simulator only after
  a representative prototype includes state conversion and correctness checks
  and demonstrates a meaningful end-to-end gain on this actual workload.
- Candidate checkpoint:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round424_selfplay_auxiliary_ppo_10k_20261030/checkpoints/latest.pt`.
  Paired side-swapped held-out evaluation against its Round423 starting policy
  completed in
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round425_candidate_vs_round423_heldout_256x2_20261030/`.
  It scored 51.46% on the cluster-weighted score (1,020 games across 256
  clusters; 95% cluster-bootstrap interval [46.29%, 56.64%]); two of 1,024
  cases timed out or errored, and no action was adjusted. This is no clear
  improvement over its start checkpoint.

## Speed profile and next optimizations (2026-10-30)

- Round424 collected 10,000 matches in 437.4 seconds across eight workers
  (22.86 aggregate rollout games/s); PPO data preparation and optimization
  took 123.5 seconds; total iteration wall time was 592.4 seconds (16.89
  games/s). Host: 16 logical CPUs and an RTX 4060 Laptop GPU with 8 GB.
- Per-opponent end-to-end rollout profiles (milliseconds per match; games/s is
  the mean per-worker shard rate, not aggregate throughput):

  | Opponent | games/s | End-to-end | Action selection | Observation encoding | Showdown roundtrip | trajectory write |
  | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
  | Random | 6.99 | 141 | 48 | 29 | 34 | 9 |
  | Max Damage | 7.27 | 136 | 50 | 26 | 29 | 9 |
  | Historical policy pool | 5.10 | 193 | 84 | 27 | 34 | 12 |
  | Public counterplay | 2.89 | 344 | 269 | 22 | 27 | 7 |

  The complete 8-worker mixed rollout achieved 22.86 aggregate games/s; the
  full iteration including PPO preparation and optimization achieved 16.89
  games/s. Per-opponent rows describe individual shard rates.

- Nested timing details: policy inference accounted for about 36 ms/match
  against Random, 35 ms vs Max Damage, 72 ms vs the historical policy pool,
  and 32 ms vs Public Counterplay. Public Counterplay's baseline scorer
  accounted for 228 ms/match (66% of end-to-end time, 85% of action-selection
  time). Inference and baseline scorer timings are inside action selection;
  don't add them a second time. Simulator roundtrips are 27-34 ms/match
  (roughly 8-24% of end-to-end time depending on opponent), so optimizing the
  remaining time has more value than a simulator-only GPU port.
- Ranked speed work:
  1. Batch policy inference across decisions from concurrent live rollouts.
     Rollout workers currently infer independently on CPU; compare CPU batches
     with a shared GPU inference service at actual batch sizes, including
     queue/transfer time, games/s, and p95 action latency.
  2. Cache and fuse observation features / static lookups, then benchmark
     precomputed team features and reusable compact-array buffers. Keep the
     player-view leakage audit.
  3. Keep eight workers as the measured best setting for the 240-game
     Max-Damage workload; 12/16 workers were slower and used more memory.
     Prototype batching across the existing live rollouts before retesting
     broader mixtures and tail decision latency.
  4. Profile and accelerate Public Counterplay candidate scoring; its scorer
     accounts for 228 ms/match in that workload. Cache static move/type data
     and batch score features while retaining switches, Protect, setup, and
     defensive responses. Recheck score parity and decision quality.
  5. After higher-cost work, benchmark buffered compact trajectory writes or
     chunk compression; the run stored about 1.8 GB and used 7-12 ms/match in
     writes.
- JAX simulator port remains a measured follow-up only. The current reference
  is local Pokémon Showdown; state conversion and parity testing add overhead.
  Prototype only if a representative end-to-end workload shows a substantial
  gain after transfer and conversion, rather than relying on GPU peak FLOPs.

  training loss fell from 0.8263 to 0.2392, with near-identical policy loss,
  value loss, KL, and win-probability loss; this is expected because the large
  hidden-set losses were no longer weighted. It does not by itself demonstrate

  this single ablation is inconclusive; keep Round430 as the validated

  complete games/s. This is evaluation throughput, not training rollout speed.

### Pre-PPO rollout scan reuse optimization (2026-10-30; end-to-end confirmation pending)

- Measured the separate sample-count pass in `train_native_rl.py` on the exact
  Round435 rollout files: 3.87 GiB and 28,000 valid records, totaling 162,366
  trainable transitions. The scan took 35.96 seconds (115.6 MB/s). This is
  outside the 159.3-second trainer preparation/aggregation timing reported for
  Round435, so it is a distinct repeated read.
- The headless training path now passes its completed preflight report into the
  PPO trainer. The report provides the exact valid-record count, trainable
  transition count, and rollout SHA-256 digest, allowing the trainer to skip
  the extra trajectory parse while preserving optimizer step budgeting and
  rollout identity. The audit's digest was verified against an independent
  recomputation over all 4,155,849,741 nonblank bytes; counts matched the
  previous scan exactly.
- Matched same-data PPO replays, using the same initial checkpoint, data,
  settings, seed, and CUDA device, took 217.98 seconds with preflight reuse
  and 260.74 seconds with the old scan (42.77 seconds / 16.4% lower wall time).
  Both produced bit-identical model parameters and identical loss, KL,
  transition, and 1,272-step metrics. The measured standalone scan was 35.96
  seconds, so treat that as the repeatable direct saving; attribute the rest
  of the wall-time difference to run variation. This measures the PPO update
  only, with rollout generation excluded.
- Artifacts:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round437_input_scan_reuse_speedbench_20k_20261030/`
  and
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round438_input_scan_control_20k_20261030/`;
  comparison summary:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round437_input_scan_reuse_speedbench_20k_20261030/comparison.json`.

### PPO input preparation: reuse cached static tensors (2026-10-30)

- `build_model_inputs` already caches each match's static team-token tensors.
  PPO preparation now reads those immutable cached tensors directly instead of
  cloning seven small tensors for every recorded state. Other callers retain
  the default clone behavior.
- A reproducible CPU microbenchmark on 1,971 real Round435 transitions
  (256 records, Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.15 CPU, six passes with the first
  excluded) measured a median 0.2780 s with clones and 0.2324 s with reuse,
  a 16.4% reduction for this input-building stage. Every returned model-input
  tensor matched exactly.
- If the saving scales linearly to Round435's 162,366 trainable transitions,
  the estimate is 3.76 seconds, or about 2.5% of the 151.5-second PPO sample
  collection time. This is a microbenchmark extrapolation, not yet an
  end-to-end PPO timing. Continue profiling record extraction and tensor
  aggregation, which remain larger costs.
- Reproduction command:
  `PYTHONPATH=. python scripts/benchmark_ppo_static_cache_reuse.py training/outputs/phase12_headless/round435_equilibrium_mixture_response_20k_20261030/rollouts/round_0001_max_damage_p1_shard000.jsonl --records 256 --transitions 1971 --repeats 6`.
- Report: `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round439_static_cache_reuse_profile_20261030/benchmark.json`.

### PPO transition extraction: replace scalar NumPy clipping (2026-10-30)

- Profiling 256 Round435 Max Damage records (1,971 transitions) showed
  `extract_player_transitions` at about 0.65 s under `cProfile`, with public
  mechanics encoding accounting for roughly 0.37 s cumulative. Scalar
  `numpy.clip` was called repeatedly for each Pokémon row.
- Replacing that scalar clip with Python `min`/`max` bounds preserved every
  public-context feature exactly and reduced median transition-extraction time
  from 0.3589 s to 0.2781 s over six measured runs after warm-up (22.5%).
- Linear extrapolation to Round435's 162,366 trainable transitions estimates
  6.66 seconds saved in transition extraction. Combined with the separate
  static-tensor reuse microbenchmark, the estimated gain is about 10.4 seconds
  or 6.9% of the 151.5-second collection stage; validate with a full PPO run.
- Reproduction script and report:
  `scripts/benchmark_public_mechanics_scalar_clip.py` and
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round440_public_mechanics_clip_profile_20261030/benchmark.json`.

### Live policy static-team token cache (Round448, 2026-10-30)

- The live `PolicyAgent` did not pass the existing static-team tensor cache to
  `build_model_inputs`, so species/move/item/ability tokens were rebuilt on
  every decision. Added a per-agent cache and wired it into both independent
  and same-model paired inference. Cache keys include the visible own and
  opponent team signatures, so updated or different rosters cannot reuse stale
  tensors; the cache is scoped to a match's agent.
- On 1,971 Round435 transitions from 256 audited match records, model-input
  construction fell from a 0.4680 s median to 0.3424 s (26.8%). Every input
  tensor was exactly equal. Linear extrapolation gives 10.34 s saved across
  162,366 transitions, but this does not measure whole-match speed.
- A live deterministic action check using Round447's checkpoint returned the
  same action `[24, 45]`, log probability, and value with caching enabled and
  disabled. The checkpoint and policy were unchanged.
- Remaining limitation: measure games/sec and p95 decision latency in paired
  full rollouts before claiming a user-visible throughput gain. Cross-match
  shared inference batching remains the larger policy-inference opportunity.
- Benchmark: `scripts/benchmark_live_team_feature_cache.py` and
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round448_live_team_feature_cache_20261030/benchmark.json`.

### Queue-aware shared inference prototype (Round449, 2026-10-30)

- Compared independent CPU inference processes with a single queue-batched GPU
  worker using 256 real closed-sheet rollout inputs, 8 or 16 concurrent
  producers, and 64 requests per producer. The shared queue includes input
  collation, host-to-device transfer, model execution, output synchronization,
  and queue wait; model inputs were already prepared in memory.
- At an 8-worker concurrency, independent CPU processes reached 2,850
  states/sec (p95 request 3.25 ms). The shared GPU queue reached 1,606
  states/sec (p95 5.29 ms) with a 1 ms max wait and 1,088 states/sec (p95
  7.82 ms) with a 3 ms wait. At 16 workers, CPU reached 3,530 states/sec
  (p95 5.72 ms); GPU reached 2,912 (p95 6.27 ms) at 1 ms and 2,089 (p95
  8.09 ms) at 3 ms.
- The GPU service batched mostly 8 or 16 requests, but its end-to-end queue
  overhead erased the isolated large-batch forward advantage. The probe
  excludes IPC serialization and live feature preparation, so it is an upper
  bound for a production service. Do not add the shared GPU broker at the
  current 8/16 worker range; revisit only if a real rollout can sustain larger
  batches and memory permits more concurrent matches.
- The active speed priorities remain CPU-side per-worker inference and
  observation/action feature preparation. The static team-token cache from
  Round448 is live, but its whole-match effect still needs measurement.
- Benchmark: `scripts/benchmark_shared_inference_queue.py` and
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round449_shared_inference_queue_20261030/benchmark.json`.

### CPU inference follow-ups (Rounds450–451, 2026-10-30)

- Dynamic int8 quantization of eligible feed-forward Linear layers (excluding
  Transformer attention internals) was tested on 256 real closed-sheet states
  from Round435 with the Round447 checkpoint. Full native action selection
  slowed from 2.295 ms to 2.511 ms median (0.91x); 5/256 actions differed
  (1.95%). Reject this quantized path for now. Report:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round450_cpu_dynamic_quantization_20261030/benchmark.json`.
- CPU `torch.compile(mode="reduce-overhead")` was tested on the same 256
  states. Full native action selection improved from 2.219 ms to 1.510 ms
  median (1.47x), p95 from 2.691 ms to 2.054 ms, with zero action
  disagreements and log-probability/value deltas below 4e-7/1.2e-7. Compile
  plus warmup took 4.92 s. This is a promising per-decision optimization, but
  remains a microbenchmark: do not enable it by default until an eight-worker
  complete-match comparison reports throughput, p95 decision latency,
  compilation overhead, and outcomes. Report:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round451_cpu_compiled_policy_20261030/benchmark.json`.
- Current end-to-end reference remains 16.49 training-iteration games/s
  (Round430, including rollout plus PPO preparation/optimization); Round424's
  measured rollout portion was 22.86 aggregate games/s. Round435 has newer
  per-opponent shard profiles but no valid aggregate rate. Do not substitute
  state-inference throughput or per-worker rates for complete-game speed.
- Updated near-term priority: benchmark optional compiled CPU inference in
  matched full rollouts. Keep the shared GPU queue, int8 quantization, and
  `torch.compile` rejected at current workloads: the 64-match, eight-worker
  Round452 comparison measured 13.15 games/s eager vs 4.30 compiled, and
  telemetry showed policy inference at 65.8 vs 944.6 ms/match. Compiled run
  peak RSS was 11.67 GiB vs 6.60 GiB eager. The 1.47x single-state
  microbenchmark did not predict multiworker rollout behavior; compile/cache
  overhead and/or repeated compilation dominates. Exact action parity in the
  256-state probe is not enough to justify this path. Round452 used the same
  policy checkpoint, seed, episode offsets, eight workers, and Max Damage
  opponent; speed only, not a strength comparison. Keep the optional switch
  for reproducibility and further profiling, but do not enable it in training.
  Next measure the Round448 static-feature cache in matched full rollouts and
  profile per-worker compile time/graph breaks only if this path is revisited.
  PPO data parsing/preparation (169.1 s in Round447) remains a major
  training-iteration cost after rollout.
- Round452 reports:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round452_compiled_full_match_20261030/`.

### PPO field-feature preparation (Round453, 2026-10-30)

- Profiling 512 audited Round435 player views (3,892 transitions) separated
  strict JSON/perspective validation, transition extraction, GAE, and model
  input construction. Under `cProfile`, preparation input construction was
  the largest measured substage in that slice; `_extract_field_features`
  performed four per-slot tensor scalar reads for active volatile features.
- Added a CPU float32 NumPy path that gathers those four active volatile rows
  together. Other device/dtype/autograd callers retain the tensor path. The
  Round453 benchmark used 1,026 real states and seven repetitions after
  warm-up: full `build_model_inputs` median fell from 114.73 ms to 106.61 ms
  (7.07%) with exact field-feature and full input-tensor parity. Empty, short,
  full-length, and NaN-active-row feature cases also matched the prior logic.
- Linear extrapolation to Round447's 162,366 transitions estimates 1.28 s
  saved, about 0.76% of its 169.12 s sample-preparation time. This is a
  microbenchmark estimate, not a complete-game throughput result. Reproduce
  the isolated probe with `scripts/benchmark_field_feature_encoding.py`; report:
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round453_numpy_field_feature_encoding_20261030/benchmark.json`.
- Replayed the exact Round447 PPO configuration on the same audited data.
  Sample preparation took 163.07 s vs 169.12 s (6.05 s / 3.58% lower); tensor
  aggregation was effectively unchanged. Losses, KL, all 1,272 optimizer-step
  metrics, transition counts, and all 82 final checkpoint tensors matched
  Round447 exactly. The complete update wall time was 228.64 s vs about 232 s
  in Round447, but remains slower than Round437's 217.98 s. One replay cannot
  separate code savings from run-to-run timing variation or attribute the full
  difference to the NumPy encoder; repeat before claiming a reliable
