### PPO sample-preparation stage profile (Round458, 2026-10-30)

- Instrumented the real PPO collection loop for the exact 20,000-game,
  Round447-matched audited dataset. Sample preparation took 162.08 s for
  28,000 valid records and 162,366 transitions; full PPO replay wall time was
  227.17 s. Loading/parse/validation took 78.51 s (48.4%), transition
  extraction 36.22 s (22.3%), model-input construction 24.97 s (15.4%), GAE
  4.71 s (2.9%), sample packaging 8.57 s (5.3%), record metadata/cache keys
  0.35 s (0.2%), with 8.74 s (5.4%) not attributed by the stage timers.
- All 28 numeric training metrics and all 82 checkpoint tensors were
  bit-identical to Round447. Instrumentation thus exposes the timing split
  without altering the PPO result. The replay is PPO-only; complete
  rollout-plus-update throughput remains the last measured 16.49 games/s from
  Round430.
- **Current bottleneck:** row loading, JSON parsing, and strict validation are
  the largest measured stage, followed by per-transition extraction and input
  construction. This exact-loop profile supersedes extrapolations from isolated
  reader probes. The standalone full-reader took 26.89 s, illustrating that
  it did not reproduce the real loop's 78.51 s; investigate storage/cache
  contention, Python object lifetime/GC, and repeated per-record overhead
  before assuming a parser-only fix.
- **Next speed-up opportunities:** (1) profile one representative full chunk
  at function level inside the loader/validator to separate seek/read, JSON
  decoding, validation, and allocation/GC; (2) reduce validated row material
  retained simultaneously, or stream compact transition arrays so decoded
  dictionaries are released promptly; (3) batch transition extraction and
  model-input construction over contiguous arrays, keeping the current
  perspective/integrity checks and parity gates; (4) evaluate safe parallel
  prefetch/decode only after measuring CPU, storage, memory bandwidth, and peak
  RSS, since parallel readers may contend with the GPU optimizer; (5) measure
  aggregation and PPO optimization separately before spending effort there.
  Re-run the same matched update and check exact sample signatures, all metrics,
  checkpoint tensors, peak memory, and full wall time after each change.
- Profile: `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round458_instrumented_full_ppo_20261030/profile.json`.

### Cyclic-GC speed experiments (Rounds459–461, 2026-10-30)

- A reader-only repeat with cyclic GC enabled took 26.84 s on the 20,000 exact
  audited records; disabling GC reduced that isolated scan to 15.54 s (42.1%),
  with identical counts. The 1,024-row-chunk experiment (Round459) disabled GC
  only while loading each chunk, then re-enabled it during extraction. It
  shifted collection work into later phases: total preparation rose to 171.74
  s from Round458's 162.08 s, so this scope is rejected.
- Round460 disabled GC only around the full PPO update and restored its prior
  enabled/disabled state in a `finally` block. On the same audited records,
  seed, initialization, and optimizer budget, sample preparation fell to 87.25
  s and complete PPO-only update wall time was 152.46 s, vs 162.08 s and
  227.17 s in Round458. That is a 46.2% sample-preparation reduction and
  32.9% full-update reduction. All 28 numeric training metrics and 82 model
  tensors matched exactly; `/usr/bin/time -v` measured peak RSS at 7.32 GiB.
- Round461 repeated the same full-update experiment. Sample preparation was
  85.45 s, full update wall time 150.66 s, and peak RSS 7.32 GiB. It also
  matched all 28 numeric metrics and all 82 tensors exactly. Across Rounds460
  and 461 the mean update was 151.56 s (range 150.66–152.46 s) vs Round458's
  227.17 s; mean preparation was 86.35 s (range 85.45–87.25 s) vs 162.08 s.
  Based on these repeatable results, the CLI now disables cyclic GC during PPO
  updates by default, restores the prior GC state in `finally`, and provides
  `--enable-gc-during-ppo-update` as an opt-out. Measure a full rollout-plus-PPO
  iteration next; do not replace the 16.49 complete-iteration games/s benchmark
  with update-only rate.
- The Round460 preparation bottleneck shifted to transition extraction (27.26
  s), model-input construction (20.46 s), and row load/parse/validation (20.24
  s); optimizer time remains about 51 s. Subsequent tuning should prioritize
  extraction and input-array construction, then measure the end-to-end
  training iteration after validating the GC mode's memory behavior.
- Reports: `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round460_gc_disabled_update_20261030/profile.json` and `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round461_gc_disabled_repeat_20261030/profile.json`.

  51.76%]. Random remains an easy-baseline check, not a strength signal. The
  Max Damage interval is below 50%; all policy-opponent intervals include 50%.

  did not demonstrate robust improvement and loses to Max Damage on this
  screen. Keep Round430 as the validated candidate, not as an optimal-play

  causal comparison.

### Decision flow: win probability is not currently an action selector

- The Round465 PPO network emits policy action logits and a separate scalar
  win-probability prediction. Training uses the probability output as an
  auxiliary loss (weight 0.1); it does not evaluate candidate actions or rank
  them by estimated win chance. The default local runner calls the direct
  policy and leaves search disabled.
- A state-value estimate cannot by itself distinguish two actions from the
  same state. To use win odds for action choice, simulate each candidate joint
  action pair across legal opposing responses and chance outcomes, evaluate
  the resulting player-view states, then select a robust or equilibrium action
  from that payoff matrix. Existing search does this with a separate learned
  value model, but earlier tests found large strength losses, so it remains
  disabled and must pass equal-budget paired evaluation before becoming part
  of default play.
- Current implication: lower auxiliary win-probability loss is not evidence of
  better move choice. Report prediction calibration and action-selection
  strength separately. The Round465 action counterfactuals above are complete
  game outcome diagnostics; they did not feed the probability head into move
  selection or alter a checkpoint.

### Round466 PPO update and held-out screen (2026-10-30)

- Resumed from Round430 for 20,000 matches: 6,000 vs Max Damage (half with
  teacher labels on P1 decisions 1 and 4), 6,000 vs public Counterplay, and
  8,000 against Round430/Round464/Round465 in equal policy-pool proportions.
  PPO used terminal outcomes, 4 epochs, minibatch 512, learning rate 5e-5,
  and the existing win-probability and hidden-set auxiliary losses. Teacher
  actions were excluded from PPO loss and weighted 0.1 as teacher targets.
- The first audit falsely rejected all 11,999 mirrored rule-based opponent
  records because they have no PPO behavior log probabilities. Fixed the audit
  and recovery validation to require those logs only on the trainable
  perspective. Replayed the one identical-team match with a disjoint rollout
  seed while retaining its record ID. Strict audit then passed: 40,000 safe
  player-view rows, 20,000 complete games, opponent mix 6k/6k/8k, and 162,363
  trainable transitions.
- PPO completed 1,272 optimizer steps (4 passes), approximate KL 0.00943,
  win-probability loss 0.4753. GPU optimization used the RTX 4060 Laptop GPU
  at about 84% utilization and 1.3 GB of 8 GB VRAM. Sample preparation took
  about 90 seconds; the optimizer took about 53 seconds. Episode-weighted
  per-worker rollout rates were 7.43 games/s for Max Damage, 5.41 for the
  policy pool, and 4.86 for public Counterplay. Mean action selection was
  48/78/120 ms respectively; observation encoding 25–26 ms, engine roundtrip
  29–33 ms, and trajectory persistence 9–13 ms. The slowest run shard took
  about 509 seconds. The earlier preflight failure prevented retaining an
  exact aggregate rollout wall-time metric, so report per-shard rates only.
- Fresh held-out screen: 128 team-pair clusters, two side-swapped outcomes
  per cluster (512 games per opponent), deterministic policies, no timeouts or
  action adjustments. Scores and 95% cluster-bootstrap intervals: Max Damage
  40.82% [33.79, 47.85], Public Counterplay 37.70% [30.66, 44.73], Round464
  57.23% [50.00, 64.45], Round465 51.17% [43.95, 58.40]. On identical
  Max Damage and Counterplay teams/seeds, Round466 vs Round430 deltas were
  +0.59 pp [-1.95, +3.32] and 0.00 pp [-2.73, +2.93], respectively. Neither
  provides evidence of a hard-opponent improvement. Keep Round430 as the
  validated strength incumbent; Round466 is a completed challenger only.

### Round467 opening-intervention transfer check (2026-10-30)

  10,000-resample paired team-cluster bootstrap. Each arm completed 512 games
  with zero action adjustments, timeouts, or errors.

  +6.84 percentage points, 95% cluster interval [0.00, +13.67]. This is
  suggestive but inconclusive at the 95% level.

  gain +12.30 points, 95% interval [+4.69, +19.73]. This is positive transfer
  evidence on this held-out set, though it is still one 128-cluster screen.

  evaluation throughput was 9.50 / 9.95 games/s (raw/hybrid) vs Max Damage and
  8.54 / 7.38 games/s vs Counterplay; the hybrid costs extra per decision
  because the Max Damage scorer runs for the opening. This is inference speed,
  not training rollout throughput.
- This confirms that the opening intervention transfers from Round430 to the
  Round467 checkpoint against these two opponents, but does not make it the
  trained policy or prove robustness to the wider population. Keep the raw
  Round467 action policy as the training checkpoint; next gather an independent

  intervention belongs in the default selector. The win-probability head is

  legacy Counterplay -0.39 pp ([-1.86,+1.03]), Public Counterplay +0.29 pp
  ([-1.03,+1.61]). This reweighting did not improve the lower tail.

  -0.63 pp ([-1.95,+0.73]), Public Counterplay +0.88 pp ([-0.20,+1.95]). All

  checkpoint population, not a Nash equilibrium of the full VGC game. Keep

### Round476 action-pattern audit (complete; descriptive only; 2026-10-31)

- Corrected the rollout analyzer to use only the 16 preflight-approved compressed
  shards and terminal-outcome labels. This excludes duplicate compressed/plain
  views, rejected records, and recovery attempts. The audit covers exactly
  20,000 completed training games, 5,000 per opponent class.
- The policy chose masked PPO action logits in battle. The predicted win
  probability remains an auxiliary training target, not an action-ranking
  score. The optional opening-search experiment may use a win-probability head
  at frontier leaves; that behavior does not apply to the default checkpoint.
- Descriptive first-action counts by eventual outcome are available in
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round476_refreshed_population_ppo_20k_20261031/action_patterns.json`.
  The action-type fractions vary between wins and losses, but terminal-state
  stratification cannot tell whether an action caused the result.
- A separate first-turn audit of the 5,000 Max Damage games with native action
  features found that the selected action's estimated damage averaged 0.227 in
  wins versus 0.211 in losses (feature scale 0–1); the best legal damage
  estimate averaged 0.344 versus 0.334. The selected move tied the best legal
  damage estimate in 34.7% of winning action slots and 32.4% of losing slots.
  These are approximate damage features, not game-state win odds or causal
  action values; they do not identify a tactical failure or justify changing
  training weights.
- Conclusion: action frequencies and approximate single-move damage rankings
  are insufficient to diagnose the plateau. Before another same-recipe PPO
  run, build a counterfactual audit on sampled decision states that compares
  complete legal joint actions under controlled outcome sampling (or an
  evaluated teacher), with matched random seeds and cluster-level uncertainty.
  Separate policy quality from team-preview selection and report where the
  current action's estimated return ranks among alternatives. Change the
  learning objective only if this audit finds a repeatable failure mode.
- Analyzer: `scripts/analyze_round476_action_patterns.py`.

### Round477: fresh multi-opponent audit of Round430's first-five Max Damage override (2026-10-31)

- Re-tested the same Round430 checkpoint with and without Max Damage actions at
  decision indices 0–4. Every arm used the Round402 selector, fresh opponent-
  specific team-seed ranges, 256 team-pair clusters, two side-swapped outcomes,
  and the override only on the evaluated Round430 player. Paired cluster

  were included: Max Damage, legacy Counterplay, Public Counterplay, historical

  [3.66,7.84] by stratified cluster bootstrap. The worst-opponent point change

  Counterplay interval rules out zero in the negative direction. Retain raw

  4.60/7.18; Round476 3.08/4.45. Evaluation throughput is opponent- and

### Round479: higher-repeat robust counterfactual follow-up (2026-10-31; not promoted)

- To test whether Round478's sparse/noisy labels caused the no-op update,
  repeated the same fixed action objective with 256 team-disjoint early-game
  states and eight chance outcomes per candidate. The response classes remained
  Max Damage, Public Counterplay, and Round476 PPO; the learner received only
  its own full team and the opponent's preview species.
- Collection completed 38,672 matches in 1,288.62 seconds (30.01 games/s
  aggregate across four CPU workers; shard rates 8.12–9.06). All 256 states
  were captured with no missing states and no rejected candidate actions. It
  averaged 6.21 candidate joint actions per state. The side-by-side speed
  figure is counterfactual branch throughput, not regular self-play throughput.
- With four of eight chance outcomes used to form targets and four held out,
  only 23/256 states had a non-incumbent candidate with positive worst-response
  advantage; incumbent target mass averaged 91.67%. The actor update stopped
  after four epochs: validation loss was best at epoch 1 (0.7996) and worsened
  thereafter. It still selected the incumbent action on all 51 held-out
  candidate sets; across all 256 states, only one candidate-set argmax changed
  and target-action probability rose by only 0.54 percentage points on average.
- This confirms that merely adding more samples to this sparse positive-minimum
  distillation target is not enough. Round479 is not promoted and was not sent
  through the full-match league because its held-out actor chose the baseline
  action in all tested candidate sets and validation worsened. Next, change the
  learning target: estimate response-conditioned state values / action payoffs
  and optimize a mixed or equilibrium-oriented objective, instead of extending
  this same conservative supervised target.
- Reproduction: `scripts/collect_round479_robust_counterfactuals.sh` and
  `scripts/train_round479_robust_counterfactual_policy.sh`. Outputs are under
  `training/outputs/phase12_headless/` with `round479_` prefixes.

  bootstrap CI [-0.78,+6.05]). Seat-specific changes were +3.13 pp and +1.95
  pp. The interval includes zero and this is one opponent only, so the result
  is promising but inconclusive; do not promote search or infer general
  strength from it.
- The search returned a matrix choice in 499/512 search-side matches; 13 cases
  safely fell back to policy after encountering unsupported possible-Illusion
  previews (10) or publicly observed Transform states (3). Aggregate
  evaluation throughput was 1,024 matches / 230.11 s = 4.45 matches/s. Search
  adapter latency median/p95 was 248.8/337.8 ms; the inner Showdown advance
  median/p95 was 154.6/240.6 ms. Value inference median was 4.85 ms.
- Added a second-opponent confirmation with Public Counterplay and the same
  Round430 policy/search pair. Across 128 fresh paired clusters and both seats
  (512 complete matches), policy-only scored 43.36% and learned search 40.63%,
  a paired change of -2.73 pp (95% team-cluster bootstrap CI [-7.82,+2.34]).
  Seat-specific changes were +2.34 pp and -7.81 pp, showing the value of the
  overall paired estimate depends on seat balance. All 512 matches completed
  with zero action corrections. The search matrix was returned in 253/256
  search-side matches; 3 cases safely fell back on possible-Illusion or
  publicly observed Transform states. Throughput was 3.42 complete matches/s;
  adapter latency median/p95 was 245.7/332.0 ms.
- The two-opponent picture is mixed: +2.54 pp vs Max Damage and -2.73 pp vs
  Public Counterplay, with both cluster intervals including zero. Search is not
  robustly improved by the Round480 evaluator and remains disabled by default.
  The launcher supports both opponent classes through `OPPONENT_STRATEGY`.
- Tested whether the Public Counterplay result was caused by a one-sample
  chance budget. Repeated the same 128 paired clusters with four independent
  outcome samples per candidate joint action. Policy-only again scored 43.36%;
  search scored 40.23%, a paired change of -3.13 pp (95% team-cluster bootstrap
  CI [-8.20,+1.95]). Only 31/256 searched decisions changed their selected
  joint action versus the one-sample run. All 512 matches completed with zero
  action corrections; the same 3 Illusion/Transform cases safely fell back.
- Four samples raised median/p95 search latency from 245.7/332.0 ms to
  782.4/1,106.8 ms and cut evaluation throughput from 3.42 to 1.80 matches/s.
  It did not improve the paired result. Keep one-sample search only for
  inexpensive experiments; additional sampling is not a promotion path by
  itself.
- Decision flow: the deployed/default PPO selects legal moves from masked
  policy logits. Its auxiliary win-probability head does not rank moves. A
  separate learned state-value model can influence a move only when optional
  search is explicitly enabled; it scores simulated successor states inside a
  payoff matrix. Search remains off by default because its results are mixed
  across Max Damage and Public Counterplay; it must pass a broader opponent
  league before default use.

### Round494: public-information boundary audit for counterfactual training (2026-10-31)

- Audited `scripts/collect_midgame_action_counterfactuals.py` and the existing
  public-compatible search-world path. The collector captures a real battle
  snapshot, then replays candidate actions from that same snapshot. Its policy
  features are player-view observations, but the simulated outcome labels are
  conditioned on the actual hidden opponent sets in that battle. This is
  legitimate for ordinary on-policy outcome data, but it does not train an
  action evaluator against a distribution of plausible hidden sets for each
  public state.
- The midgame search path is safer for that purpose: it calls
  `ClosedSheetBeliefTracker` using observed battle events, samples sets from
  public preview species plus revealed facts, and asks
  `buildSanitizedSearchWorlds` to align public facts into reconstructed worlds.
  The sampler uses the local Showdown random-champions set builder and legal
  team validation. It is a particular prior, not a complete model of all
  plausible legal tournament sets; policy-value gains against it alone would
  not establish robustness.
- This audit explains a key source of apparent transfer failure: training
  counterfactual rankings on actual hidden sets can reward choices that fit
  those sampled opponents while evaluation changes the team/set distribution.
  Max Damage remains a useful regression opponent, but its win rate is not a
  sufficient measure of general strength. The Round485 70%-Max-Damage training
  exposure change did not measurably improve either that matchup or the broader
  league.
- Next experiment gate: make action outcomes aggregate over multiple
  independently sampled, public-compatible hidden worlds per public state,
  with paired chance seeds across candidate actions. Keep each world’s private
  sets out of model inputs. Include more than one legal set prior or report the
  random-champions prior explicitly; compare the learned selector with the
  incumbent on fresh teams, held-out public-compatible worlds, and the full
  opponent league before promotion. Track wall-clock branches/s and end-to-end
  matches/s because world preparation and replay may become the new bottleneck.

### Round496: repair sampled-world parser move cache (2026-10-31; targeted replays pass)

- Reproduced all five Round495 empty-mask branches from the original seeds and
  checkpoints. In a resumed sampled world, Showdown's private request for P2
  correctly described the sampled set, but the reused poke-env `Pokemon` object
  retained the source match's move cache. When every move in the request was
  absent from that stale cache, the native action mask was empty even though
  Showdown had valid move orders.
- Updated `HeadlessShowdownProcess` to optionally rebuild a selected side's
  active move cache from each of its own current requests during branch replay.
  The option is enabled only for P2 in public-world counterfactual branches;
  it uses that side's private request and is not exposed to P1 policy inputs.
  Refreshing each request is needed because a sampled bench Pokemon can enter
  after the branch's initial state. Private move IDs are deliberately excluded
  from saved diagnostics; records retain only the player side, active slot, and
  legal-action counts.
- Replayed the five formerly failing cases (step/cluster 3/9, 3/17, 3/18,
  5/13, and 5/18) with their original team generation seeds, checkpoints,
  worlds, response classes, and chance repeats. All five states were captured;
  their replay counts were 362, 322, 362, 362, and 162 respectively, with no
  invalid resumed branch and no rejected candidate action. These targeted
  replays show the specific parser mismatch is repaired; they do not replace a
  fresh full collection or establish policy strength.
- Speed: the last full Round495 collection measured 38.412 branch matches/s
  across eight workers (12,374 branches; 20.609 s total hidden-world prep).
  Targeted replay rates are not directly comparable because each run uses one
  cluster and different match lengths. Re-measure aggregate throughput on the
  next full batch after this fix; branch simulation remains the measured
  bottleneck, while public-world preparation was about 6% of measured branch
  time.
- Next: implement a second public-compatible legal-set prior, then collect at
  least 128 usable held-out states across decision steps and both priors. Fit
  action values without mixing correlated worlds across train/test, evaluate
  on fresh team clusters, and require a broad full-match opponent league before

  14 actions and improved the empirical worst-response rate by 2.78 pp, but
  its 95% team-cluster interval was [-2.78,+9.72] pp. Equal-weight selection's
  worst-response delta was 0.00 pp [-5.56,+6.94]. Per-response test Brier was
  worse than the constant-rate baseline for the Round476 policy head and
  nearly tied for most others. This is a small, noisy feasibility fit, not
  evidence of better play; no checkpoint is promoted. Fit report and weights
  are under `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round497_showdown_prior_action_value_fit_20261031/`.
- Opponent-diversity limit: although these counterfactual labels cover five
  response classes, only one is a learned PPO policy (Round476); the other four
  are heuristic policies. This is broader than a Max Damage-only target, but
  it can still overfit to Round476 as the sole learned response. Before using
  action values to update or promote the battle policy, add separate heads for
  the Round430 incumbent and an older held-out PPO generation (Round102), keep
  one generation out of fit when possible, and require full-match screens
  against all of them plus public/legacy Counterplay and random. Do not treat
  more response labels as proof of Nash or optimal play.
- Uniform-prior retry: the initial step-1 shard failed when publicly revealed
  moves/items/abilities had no compatible variant in the 20k-team corpus. The
  collector now records this as `hidden_set_prior_support_gap` and skips the
  affected state; it does not silently fall back to the Showdown prior. A
  replay of the exact six-cluster shard captured two usable states, recorded
  two support gaps and two forced switches, and rejected zero actions. The
  retry uses a separate output root ending in `_retry1`, preserving the failed
  partial artifacts for diagnosis.
- Under the uniform full-set prior, decision step 1 captured 30/48 states,
  prepared 120 worlds, and executed 10,758 branches in 302.11 seconds (35.61
  matches/s). Eighteen states were skipped: 14 forced switches and four prior
  support gaps. Step 3 captured 20/48 states, prepared 80 worlds, and executed
  7,268 branches in 184.08 seconds (39.48 matches/s). Twenty-eight states
  were skipped: 21 forced switches, five prior support gaps, one unreached
  decision, and one possible-Illusion preview. No candidate actions were
  rejected. The step-5 phase is still running.
- Uniform-prior decision step 5 has completed: 26/48 states, 104 worlds, and
  7,994 branches in 102.07 seconds (78.318 matches/s); world preparation took
  11.77 seconds and zero candidates were rejected. The 22 skipped states were
  ten forced switches, seven unreached decisions, and five support gaps. The
  full uniform-prior corpus has 76/144 usable states, 304 worlds, and 26,020
  branches in 588.26 seconds (44.23 aggregate matches/s); 68 states were
  skipped, including 14 support gaps (9.7% of requests). Across both priors,
  there are 166/288 usable states, 664 worlds, and 56,454 branches in 1,222.56
  seconds (46.18 aggregate matches/s), with zero rejected candidate actions.
- The uniform-prior feasibility fit used 49/12/15 train/validation/test
  clusters, stopped at epoch 8, and had pooled validation Brier 0.1856. On its
  15 test clusters, maximin selection was -3.33 pp vs the incumbent action
  [-8.33,0.00]; equal-weight was also -3.33 pp [-8.33,0.00]. These are too
  small to establish a regression, but they provide no support for promotion.
- Cross-prior replay evaluated each fitted selector on the other prior's
  outcomes for the same public team clusters. The Showdown-trained model was
  -3.95 pp maximin [-9.21,+0.82] on uniform-prior outcomes and -2.47 pp
  equal-weight [-6.25,+0.82]. The uniform-trained model was +1.81 pp maximin
  [-1.11,+4.86] and +2.08 pp equal-weight [-0.97,+5.14] on Showdown-prior
  outcomes. Every interval includes zero. Because the public states and team
  clusters are shared across priors, this is a prior-sensitivity diagnostic,
  not independent generalization or full-match strength evidence. Neither
  action-value model is promoted.
- Promotion remains gated on a fresh, side-swapped full-match league across
  varied opponents and held-out teams. Report per-opponent win rates and
  confidence intervals, mean and lower-tail performance, invalid actions, and
  latency. A Max Damage-only gain cannot promote a checkpoint; regressions
  against the incumbent or broad-policy opponents block promotion even if the
  Max Damage result improves.

### Round498: learned-opponent response diversity (complete; no promotion)

- Round497 varied hidden-set priors and included five response classes, but
  only one was a learned PPO policy (Round476). The preliminary PPO-head Brier
  and cross-prior selector results provide no reliable strength gain. The next
  action-value data batch adds separate Round430 incumbent and Round102
  historical PPO response heads; Round476 remains as the newer population
  response, alongside Max Damage, Public Counterplay, random, and legacy
  Counterplay.
- A three-state pipeline pilot captured three usable states, prepared six
  worlds, executed 847 branches in 72.12 seconds (11.74 matches/s on one
  worker), and rejected zero actions. The saved rows contain all seven named
  response heads. This confirms the extra policy checkpoints run through the
  branch collector; it is not policy-strength evidence.
- Full collection is running from `scripts/collect_round498_policy_ensemble_counterfactuals.sh`:
  48 clusters at decision steps 1/3/5 under both Round497 hidden-set priors,
  four worlds per state, two chance repeats, and eight CPU workers. The same
  seeds are used under both priors. Reports must group by team cluster, include
  support-gap/skipped-state counts, and compare all three PPO generations
  separately. Keep Round430 as the active policy; do not use action-value
  selector results to promote without held-out full-match confirmation against
  the broad opponent league.
- The first Round498 phase (decision step 1, Showdown prior) completed with
  24/48 usable states, 96 worlds, and 11,888 branches in 264.11 seconds
  (45.012 matches/s across eight workers). Twenty-four states were skipped:
  23 forced switches and one public Transform state. No candidate action was
  rejected. This is the first throughput measurement with seven response
  classes; compare later phases by response count and decision step before
  interpreting rate changes.
- Decision step 3 under the Showdown prior completed with 34/48 usable states,
  136 worlds, and 16,266 branches in 328.12 seconds (49.573 matches/s). The 14
  skipped states were 11 forced switches, two possible-Illusion previews, and
  one unreached decision; no candidate actions were rejected. Across the first
  two phases, 58/96 states were usable and 28,154 branches ran in 592.23
  seconds (47.54 aggregate matches/s).
- Decision step 5 under the Showdown prior completed with 36/48 usable states,
  144 worlds, and 14,812 branches in 226.11 seconds (65.509 matches/s). Twelve
  states were skipped (five forced switches, seven unreached decisions); no
  actions were rejected. The full Showdown-prior batch captured 94/144 states
  and ran 42,966 branches in 818.34 seconds (52.504 aggregate matches/s), with
  376 worlds and no rejected actions.
- The seven-response model fit on those 94 states used 60/15/19 train,
  validation, and test clusters, stopped at epoch 1, and had validation Brier
  0.2190. On 19 test clusters, maximin's paired worst-response delta was 0.00
  pp [-6.58,+7.89]; equal-weight was -1.32 pp [-7.89,+6.58]. It changed
  actions in 16 states without showing a strength gain. Held-out response Brier
  beat a constant-rate baseline for all seven heads, but this better prediction
  did not improve action selection. Do not promote from this fit.
- Round498's first uniform-prior phase (decision step 1) completed with 21/48
  usable states, 84 worlds, and 10,709 branches in 248.09 seconds (43.165
  matches/s). Twenty-seven states were skipped: 23 forced switches, three
  full-set-prior support gaps, and one public Transform state. No actions were
  rejected; the remaining uniform-prior phases are running.
- Round498's uniform-prior decision step 3 completed with 30/48 usable states,
  120 worlds, and 14,414 branches in 260.11 seconds (55.415 matches/s). Its 18
  skipped states were 11 forced switches, four support gaps, two possible-
  Illusion previews, and one unreached decision. No actions were rejected.
  Across all five completed Round498 phases, 145/240 states were usable and
  68,089 branches ran in 1,326.54 seconds (51.33 aggregate matches/s); seven
  uniform-prior states so far were excluded for lack of a compatible corpus
  set. The final phase is still running.
- The final uniform-prior phase (decision step 5) completed with 32/48 usable
  states, 128 worlds, and 13,296 branches in 218.10 seconds (60.963 matches/s).
  The 16 skipped states were five forced switches, four support gaps, and
  seven unreached decisions. No actions were rejected. The full uniform-prior
  batch captured 83/144 states and ran 38,419 branches in 726.30 seconds
  (52.897 aggregate matches/s), with 332 worlds and 11 support gaps. Across
  both priors, Round498 captured 177/288 states, prepared 708 worlds, and ran
  81,385 branches in 1,544.64 seconds (52.689 aggregate matches/s); 111 states
  were excluded by documented request/eligibility/support causes, with zero
  rejected candidate actions.
- Fits were completed separately for the Showdown and uniform-set priors. The
  Showdown fit used 60/15/19 train/validation/test team clusters, stopped at
  epoch 1, and changed the incumbent action in 16 of 19 test states; its
  maximin delta was 0.00 pp [-6.58,+7.89]. The uniform fit used 53/13/17
  clusters, stopped at epoch 1, changed 16 of 17 actions, and measured +2.94 pp
  maximin [-5.88,+11.76]. Both intervals include zero; equal-weight selection
  showed no reliable gain. The small cluster counts prohibit a strength claim.
- To check whether separate prior-specific fits were hiding a robust selector,
  `scripts/merge_round498_hidden_prior_outcomes.py` aligned the 83 public
  states common to both priors and made 14 response heads: seven opponents
  under each prior. Eleven Showdown-prior states had no uniform-prior match;
  no uniform-only states remained. The combined fit used 53/13/17 clusters,
  stopped at epoch 1, and changed actions in 14 of 17 held-out states. Its
  worst-response delta was -1.47 pp [-5.88,+2.94], so the selector did not
  beat Round430. These intervals are cluster-bootstrap estimates from only 17
  held-out team clusters and are not a final match-level evaluation.
- This experiment confirms that Round497's single learned PPO response was a
  real coverage gap, which Round498 corrected with Round476, Round430, and
  Round102. Broadening the opponent set did not, by itself, improve action
  selection. Keep Round430 active; do not promote the action-value model.
  Next, increase held-out team coverage and evaluate any policy change in
  paired, side-swapped full matches across the whole opponent pool and both
  hidden-set priors. Max Damage remains one diagnostic opponent, not the
  optimization objective.

### Round499: expand held-out team coverage (Showdown prior complete)

- Round498's pooled-prior selector had only 17 held-out team clusters, so its
  confidence interval was too wide to establish a modest action-selection
  gain or loss. Round499 repeats the seven-response, two-prior collection at
  three times the requested team clusters: 144 per decision step (1/3/5) per
  prior, 864 requested states total. It keeps the incumbent Round430 as the
  candidate policy and uses Round476, Round430, Round102, Max Damage, Public
  Counterplay, random legal, and legacy Counterplay as separate responses.
- Each state uses four hidden worlds and two chance repeats, with eight CPU
  workers. Seeds are distinct from Round498 and aligned between priors. The
  output is written to `training/outputs/phase12_headless/round499_policy_ensemble_144x4x2_20261031`.
- Reproduction: `scripts/collect_round499_policy_ensemble_144x4x2.sh`.
  The Showdown-prior decision-step-1 phase completed with 81/144 usable states,
  324 worlds, and 41,777 branch matches in 1,052.34 seconds (39.699 matches/s
  across eight CPU workers). It skipped 61 forced-switch states and two public
  Transform states; no candidates were rejected. Decision step 3 under the
  same prior completed with 84/144 usable states, 336 hidden worlds, and 41,612
  branches in 634.29 seconds (65.604 matches/s across eight CPU workers). It
  skipped 57 forced-switch and three possible-Illusion states, with zero
  rejected actions. Decision step 5 completed with 93/144 states, 372 worlds,
  and 40,837 branches in 520.27 seconds (78.492 matches/s); 51 states were
  skipped and no actions were rejected. Across all three Showdown-prior phases,
  258/432 states were usable, 1,032 worlds were prepared, and 124,226 branches
  ran in 2,206.90 seconds (56.290 aggregate matches/s), with zero rejected
  candidates. Uniform-prior decision step 1 is running. Five of eight worker
  shards have reported 48 cluster attempts, 14 usable states, and 7,398
  branches. Two partial requests had no support under the full-set prior; these
  are preliminary counts, not the phase total. The complete two-prior dataset will be fit jointly
  across both priors and all 14 opponent/prior heads, then compared to Round430

  side-swapped full-match evaluation across opponents.
